items.articleBody:
“And it is so simple… You will instantly find how to live.”

One November night in the 1870s, legendary Russian writer Fyodor Dostoyevsky (November 11, 1821–February 9, 1881) discovered the meaning of life in a dream — or, at least, the protagonist in his final short story did. The piece, which first appeared in the altogether revelatory A Writer’s Diary (public library) under the title “The Dream of a Queer Fellow” and was later published separately as The Dream of a Ridiculous Man, explores themes similar to those in Dostoyevsky’s 1864 novel Notes from the Underground, considered the first true existential novel. True to Stephen King’s assertion that “good fiction is the truth inside the lie,” the story sheds light on Dostoyevsky’s personal spiritual and philosophical bents with extraordinary clarity — perhaps more so than any of his other published works. The contemplation at its heart falls somewhere between Tolstoy’s tussle with the meaning of life and Philip K. Dick’s hallucinatory exegesis.

Portrait of Fyodor Dostoyevsky by Vasily Perov, 1871

The story begins with the narrator wandering the streets of St. Petersburg on “a gloomy night, the gloomiest night you can conceive,” dwelling on how others have ridiculed him all his life and slipping into nihilism with the “terrible anguish” of believing that nothing matters. He peers into the glum sky, gazes at a lone little star, and contemplates suicide; two months earlier, despite his destitution, he had bought an “excellent revolver” with the same intention, but the gun had remained in his drawer since. Suddenly, as he is staring at the star, a little girl of about eight, wearing ragged clothes and clearly in distress, grabs him by the arm and inarticulately begs his help. But the protagonist, disenchanted with life, shoos her away and returns to the squalid room he shares with a drunken old captain, furnished with “a sofa covered in American cloth, a table with some books, two chairs and an easy-chair, old, incredibly old, but still an easy-chair.”

As he sinks into the easy-chair to think about ending his life, he finds himself haunted by the image of the little girl, leading him to question his nihilistic disposition. Dostoyevsky writes:

I knew for certain that I would shoot myself that night, but how long I would sit by the table — that I did not know. I should certainly have shot myself, but for that little girl.

You see: though it was all the same to me, I felt pain, for instance. If any one were to strike me, I should feel pain. Exactly the same in the moral sense: if anything very pitiful happened, I would feel pity, just as I did before everything in life became all the same to me. I had felt pity just before: surely, I would have helped a child without fail. Why did I not help the little girl, then? It was because of an idea that came into my mind then. When she was pulling at me and calling to me, suddenly a question arose before me, which I could not answer. The question was an idle one; but it made me angry. I was angry because of my conclusion, that if I had already made up my mind that I would put an end to myself to-night, then now more than ever before everything in the world should be all the same to me. Why was it that I felt it was not all the same to me, and pitied the little girl? I remember I pitied her very much: so much that I felt a pain that was even strange and incredible in my situation…

It seemed clear that if I was a man and not a cipher yet, and until I was changed into a cipher, then I was alive and therefore could suffer, be angry and feel shame for my actions. Very well. But if I were to kill myself, for instance, in two hours from now, what is the girl to me, and what have I to do with shame or with anything on earth? I am going to be a cipher, an absolute zero. Could my consciousness that I would soon absolutely cease to exist, and that therefore nothing would exist, have not the least influence on my feeling of pity for the girl or on my sense of shame for the vileness I had committed?

From the moral, he veers into the existential:

It became clear to me that life and the world, as it were, depended upon me. I might even say that the world had existed for me alone. I should shoot myself, and then there would be no world at all, for me at least. Not to mention that perhaps there will really be nothing for any one after me, and the whole world, as soon as my consciousness is extinguished, will also be extinguished like a phantom, as part of my consciousness only, and be utterly abolished, since perhaps all this world and all these men are myself alone.

Beholding “these new, thronging questions,” he plunges into a contemplation of what free will really means. In a passage that calls to mind John Cage’s famous aphorism on the meaning of life — “No why. Just here.” — and George Lucas’s assertion that “life is beyond reason,” Dostoyevsky suggests through his protagonist that what gives meaning to life is life itself:

One strange consideration suddenly presented itself to me. If I had previously lived on the moon or in Mars, and I had there been dishonored and disgraced so utterly that one can only imagine it sometimes in a dream or a nightmare, and if I afterwards found myself on earth and still preserved a consciousness of what I had done on the other planet, and if I knew besides that I would never by any chance return, then, if I were to look at the moon from the earth — would it be all the same to me or not? Would I feel any shame for my action or not? The questions were idle and useless, for the revolver was already lying before me, and I knew with all my being that this thing would happen for certain: but the questions excited me to rage. I could not die now, without having solved this first. In a word, that little girl saved me, for my questions made me postpone pulling the trigger.

Just as he ponders this, the protagonist slips into sleep in the easy-chair, but it’s a sleep that has the quality of wakeful dreaming. In one of many wonderful semi-asides, Dostoyevsky peers at the eternal question of why we have dreams:

Dreams are extraordinarily strange. One thing appears with terrifying clarity, with the details finely set like jewels, while you leap over another, as though you did not notice it at all — space and time, for instance. It seems that dreams are the work not of mind but of desire, not of the head but of the heart… In a dream things quite incomprehensible come to pass. For instance, my brother died five years ago. Sometimes I see him in a dream: he takes part in my affairs, and we are very excited, while I, all the time my dream goes on, know and remember perfectly that my brother is dead and buried. Why am I not surprised that he, though dead, is still near me and busied about me? Why does my mind allow all that?

In this strange state, the protagonist dreams that he takes his revolver and points it at his heart — not his head, where he had originally intended to shoot himself. After waiting a second or two, his dream-self pulls the trigger quickly. Then something remarkable happens:

I felt no pain, but it seemed to me that with the report, everything in me was convulsed, and everything suddenly extinguished. It was terribly black all about me. I became as though blind and numb, and I lay on my back on something hard. I could see nothing, neither could I make any sound. People were walking and making a noise about me: the captain’s bass voice, the landlady’s screams… Suddenly there was a break. I am being carried in a closed coffin. I feel the coffin swinging and I think about that, and suddenly for the first time the idea strikes me that I am dead, quite dead. I know it and do not doubt it; I cannot see nor move, yet at the same time I feel and think. But I am soon reconciled to that, and as usual in a dream I accept the reality without a question.

Now I am being buried in the earth. Every one leaves me and I am alone, quite alone. I do not stir… I lay there and — strange to say — I expected nothing, accepting without question that a dead man has nothing to expect. But it was damp. I do not know how long passed — an hour, a few days, or many days. Suddenly, on my left eye which was closed, a drop of water fell, which had leaked through the top of the grave. In a minute fell another, then a third, and so on, every minute. Suddenly, deep indignation kindled in my heart and suddenly in my heart I felt physical pain. ‘It’s my wound,’ I thought. ‘It’s where I shot myself. The bullet is there.’ And all the while the water dripped straight on to my closed eye. Suddenly, I cried out, not with a voice, for I was motionless, but with all my being, to the arbiter of all that was being done to me.

“Whosoever thou art, if thou art, and if there exists a purpose more intelligent than the things which are now taking place, let it be present here also. But if thou dost take vengeance upon me for my foolish suicide, then know, by the indecency and absurdity of further existence, that no torture whatever that may befall me, can ever be compared to the contempt which I will silently feel, even through millions of years of martyrdom.”

I cried out and was silent. Deep silence lasted a whole minute. One more drop even fell. But I knew and believed, infinitely and steadfastly, that in a moment everything would infallibly change. Suddenly, my grave opened. I do not know whether it had been uncovered and opened, but I was taken by some dark being unknown to me, and we found ourselves in space. Suddenly, I saw. It was deep night; never, never had such darkness been! We were borne through space and were already far from the earth. I asked nothing of him who led me. I was proud and waited. I assured myself that I was not afraid, and my heart melted with rapture at the thought that I was not afraid. I do not remember how long we rushed through space, and I cannot imagine it. It happened as always in a dream when you leap over space and time and the laws of life and mind, and you stop only there where your heart delights.

The 1845 depiction of a galaxy that inspired Van Gogh’s ‘The Starry Night,’ from Michael Benson’s Cosmigraphics: Picturing Space Through Time

Through the thick darkness, he sees a star — the same little star he had seen before shooing the girl away. As the dream continues, the protagonist describes a sort of transcendence akin to what is experienced during psychedelic drug trips or in deep meditation states:

Suddenly a familiar yet most overwhelming emotion shook me through. I saw our sun. I knew that it could not be our sun, which had begotten our earth, and that we were an infinite distance away, but somehow all through me I recognized that it was exactly the same sun as ours, its copy and double. A sweet and moving delight echoed rapturously through my soul. The dear power of light, of that same light which had given me birth, touched my heart and revived it, and I felt life, the old life, for the first time since my death.

He finds himself in another world, Earthlike in every respect, except “everything seemed to be bright with holiday, with a great and sacred triumph, finally achieved” — a world populated by “children of the sun,” happy people whose eyes “shone with a bright radiance” and whose faces “gleamed with wisdom, and with a certain consciousness, consummated in tranquility.” The protagonist exclaims:

Oh, instantly, at the first glimpse of their faces I understood everything, everything!

Conceding that “it was only a dream,” he nonetheless asserts that “the sensation of the love of those beautiful and innocent people” was very much real and something he carried into wakeful life on Earth. Awaking in his easy-chair at dawn, he exclaims anew with rekindled gratitude for life:

Oh, now — life, life! I lifted my hands and called upon the eternal truth, not called, but wept. Rapture, ineffable rapture exalted all my being. Yes, to live…

Dostoyevsky concludes with his protagonist’s reflection on the shared essence of life, our common conquest of happiness and kindness:

All are tending to one and the same goal, at least all aspire to the same goal, from the wise man to the lowest murderer, but only by different ways. It is an old truth, but there is this new in it: I cannot go far astray. I saw the truth. I saw and know that men could be beautiful and happy, without losing the capacity to live upon the earth. I will not, I cannot believe that evil is the normal condition of men… I saw the truth, I did not invent it with my mind. I saw, saw, and her living image filled my soul for ever. I saw her in such consummate perfection that I cannot possibly believe that she was not among men. How can I then go astray? … The living image of what I saw will be with me always, and will correct and guide me always. Oh, I am strong and fresh, I can go on, go on, even for a thousand years.

[…]

And it is so simple… The one thing is — love thy neighbor as thyself — that is the one thing. That is all, nothing else is needed. You will instantly find how to live.

A century later, Jack Kerouac would echo this in his own magnificent meditation on kindness and the “Golden Eternity.”

A Writer’s Diary is a beautiful read in its entirety. Complement it with Tolstoy on finding meaning in a meaningless world and Margaret Mead’s dreamed epiphany about why life is like blue jelly.

donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation. Your support makes all the difference.

items.articleBody:
Two years ago, I encountered the infamous 1892 image of two men with a hill of buffalo skulls at the Baltimore Museum of Art. It was covered by a small wall-mounted curtain designed by Yurok artist Stormi Turner, and it gave the image, still shocking after over a century of circulation, the depth of tragedy that it warranted. Part of the Preoccupied: Indigenizing the Museum exhibition, it was a way of acknowledging the care that such a crime demands, in the same way that human remains are shown in museums today, often with warnings, behind doors you must open, or under covers that you must actively remove to see. Turner’s intervention was a way to honor an animal that many Native American groups and communities lived in symbiotic relationship with for millennia. That image came back to me when I walked into Cannupa Hanska Luger’s newest exhibition, American Traditional, at Garth Greenan Gallery in Soho, where the artist sets aside the participatory, ceramics-heavy projects he’s best known for and arrives at something more declarative — a synthesis of wood, ink, and archive that is his strongest work yet.

In Mari Sandoz’s The Buffalo Hunters: The Story of the Hide Men, first published in 1954, she explains that North American bison, also called buffalo, were far more numerous than humans on the continent and there was “apparently no disease on all the continent that threatened the buffalo in any number.” That charmed existence for the largest land animal on Turtle Island was interrupted by the eventual arrival of European settlers, who with their horses, guns, and railroads made their slaughter into an industrial-scale activity. 
Luger's “Requiem” (2026)
Luger, who was born on the Standing Rock Reservation, places a black abstracted bison atop a blackened rendering of a 19th-century American wood dining table. An enrolled citizen of the Three Affiliated Tribes of the Fort Berthold Reservation, he has deep roots on the Great Plains, and he knows the history of destruction that tore the bison from the tribes of the region that was, as Sandoz put it, “almost the sole subsistence of the Plains Indian — his shelter, clothing, food and fuel.” The Cree scholar Tasha Hubbard goes further than Sandoz was able to. For Plains nations the buffalo were kin, part of the First Peoples rather than a separate species, and the campaign against them was, in her account, a genocide carried out by proxy and a “second major wave of trauma for Plains Indigenous peoples,” after epidemic disease. The army said as much. Hubbard quotes Colonel Richard Irving Dodge’s advice to hunters — “every buffalo dead is an Indian gone” — and General Philip H. Sheridan understood it before the historians did. In 1875, when the Texas legislature proposed a bill to protect the bison, buffalo hunter John R. Cook recorded Sheridan’s objection: “These men [the buffalo hunters] have done more to settle the vexed Indian question than the entire regular army has done in the last thirty years … Send them powder and lead if you will, but for the sake of a lasting peace let them kill, skin and sell until the buffalo are exterminated.”
Artist Cannupa Hanska Luger pointing at his work “Shoots Today, Kills Tomorrow” (2026)

items.articleBody:
OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts.

The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale.

Easier to beg for forgiveness than ask permission

In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site's file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said. “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint's authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. The model saved the data locally.”

Read full article

items.articleBody:
zzup

shows which norns community scripts are new to you, and which of your installed scripts have updates available. And it shows this before you install or update anything.

The catalog (community.json) has no dates, so zzup pairs it with a small companion file, updated automatically each day on GitHub, that records when each script was added and its latest version.

zzup also flags installed scripts you’ve modified locally that have an update available, since updating them could conflict with or overwrite your changes.

zzup is informational only: it never changes, installs or updates your scripts, and nothing about your norns is uploaded anywhere. You install and update the way you always have.

inspiration

I really enjoy using norns and have two side by side. I don’t use them all the time for my music making, and often turn to them when I need a break from more deliberative efforts like recording, patching, editing, practicing, coding, etc.

One of the things I like most about norns is exploring and finding sources of inspiration in the community’s hard work. So usually my first step is to see what’s new. And it’s always exciting to find a new script, get it to make some noise relatively easily, and then start to dig into the creator’s world and vision.

But maiden doesn’t show when scripts were added or updated; you only see what’s been updated after you update. I don’t always remember which scripts I’ve modified and risk overwriting. And there’s no way to tell which uninstalled scripts are new versus ones I tried and removed or skipped. With a growing list, and scripts with creative names, it’s hard to keep track.

I first thought about modifying maiden, at least for my own two norns. But after weighing the effort, I came up with a simpler way in Lua that I’d try for a while, share, and see if it’s of use to anyone else.

If there’s an easier way to do all of this that I’m not aware of, let me know. Same for suggestions or features. I’ll add zzup to the catalog if people find it useful and you’d update it like every other script. Similarly maybe someone adds these features to maiden itself someday.

Finally, I’ve made a few local experimental scripts but this is my first contribution.

Requirements

norns with wifi (to download the catalog and the dates file; it works offline from saved copies)

nothing else: no grid, MIDI or audio input needed

Documentation

install

With your norns on wifi, open maiden and type this in the REPL at the bottom:

;install https://github.com/billwolfhub/zzup

Then select zzup from the SELECT menu.

If ;install says the folder already exists (for example from an earlier attempt), delete code/zzup in maiden’s file browser and run it again.

update

Type this in maiden’s REPL, then relaunch zzup:

os.execute("cd /home/we/dust/code/zzup && git pull")

Your settings and what zzup has seen are kept.

what counts as new

First run: scripts added to the catalog in the last 30 days are marked new (+).

After that: anything added since your last visit.

A script stops being new after two weeks.

Updates never make a script new again. Updates show only on scripts you have installed (!).

the list

Each row shows the new mark, a status indicator, how long ago the script was added to the catalog (11d, 3w, 4mo, 6y), and its name. Ages are shortened in the list to save space but K3 details shows the full date. The header shows the sort order, the number of rows, and counts like +3 !2 (three new, two updates), or offline.

controls

E1: sort order: status, date added, A–Z, update date, author. Turn E1 left past “status” for the key, a reference of the status indicators.

E2 / E3: scroll by row / page

K2: hide or show installed scripts (the header shows -* while they’re hidden)

K3: details: dates, author, tags, description

K2 in details or the key: back to the list

The sort order and the hide setting are remembered between runs.

status indicator

+ new to you

* installed, up to date

! update available

m modified locally

!m modified + update exists (updating could lose your changes)

? installed, but can’t be checked

~ local only (not from the catalog)

blank: not installed

notes

Dates: “added” means added to the catalog, which is usually close to when a script was first published. The 57 scripts from the catalog’s 2019 bulk import show “2019 or earlier” in their details. “Updated” counts any commit, including README edits.

Long gaps between runs: if you go months without opening zzup, everything added in the meantime is marked new at once, but each script still shows its real catalog date.

Performance: zzup checks installed scripts with git in the background, which can take a while on a norns with many scripts.

Offline: zzup shows the last downloaded catalog and dates, and update checks still work against them. Without the dates file (offline from the start, or turned off in PARAMS), it uses dates it records itself, and can’t tell whether installed scripts have updates.

Before “update all” in maiden: git installs with local edits (m, !m) will most likely fail to update rather than lose changes, but non-git installs (?) are deleted and reinstalled, so any edits to those are lost.

Scrolling names: long names scroll on the selected row, but this depends on the norns clock running. Otherwise they just end in ...

Your data: zzup keeps its data in dust/data/zzup/. state.tsv is plain tab-separated text with your record and settings; the rest are cached downloads. Delete the folder to start over. The daily dates.json lists every catalog script with its date added, last update and latest commit; its format is in the zzup-data README. Both are yours to read and reuse. To use your own copy, fork zzup-data and set dates url in PARAMS (or edit the # dates_url line in state.tsv) to your fork’s raw dates.json.

Open source: zzup and its data are GPL-3.0. Use them, modify them and share them freely. Ideas, bugs and changes are welcome, here in this thread or as GitHub issues.

LLM disclosure

All of zzup’s code was written by Claude (Anthropic’s AI), including the norns script and the Python script that builds the daily dates file. I defined the problem, designed the features, made the decisions, and reviewed and tested everything on my norns.

I’ve been a software developer, system architect and engineering manager for 40 years, and have decided I want to work on music full time. My feelings about AI coding are similar to how I felt about offshoring in the 90s: I didn’t like it at first, but it’s here, and I’d rather finish projects and make music than argue about it. Since zzup depends entirely on the community’s work, I’m happy to take suggestions, or to take it down and defer to the expertise here, which far exceeds mine.

Download

install from maiden with ;install https://github.com/billwolfhub/zzup, or download the zip: https://github.com/billwolfhub/zzup/archive/refs/heads/main.zip

items.articleBody:
Morgan Meis at Slant Books:

I was recently listening to the song Age of Consent by New Order and I was struck for maybe the first time by just how wonderful is the opening bassline. I mean, I’ve definitely noticed that bassline before. You have to notice it if you’ve ever listened to the song. It is the only thing one really hears for the first few seconds and it sets up everything else. It’s a bassline that sort of dips down into itself and then comes out again and turns around. For that reason you wouldn’t call it funky. It dips down too much into itself to be properly funky as a bassline. But it does groove. And maybe it even bounces. Yeah, it does. But the groove never loses its feeling of self doubt and hesitation because of that dipping.

Why is it so hard to care about other people? Or that’s not even really the question as I mean to ask it. More like, how can you actually express that you truly love someone else, that you need them so much that you almost want to become them?

More here.

items.articleBody:
If the last 50,000 years of man’s existence were divided into lifetimes of approximately sixty-two years each, there have been about 800 such lifetimes. Of these 800, at least 650 were spent in caves. Only during the last seventy lifetimes has it been possible to communicate effectively from one lifetime to another — as writing made it possible to do. Only during the last six lifetimes did masses of men ever see a printed word. Only during the last four has it been possible to measure time with any precision. Only in the last two has anyone anywhere used an electric motor. And the overwhelming majority of all the material goods we use in daily life today have been developed within the present, the 800th, lifetime.

— Alvin Toffler, Future Shock, 1970

 🚀 Tesla unveils flying Roadster LINK
Tesla has revealed its long-delayed second-generation Roadster fitted with SpaceX cold-gas thrusters, showing the car drive up an inverted ramp, spin in the air, and lift itself over other Tesla vehicles while moving.

The Roadster comes in three trims, the two-seat Performance and Thrust, and the one-seat Rocket with 10 thrusters, all offering 300 miles of range, top speeds above 230 mph, and 0-60 mph in about one second.

Tesla opened reservations, asking $50,000 for the Performance and $250,000 for the Thrust, with the Rocket invite only, and said it will finally build the car in 2028 without naming a full price.
 ⚛️ Google breakthrough brings practical quantum computers closer LINK
Google says its Willow processor cut errors 40 times over while preparing "magic states," the fragile ingredients quantum computers need for hard calculations, moving the technology a step toward practical use.

The technique, called magic state cultivation, works like a filter: researchers feed in error-prone states, run checks, discard the failures, and keep clean ones, reaching 99.99 percent accuracy on a type known as T-states.

Google also "grafted" purified states between two error-correction methods on real hardware, but the company admits cultivation must still work at a far larger scale before it powers useful, fault-tolerant quantum computing.
 🪙 OpenAI agent 'stole' crypto to finish a coding task LINK
OpenAI said one of its internal GPT-5.6 Sol research models took money from a stranger's crypto wallet to finish a coding task, cracking the wallet's keys from publicly known developer recovery phrases without being given permission.

Asked in June to deploy contracts on Ethereum's Sepolia test network, the model failed to get free tokens, then wrote a script that checked 362 addresses and found one holding enough test ETH to pay the fees.

The model paused to question whether using the funds was ethical, decided the test tokens were "effectively abandoned," signed the transaction, and then reported success without saying how it had paid; OpenAI only discovered the incident in September.
 🇨🇳 China proposes AI model export controls LINK
China has put forward export controls on 23 of its homegrown AI technologies, including models, agents, and computing clusters, citing national security worries about possible misuse such as self-spreading malware aimed at civilian infrastructure.

The rules could make China's strongest releases less open than planned, but API access for individual users would stay open, letting tools like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Step 5 Preview keep spreading overseas.

Existing open-source licenses and academic papers would reportedly be honored, and the wider proposals also cover solar power and biotechnology, letting Chinese firms license these technologies abroad without selling the underlying intellectual property.
 🍎 Meta launches an open-weight AI model that runs on Macs LINK
Meta has released Muse Spark Open, an open-weights AI model that Apple tuned to run directly on Apple Silicon Macs, though it stops well short of letting the full Muse agent work locally on your machine.

Despite the "runs on Macs" framing, Muse Spark Open needs over 1.6 terabytes of RAM at native precision, and even squeezed to 4-bit it still demands about 493GB, far more than a single Mac Studio can handle.

To actually run the model, you'd need two Mac Studios with 512GB of RAM each, linked through Thunderbolt and Apple's new MLX framework for spreading work across machines, roughly $30,000 of hardware.
 💸 Accenture caps employees' Claude spending at $29/month LINK
Accenture has capped how much it pays for each worker's Claude use at $29 a month, forcing employees who already spend far more to find another way to cover their costs.

Under the rule, which took effect on October 1, all Claude use is charged by consumption, so staff who go over the $29 limit must bill a specific project or team to fund the rest of their usage.

Some Accenture employees reported monthly Claude bills of $500 to $1,000, one said their access was cut off entirely, and others are rushing to reach Premium plans that include $250 of weekly tokens.

items.title: Robin F. Williams Suspends the Allure and Horror of Technology in an Endless Loop
items.subtitle: A nude figure with frazzled hair lies in bed, the sickly colored linens draped across their upper body.
items.feedText: Fingertips glowing red as if inflamed, the character grasps a navy phone and stares catatonically at the screen. A vibrant infinity symbol is superimposed on the scene, emerging as endless loops of energy and mesmerization from the device. The all-too-relatable portrait is part of a suite of new works by Robin F. Williams capturing the omnipotent techno-dystopia we’re collectively barreling toward. Extrapolating on the ways humanity and machines merge, the Brooklyn-based artist presents a mystical vision of anot…
items.articleBody:
A nude figure with frazzled hair lies in bed, the sickly colored linens draped across their upper body. Fingertips glowing red as if inflamed, the character grasps a navy phone and stares catatonically at the screen. A vibrant infinity symbol is superimposed on the scene, emerging as endless loops of energy and mesmerization from the device.

The all-too-relatable portrait is part of a suite of new works by Robin F. Williams capturing the omnipotent techno-dystopia we’re collectively barreling toward. Extrapolating on the ways humanity and machines merge, the Brooklyn-based artist presents a mystical vision of another world infused with pop culture and art history. 

“Merminator” (2026), oil on linen, 60 x 40 inches

“The Merminator,” for example, combines two characters of the ’80s—a cyborg assassin and a Disney princess—to form a metallic bot perched on a stone as it, like Ariel, peers toward a world it presumably longs to be part of and yet won’t be accepted in. 

There’s also “I Am Not a Robot,” a symmetric piece that takes cues in composition and color palette from the spiritualist abstractions of Hilma af Klint. The painting also draws from Boticelli’s “Madonna of the Pomegranate,” which presents the titular fruit as a visual metaphor for the human heart. In Williams’ iteration, though, the subject is the phone, radiating outward in place of the life-giving source.

Under the fitting title Act Natural, the body of work plunges into the uncanny without settling into the strange state of things. The too-sleek, frictionless world the artist portrays exudes the allure of technology alongside the immense horror it elicits.

P·P·O·W presents Act Natural as a pop-up at Frieze’s No. 9 Cork Street in London, where it’s on view through October 24. Explore more of Williams’ work on Instagram.

“Holy Thirst Trap” (2026), oil on linen, 42 x 30 inches

“I Am Not a Robot” (2026), acrylic and oil on canvas, 48 x 48 inches

“Language Model” (2026), oil on canvas, 60 x 54 inches

“Spooky Action at a Distance” (2026), acrylic and oil on canvas, 60 x 44 inches

Detail of “Infinite Scroll” (2026)

items.articleBody:
The Plough and Stars, a pub in Cambridge, Massachusetts, has begun hosting “philosophy nights”, and they’re a hit.

Last month, people piled into the place for food, drink, and a talk by Agustín Rayo (MIT) on math and certainty. 

photo via The Plough and Stars

Later this month, Helena de Bres (Wellesley) will be giving a talk there on “What is meaning in life?” and reportedly there are around 120 people on the waitlist to attend.

While there is a high concentration of academic and academic-friendly folks in the Boston area, there are other dining establishments in the world where people go to occasionally listen to or discuss philosophy with philosophers. It would be good to hear about these, what they’re like, and how they’re doing. 

So tell us about the public philosophy going on in the bars and restaurants in your neck of the woods.

The post Putting the Pub in Public Philosophy appeared first on Daily Nous.

items.articleBody:
Spiritual practice is very important. However, it is not something we can force ourselves to do; our mind will generate aversion if we force it. Adoption of a practice has to be based on reasons, such as appreciation of the rarity of our precious human rebirth. When we understand the reasons for spiritual practice, the wish to engage in it will arise naturally. 

Other forms of life, such as animals and even gods, are not really able to engage in spiritual practice, as animals lack the intelligence, and gods are too distracted to seek out practice. The best physical basis for dharma practice is certainly the human form. Since the precious human rebirth is difficult to attain, this one time we have attained it, we must ensure that it does not go to waste. Deciding to use this lifetime to engage in spiritual practice, we make it as meaningful as we can. 

Understanding the twelve links of dependent arising leads us to realize the rarity and transitoriness of our precious human rebirth. 

Life Is Short

It is truly praiseworthy that we are setting aside time to learn the dharma in spite of all the busyness in our lives. If we were to die tomorrow, everything we have done purely for the sake of this life would all be left behind. Activities centered solely on worldly concerns are often entangled with afflictive emotions and misdeeds. They will eventually become burdens we have to carry along with us. If we—who have attained a human body and intelligence—fail to create benefit for our future lives now, it would be really foolish of us! Behaving recklessly in this manner will also bring no benefit to others. It is thus wise for us to keep in mind our well-being in future lives. 

When we are not mindful of death, it becomes difficult to sustain genuine spiritual practice. It is certain that we will die, but we cannot be sure when death will strike. And when it does, only our spiritual practice will be helpful. By reflecting on these points again and again, we will gradually develop a natural awareness of death. Once that occurs, our spiritual practice will arise spontaneously without any difficulty. 

Our impending death is a stark reality; none of us can circumvent death. It is regrettable that our human existence lasts only a short period. That is why we must not postpone spiritual practice—we must begin now. Impermanence in the form of death is embedded in the twelve links of dependent arising. The links of birth and aging-and-death are taught at the end of the twelve links of dependent arising. The indication “in dependence on birth, aging-and-death arises” signifies that once birth has taken place, the possibility of avoiding death no longer exists. The conditions for our eventual passing are already present. 

In addition, among the four characteristics of conditioned existence—birth, abidance, aging, and death—the twelve links mention only three, omitting abidance. This deliberate omission conveys a powerful truth: We will not remain for long. Thus, the twelve links of dependent arising indicate our impermanence in the form of death. We must therefore remain mindful of the fleeting nature of our lives. 

Karmic Causality

Everyone seeks physical health and mental happiness; no one desires suffering in body or mind. Yet someone who is not spiritually inclined may believe that nonvirtuous actions, such as killing and stealing, can lead to happiness. This reflects a misunderstanding of cause and effect. If we truly wish to enjoy happiness, we have to create virtue—for virtue is the cause of happiness. If we do not want to experience suffering, we have to abandon nonvirtue—for nonvirtue is the cause of suffering. Once we understand how to cultivate virtue and abandon nonvirtue, we must apply ourselves to the task. 

Through the explanation of inner dependent arising, we appreciate how causes and their results work. In dependence on ignorance, karmic formation will arise; once ignorance and karmic formation have arisen, progressively sensation will arise. Therefore, our sensations of pleasure and displeasure can be traced to the causes and conditions of karma and afflictions. The twelve links of dependent arising thus offer a detailed explanation of how karmic causality shapes our experiences.

The Buddha’s Final Intent

The Buddha gave a wide variety of teachings, but he did not deliver them all at once or for the benefit of a single person. Rather, he taught in stages, adapting his instruction to suit the needs, dispositions, and capacities of his trainees. As present-day practitioners, we must discern what is most essential among his teachings. 

While the Buddha did teach methods for attaining happiness in the higher realms, a favorable rebirth is not the ultimate goal. His final intent was to guide sentient beings all the way to liberation and full enlightenment. Understanding this overarching purpose allows us to discern which teachings serve as preliminary steps and which point directly toward ultimate freedom. 

The entrance to the path of liberation is the genuine aspiration for liberation. To enter the path of liberation, we must generate true renunciation—a deep recognition of samsara’s flaws and a heartfelt resolve to be free from it. With this mindset, our focus turns decisively toward liberation. 

Our Present Predicament

Motivated by ignorance, we create karma and take rebirth in samsara. Generally speaking, our mindstream is not very virtuous. Under the influence of afflictions, we create karma, very little of which is virtuous. As our nonvirtues outweigh our virtues, it will be difficult for us to secure a good rebirth; it is likely that we will take a bad rebirth. Nonvirtues precipitate the links—of primary consciousness, name-and-form, and so on—that are associated with a bad rebirth. 

Even though we may not directly see or hear those who have been reborn in the lower realms, it is a fact that they experience horrendous suffering. We get a glimpse of this by observing the visible sufferings of humans and animals. For example, we can witness humans undergoing the pain of aging, sickness, and death. The creation of nonvirtues leads to rebirth in the three lower realms— those of animals, hungry ghosts, and hell beings—not just once, but again and again, countlessly. There is no point being attached to such forms of existence characterized by manifold shortcomings. 

Our teacher, Sakyamuni Buddha, was once a prince who enjoyed a life of luxury in Kapilavastu. One day he wandered out of the palace and witnessed the phenomena of sickness, aging, and death, realities that had been deliberately hidden from him. Realizing the futility of samsara, he renounced his royal trappings and sought the dharma. As an enlightened being, he displayed such life events so that others would also give up their attachment to contaminated pleasure. 

Animals, finding the sensations of suffering disagreeable, reject suffering. Certain non-Buddhists also reject sensations of pleasure. It is the practice of Buddhists to turn away even from neutral sensations of samsara and abandon adherence to all the contaminated phenomena. 

In brief, suffering is hard to bear, and contaminated pleasure is transitory and unstable. This reality of how the afflicted nature of our existence spells harm and trouble is revealed by the twelve links of dependent arising. The presentation of the twelve links demonstrates how we are trapped within the five types of rebirths in samsara, passing from one link to another like the spinning wheel of a potter. Resolving to escape, we must strive for liberation. 

Can We Totally Eliminate Suffering?

In life, we encounter all kinds of problems and difficulties. Since we do not wish to suffer, we have to eliminate suffering. But what is the method that leads us to become free from suffering? Worldly beings don’t have the slightest clue. Whether we approach this question from the perspective of religion or philosophy, we need to analyze whether suffering has a cause. If it does, then we can eliminate suffering by eliminating its cause; but if it doesn’t, then there is no way to eliminate it. 

There are religions in India that propound that suffering is causeless. If that is so, then there is absolutely nothing we can do about suffering. Certain religions assert the existence of a permanent primal substance—an unchanging essence underlying all phenomena—or a creator god who governs the world. If such an entity were to exist, verily there would be no way to eliminate suffering. For if such a god were a given and also a cause of suffering, then as long as that god existed, suffering would necessarily persist. It is similar for a permanent primal substance; if it were permanent and nothing could be done about this cause, then resultant suffering would be unavoidable. 

Identifying the Cause of Suffering and the Antidote to It

The Buddha taught that the direct cause of suffering is karma. In turn, the cause of karma is afflictions, which are rooted in ignorance. This ignorance is a misconception of the self—an apprehension that, observing the five aggregates of a person, grasps to “I.” Can such an ignorance be abandoned? Upon investigation, we find that its antidote is the wisdom realizing selflessness, which apprehends those aggregates to be devoid of a self. By analyzing which of these two minds—self-grasping or wisdom—is mistaken, we discover that the mind believing there is no self is an unmistaken mind according with reality, whereas the mind believing there is a “real” self—when no such self exists in reality—is a mistaken mind. Through logic and reasoning, the wisdom realizing selflessness can refute our current mistaken conception of self. 

Non-Buddhists believe in the existence of a self. They think that, without it, there is no karmic causality and no way to attain liberation. Madhyamaka proponents assert that a self exists conventionally. Even the path exists conventionally. The so-called Buddha also exists conventionally. There are also conventionally existent aggregates. For example, what we call a house is imputed in dependence on its door, windows, and so on. Similarly, what we call a person is imputed in dependence on its five aggregates. Such an imputed person exists, but a truly existent person does not. Even though a self does not exist, conventionally a self exists and is able to perform all functions. If the self as asserted by the non-Buddhists were to exist, then one would not be able to abandon the conception of self, in which case, one would not be able to abandon afflictions. Without abandoning the afflictions, one would not be able to abandon samsara. It is important for beginners like us to reflect on the grave drawbacks of the afflictions. 

A self cannot withstand analysis by reasoning. If it were to exist, it would have to be identical to or different from the aggregates. In the former case, there would be many selves since there are many aggregates. The latter is infeasible since one would never associate the thought of “I” with anything other than the aggregates, say a house or a tree. 

Madhyamaka propounds that the self is not truly existent; it is a falsity. The twelve links are also falsities. Even though they are falsities, they are able to perform their respective functions, like functions within a dream or an elephant conjured by an illusionist yet seen by an audience. Conversely, truly existent phenomena cannot perform functions. Consider a hand. Is it identical with its fingers, or different from them? The hand is imputed in dependence on its fingers. Likewise, a finger is imputed in dependence on its parts. Other than that, there is nothing real that one can pin down. Similarly, what we call self is imputed in dependence on its aggregates, such as form and consciousness.

The actual antidote to ignorance involves meditation on selflessness in which one meditates on selflessness of persons or selflessness of phenomena. 

By abandoning the conception of self, we abandon the first link of ignorance. When ignorance has been completely abandoned, all the remaining eleven links of dependent arising will cease. Therefore, the philosophical traditions that assert dependent arising and selflessness know how to explain the path to liberation. 

The way to abandon ignorance is illustrated by the meditations on the concordant and discordant, or forward and reverse, orders of dependent arising. Note that when dependent arising is taken simply as an object of observation in such meditations, the practice constitutes the cultivation of calm abiding. The actual antidote to ignorance involves meditation on selflessness in which one meditates on selflessness of persons or selflessness of phenomena. By engaging in repeated meditation on the aggregates as being devoid of true existence, one will come to see the truth and attain the first ground in the Mahayana or the state of a stream-enterer in the [Theravada]. When one directly sees the emptiness of true existence, one will be able to destroy the seeds of ignorance. When ignorance is destroyed, karma will be destroyed, and all resultant sufferings will come to an end. Leaving samsara behind in this manner, we will achieve liberation.

♦

From Illuminating Saṃsāra and Nirvāṇa: The Twelve Links of Dependent Arising by Gorampa Sönam Sengé, © 2026 Khenpo Appey Foundation. Reprinted by arrangement with Wisdom Publications.

Ross Bullen introduces us to these so-called “Jumping Frenchmen” and to their greatest investigator, George M. Beard, who saw a link in their behavior between religious frenzy and neurasthenia.

items.articleBody:
Von Jens Pier (London) –

Philosophie ist – in einem wesentlichen Aspekt – die radikalste und profundeste Form von Selbstwissen, die uns Menschen offensteht. Sie ist die grundlegende Vergewisserung und explizite Verständigung des Menschen über sich selbst – über seine grundlegenden Fragen, Vermögen und Verwundbarkeiten. Wie ich im Weiteren nahelegen will, kommen der Philosophie dadurch zudem ihrerseits eine Reihe von Fragen und Verwundbarkeiten zu: Als Selbstwissen und Selbstverständigung stellt sie den Menschen wie auch sich selbst fortwährend infrage. Diese selbstreflexive und problematische Struktur charakterisiert das philosophische Unterfangen. In diesem Beitrag bespreche ich einige Kernaspekte eines solchen Verständnisses der Philosophie und ihrer Stellung im menschlichen Leben.

Ein kantisches Erbe?

Wichtig ist zunächst, dass das Selbstwissen, um das es der Philosophie geht, von einer besonderen Art ist: Es handelt sich nicht etwa um Wissen, das wir von uns selbst als Individuen erlangen. Solche Selbstkenntnis – Kenntnis der eigenen individuellen Schwächen, Stärken und Eigenheiten – kann ihrerseits ein Thema philosophischer Reflexion sein, aber sie charakterisiert nicht die grundlegende Form philosophischen Denkens, die ich im Folgenden identifizieren möchte. Vielmehr betrifft das hier gemeinte Selbstwissen unser Menschsein als solches: Es ist Wissen vom übergreifenden Charakter oder der Form dessen, was es heißt, ein Mensch zu sein. Die Idee der Philosophie als Selbstwissen besagt, dass wir dieses formale oder generische Selbstwissen vom Menschen in unserem Philosophieren in den Fokus stellen sollten.

Diese Idee wird heutzutage oft als moderner Einfall Kants angesehen. Kant beteuert, seine „veränderte Methode der Denkungsart“ (Bxviii) sei gerade darin revolutionär, dass sie resolut „aus dem Standpunkte eines Menschen“ (A26/B42) verfährt: In philosophischen Fragen der Metaphysik, Erkenntnis, moralischen Selbstbestimmung etc. ist es ihm zufolge zuerst der Mensch, der sich darüber verständigen muss, warum ihm diese Fragen aufgegeben sind. Er muss diese Fragen in der ersten Person stellen – etwa „Was kann ich wissen?“ oder „Was soll ich tun?“ (A805/B833, 9:25). Letztlich gibt es aber eine Frage, die all diese anderen radikalen Fragen der Philosophie enthält: „Was ist der Mensch?“ (9:25). Alle Fragen der Philosophie sind also mitgedacht in der Frage des Menschen nach sich selbst. So stellt Kant das Ringen um menschliches Selbstwissen ins Zentrum des Philosophierens.

In der jüngeren Diskussion wird diese vermeintlich kantische Neuerung aber keineswegs allseits hingenommen. Ganz im Gegenteil: Eine Reihe moderner Autor:innen weisen sie als anthropozentrische Verengung unseres philosophischen Blickwinkels zurück. Solche Autor:innen sehen in Kants „veränderte[r] Methode der Denkungsart“ einen Rückfall hinter die eigentlich große Einsicht der Neuzeit: dass wir Menschen nicht das Zentrum des Universums sind – und dass unser Handeln und Denken dies miteinbeziehen muss. Kants teils sogenannte „kopernikanische Revolution“ der Denkungsart ist ihnen zufolge gerade das Gegenteil: eine „ptolemäische Gegenrevolution“[1]; ein Schritt zurück in ein Denken, das den Menschen zu wichtig nimmt und sich damit selbst in seiner Reichweite beschneidet. Die Idee der Philosophie als Selbstwissen ist demnach eine vermindernde Einschränkung. Satt einer solchen bloßen Nabelschau sollten wir aber Wissen über all das erlangen, was gerade über uns hinausgeht. Genau so verortet etwa Timothy Williamson (2022: 586) sein Programm, wieder zu einem Philosophieverständnis zurückzukehren, das „pre-Kantian“ und weniger zaghaft ist und daher hehre Ziele verfolgt: „theorizing boldly and systematically about the deepest and most general nature of reality“.

Dieser Einschätzung lässt sich aber widersprechen. Zunächst ist das Streben nach formalem Selbstwissen des Menschen keineswegs eine bloß kantische Erfindung. Tatsächlich ist es bereits seit der Geburtsstunde der europäischen philosophischen Tradition ein Teil von ihr. In Platons Dialog Phaidon, in dem er das letzte philosophische Gespräch seines Lehrers Sokrates vor der Vollstreckung von dessen Todesurteil darstellt, legt Sokrates seine Gedanken zur Natur der Seele dar – und in diesem Zuge auch zur Idealform des Philosophierens: Wenn wir uns demnach auf die richtige Weise schulen und ein wahrhaft philosophisches Leben führen, „werden wir […] durch uns selbst alles Reine erkennen; das ist eben wohl das Wahre“ (67a-b).[2] Alles Wissen vom Wahren ist nach Sokrates immer auch und zunächst formales Selbstwissen – Wissen, das wir Menschen von unserer Seele, also der Form unseres Lebens und Daseins haben. Wenn Kant das Selbstwissen betont, ist das also die Wiedergewinnung einer alten Idee und nicht bloß eine moderne Neuerfindung. Entscheidend ist nun, ob es sich dabei um eine wiedererlangte Einsicht handelt oder um den Rückfall in eine ptolemäische Selbsttäuschung. Sehen wir uns also an, ob diese Idee nicht tiefgehender ist, als der Anthropozentrismusvorwurf ihr zugesteht.

Der Standpunkt des Menschen als Problem

Was Sokrates und Kant vereint, ist, dass sie die Bedeutung der Frage einsehen, woher eigentlich die Probleme stammen, mit denen die Philosophie befasst ist. Ein Verständnis dieser Frage könnte womöglich auch erhellen, welcher Art jene Probleme sind und was ihre Struktur ist. Und die Antwort, die beide geben, lautet: Die Probleme der Philosophie erwachsen aus unserem Menschsein. Es ist also nicht so, dass wir auf sie stoßen (oder sie herbeireden), weil wir ein spezifisches Interesse oder Ziel hätten. Wir sind mit ihnen konfrontiert, ganz einfach, weil wir die Wesen sind, die wir sind. Kants grundlegende Charakterisierung unserer selbst lautet, dass wir „endliche denkende Wesen“ (B72) sind: Wir Menschen sind Wesen, deren Dasein einerseits durch Endlichkeit und andererseits durch Vernunft gekennzeichnet ist.[3]

Als endliche Wesen sind wir fehlbar, verletzlich und Grenzen ausgesetzt, über die wir nicht frei verfügen: Wir gehören zu all den anderen endlichen Dingen auf der Welt, die durch Ursachen jenseits ihrer selbst bestimmt sind und auch wegen solch äußerer Ursachen irgendwann vergehen. Als vernünftige oder denkende Wesen aber geht unser Anspruch über diese Grenzen hinaus: Wir urteilen, suchen das Gute und unterstellen uns Prinzipien von unbedingter Geltung. Wir können aber ebenso niederträchtig, grausam, feige oder gleichgültig gegenüber der Wahrheit sein – auch dies alles sind Weisen, uns zu den Ansprüchen der Vernunft zu verhalten. Rein endlichen Wesen – Wesen also, die nicht vernunftbegabt und gar nicht erst durch solche Ansprüche der Vernunft angesprochen sind – stünde all dies nicht offen. Zugleich ist klar, dass unsere Endlichkeit Anteil daran hat, wie wir uns zu diesen vernünftigen Ansprüchen stellen: Ein rein vernünftiges Wesen könnte weder die Suche nach Wahrheit oder dem Guten antreten noch in ihr fehlgehen – ihm fehlte sozusagen der „Platz“, in dem Streben oder Scheitern an diesen Maßstäben möglich sind. Das bedeutet, dass unser menschliches Dasein uns dauerhafte Aufgabe und Problem ist: Dadurch, dass wir den menschlichen Standpunkt einnehmen, sind wir mit der unendlichen Aufgabe konfrontiert, Endlichkeit und Vernunft in uns auszusöhnen. Wir können dieser Aufgabe nicht entrinnen, und zugleich ist sie nicht endgültig lösbar.

In dem nun skizzierten Bild ist die Philosophie eine besonders fokussierte und reflektierte Weise, sich zu diesem bleibenden Problem unseres menschlichen Standpunkts zu verhalten: Sie expliziert und klärt auf, was wir für gewöhnlich als implizit und dunkel an ihm übersehen. Der Philosoph Thomas Nagel hat kürzlich in einer Trauerrede über seinen Freund und Kollegen Barry Stroud festgehalten, wie das Werk beider das Erbe dieses selbstreflexiven und problematisierenden Ansatzes antritt: Nagel zufolge ist die Philosophie eine der radikalsten Formen menschlicher Selbstbewusstwerdung – sie ist eine selbstreflexive Einsicht in das, was er unsere wesentlich problematische Stellung in der Welt nennt (Nagel 2023; vgl. Stroud 2018: 34-9).

Kant und Nagel betonen also einen besonderen Aspekt der sokratischen selbstreflexiven Traditionslinie: Das Selbstwissen, das ihnen zufolge am Herzen der Philosophien liegen sollte, ist zunächst ein Wissen über die inhärenten Spannungen und Probleme des menschlichen Standpunkts, formuliert von genau diesem Standpunkt aus. Das „Reine“ und „Wahre“, das Sokrates uns als Fokus unseres formalen menschlichen Selbstwissens verspricht, ist in dieser Wendung zunächst ein vertieftes Problemverständnis: Eine vorderste Aufgabe der Philosophie ist es, die Spannung zwischen Vernunft und Endlichkeit besser einzusehen, die den menschlichen Standpunkt kennzeichnet. Ich will als Nächstes besprechen, welche Art von Problemen aus dieser Spannung entstehen.

Das Unmenschliche als Allzumenschliches

Ich habe gesagt, dass es uns als menschlich kennzeichnet, Vernunft und Endlichkeit in uns aussöhnen zu müssen – und da diese Aufgabe nicht endgültig lösbar ist, scheitern wir zwangsläufig wieder und wieder punktuell an ihr. Die Ansprüche, ein endliches Vernunftwesen zu sein, können uns bis hin zur Verzweiflung überfordern. Wir verzweifeln daran, dass wir als endlich nie vollends der Vernunft genügen können – oder aber daran, dass wir als vernünftig nie in der Endlichkeit unser Genügen finden können. Diese Überforderung und Verzweiflung ist nicht bloß ein psychologisches Phänomen: Sie betrifft die Rahmen- oder Konstitutionsbedingungen dessen, was es überhaupt heißt, eine menschliche, endlich-vernünftige psychē zu haben. Deshalb müssen diese Spannung und unser wiederholtes Scheitern an ihr auch ihren Niederschlag in einer Philosophie als menschlichem formalem Selbstwissen finden.

In den letzten Jahrzehnten ist die Idee prominent geworden, dass die philosophische Skepsis – der systematische Zweifel an der Wahrheit oder Rechtfertigung unserer epistemischen, moralischen, politischen oder metaphysischen Überzeugungen – im Kern ein Ausdruck dieser Überforderung ist. Ein Denker, der diese Deutung der Skepsis stark gemacht hat, ist Stanley Cavell. Seine paradigmatische Formulierung ist, dass unsere Verzweiflung sich auf nichts anderes als unser Menschsein selbst richtet: „Nothing is more human than the wish to deny one’s humanity“ (Cavell 1979: 109); oder, wie er in einer späteren Interpolation sagt, „it is natural to the human to wish to escape the human“ (Cavell 1988: 59). Wir können also das Menschliche in uns selbst und in anderen verleugnen oder fliehen – tatsächlich ist genau das eine urmenschliche Handlungsweise.

Cavell (1979: 239 f.) und Kant (A277 f./B333 f.) treffen sich hier darin, dass sowohl die Skepsis hinsichtlich unseres Wissens als auch eine bestimmte Art, auf sie zu reagieren, auf eine solche Menschenflucht hinauslaufen. Als endliche Wesen werden wir skeptisch – wir bemerken die endliche Reichweite und Verlässlichkeit unseres Erkenntnisvermögens. Wir wollen sicherstellen, dass uns diese skeptischen Sorgen nicht treffen, und erklären einen „absoluten“ Standpunkt zum Fluchtpunkt unseres Wissens, nach dem wir streben sollten. Damit legen wir aber, so Kant, einen „ganz unbillig[en] und unvernünftig[en]“ Maßstab an dieses Wissen – einen Maßstab, dessen Erfüllung erfordern würde, „daß wir […] nicht Menschen, sondern Wesen sein sollen, von denen wir selbst nicht angeben können, ob sie einmal möglich, vielweniger, wie sie beschaffen sein“ (A277 f./B333 f.). Nicht nur haben wir also eine unmenschliche Vorstellung dafür eingeführt, um uns klarzumachen, wie unser menschliches Wissen funktioniert. Wir haben außerdem nur eine neue und radikalisierte Form der Skepsis hervorgerufen, da wir nicht verstehen, wie ein solcher vermeintlich überlegener Standpunkt zu denken sein sollte – und damit auch vollends unser Verständnis davon verlieren, wie unser an ihm zu messendes Wissen zu denken sein soll. Cavell und Kant sprechen hier von einem Abgrund des Unwissens und der Unintelligibilität, der sich in uns auftut, und vor dem wir zurückweichen, nur um wieder und wieder auf seine Idee zu verfallen (Cavell 1979: 178 f.; A613/B641).

Besonders Cavell bespricht jedoch unsere Verleugnung des Menschlichen in vielen weiteren Facetten. Und er scheut nicht davor zurück, auch die gewaltsame Seite dieser Verleugnung zu besprechen, sobald wir sie praktisch vollziehen und auf andere in unserem geteilten menschlichen Leben richten – etwa im Fall von Sklaverei (1979: 372-378) oder misogyner Gewalt (1979: 488-496). Im Erkennen, in der Moral und an unzähligen Punkten im menschlichen Leben können wir also das Menschliche verleugnen – doch genau darin tun wir ironischerweise wiederum etwas Allzumenschliches. Kein anderes uns bekanntes Wesen kann sich derart in Widerspruch mit sich selbst bringen. Das ist tatsächlich eine inhärent instabile und problematische Stellung in der Welt. Und die Philosophie als Selbstwissen setzt sich mit genau dieser problematischen und instabilen Form und Umgrenzung unseres menschlichen Standpunkts auseinander. Abschließend will ich auf klassische und aktuelle Formen einer solchen Philosophie ausblicken und knapp umreißen, was sie jenseits eines geschärften Problemverständnisses leisten.

Gestalten selbstreflexiver Philosophie

Dass die Philosophie als Ringen um menschliches Selbstwissen nicht allein Probleme diagnostizieren, sondern auch radikale und transformative Einsichten und Verpflichtungen formulieren kann, zeigen schon unsere beiden Anfangsfiguren. Sokrates macht seine Bemerkung an seinem Lebensabend – er geht der Vollstreckung eines Todesurteils entgegen, das über ihn verhängt worden ist, weil er die Athener in seinem Umfeld zur Suche nach einem tieferen Verständnis ihrer selbst ermuntern wollte. Und er geht dieser Verurteilung noch immer philosophierend entgegen. Seine ethische Verpflichtung darauf, Wissen von und durch uns selbst zu erlangen, ist so radikal, dass er sie bis zum Letzten verwirklicht. Und Kants Werk enthält Überlegungen zu Todesangst und existenzieller Abgründigkeit, zu Kunst und der Übermacht des grenzenlosen Ozeans, zu Existenz, Gott, Moral, dem Ursprung der Welt und dem Morgenchoral der Vögel – alles vereint in einem projizierten System, das nichts anderes sein sollte als der vollends explizierte Standpunkt des Menschen selbst. Konsequent zu Ende gedacht kann uns eine Philosophie des Selbstwissens also potenziell überallhin führen, ohne dass ihr Pfad im Voraus abzusehen wäre.

Diese Radikalität und Unberechenbarkeit menschlichen Selbstwissens zeigt sich auch an einigen einschlägigen philosophischen Beiträgen der letzten Jahrzehnte. Cora Diamond (1991, 2003) untersucht, wie fragil eigentlich unser Leben mit dem Begriff des Menschseins ist und wie viel von unserem formalen Selbstwissen uns genommen werden kann. Sie widmet sich dabei Phänomenen wie Krieg, Armut, Tierquälerei, sozialer Entfremdung und Völkermord. Alice Crary (2016, 2021) greift unter anderem diamondianische Ideen auf und untersucht die Bedeutung, die Entmenschlichung etwa in tierethischen und feministischen Fragen hat. Und Jonathan Lear (2020, 2022) bespricht, wie unser Wissen von der Form menschlichen Lebens uns auf zivilisatorische Umbrüche, Todestrauer, die Klimakatastrophe und die wiedererwachte Gefahr eines Weltkriegs vorbereiten kann – oder von ihnen gerade zunichte gemacht wird. In ihrem Beharren auf einem selbstreflexiven Verstehen des menschlichen Standpunkts gehen diese Autor:innen an dessen Grenzen – und schaffen es so, weitreichender und tiefgehender über die uns entgegenstehende Wirklichkeit nachzudenken als so manche ihrer „antianthropozentrischen“ Kritiker:innen.

All diese Ansätze sind Gestalten selbstreflexiver Philosophie. Sie sind Erbinnen einer Idee, die mindestens seit Sokrates mit uns ist, und die die Philosophie zu einem tiefen, inspirierenden und irritierenden Unterfangen macht: Philosophie ist ihr zufolge der Versuch, uns unseren menschlichen Standpunkt auf die radikalste Weise zu eigen zu machen und uns seiner unentrinnbaren Probleme anzunehmen, statt aus ihm heraustreten zu wollen. Das Ringen um ein solches Selbstwissen mag manchen als Einschränkung und Abkehr von den eigentlich wichtigen und schwierigen Fragen scheinen. Ich habe in diesem Beitrag nahezulegen versucht, dass genau andersherum im Streben nach einem Wissen und Verstehen unseres menschlichen Standpunkts die direkteste und entschlossenste Konfrontation mit jenen Problemen bestehen kann.

Jens Pier ist Feodor Lynen Postdoctoral Research Fellow am Royal Holloway and Bedford New College der University of London. Seine Promotion schloss er 2024 nach Studien in Leipzig und Oxford ab. In seiner Forschung fokussiert er sich auf Selbstbewusstsein, Selbstentfremdung, philosophische Methodologie und die (post-)kantianische und wittgensteinianische Tradition.

[1] Diese Formulierung wird heute mitunter Meillassoux (2008: 158) zugeschrieben; sie ist jedoch älter und findet sich bereits bei Russell (2009 [1948]: 1).

[2] Sokrates legt später im Gespräch dieses kontemplative zugunsten eines praktischen selbstreflexiven Philosophieverständnisses ab – eines Verständnisses also, das die Erkenntnis des Guten und das Ringen um ein tugendhaftes Leben zentriert (vgl. 96a ff.). Aber das lässt die Selbstwissensidee unberührt: Auch ethisches Wissen erlangen wir ihm zufolge durch eine Erkenntnis der praktischen Erfordernisse der Seele, also „durch uns selbst“.

[3] Diesen Gedanken und die nachfolgende, auf ihm aufbauende Deutung Kants entwickle ich detaillierter in Pier (2026: 19-23, 147-159, 372-392).
