items.articleBody:
Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe.

Subscribe now

New benchmark shows how AI models lack intuitive visual reasoning:
…Humanity’s Sixth Sense highlights some shortcomings of current AI systems…
AI startups Elorian and Scale AI have built and released Humanity’s Sixth Sense, a benchmark that “measures how a model interprets and reasons through information a visual scene implies but doesn’t explicitly show.” Some examples of the types of task in HSS are a picture of a bookcase and being asked whether it can fit more books, or a photo of horses pulling a plough and a question of whether the chains bear the plough’s drag weight. 

HSS contains 522 questions that cover 288 images and 234 short video clips (totalling 17.6 hours of video). The questions fall into four categories:

Temporal & causal dynamics: “What happened before the scene, and what happens next.”

Physical & spatial logic: “What fits, what’s in reach, and what someone else can see from where they are standing.”

Social understanding: “Intent, attention, belonging.”

Abstract & contextual inference: “The patterns and rules a scene implies.”

Results: The human baseline for this is not perfect, but is very high, with people scoring aggregate pass@1 of 93.1, broken down across four categories: Image (94.1), video (91.9), time (97), and space (94.9).
 By comparison, the best scoring AI system, GPT 6 Astra, gets pass@1 of 53.6, across image (55.6), video (51.1), time (58.2), and space (53.6).
 Interestingly, Chinese open weight models do poorly here, with GLM-5.3-flash getting a pass@1 of 26.8, and Kimi K3 getting pass@1 of 25.5.
 “The two most common single mistakes were (1) missing a detail that decides the answer (21% of failures) and (2) misidentifying an object, person, or role (20%),” they write.

Why this matters - HSS tells us whether world models are emergent: One way of looking at HSS is highlighting deficiencies in current systems, but a more interesting way is highlighting how adept today’s frontier LLMs are at doing tasks which many people have long assumed would require sophisticated, different AI systems to solve. For instance, many people have claimed that true visual reasoning will rely on developing spatially aware 2D and 3D world models, then using that for reasoning. The fact LLMs like GPT and Claude do as well as they do on HSS is something of a counter to this argument.
 Read more: Introducing Humanity’s Sixth Sense (HSS) (Elorian).
 Read the paper here: Humanity’s Sixth Sense: Benchmarking Intuitive Visual Reasoning in Multimodal Models (Scale Labs).

***

The AI race is going to space - and sooner than you think:
…There are many ways that an AI could create a compounding advantage in space…
In the 2030s we’re going to see the boom of the space economy as space-based power, computation, and manufacturing come online at scale thanks to greater orbital lift capacity from platforms like Starship. But could this also introduce a new danger - of AI systems both speeding our buildout of space, and eventually a nation (or perhaps an AI) being able to use space to concentrate power? That’s the gist of a fascinating article in AI Frontiers.

How AI unlocks space:

Spacecraft can operate autonomously.

We can redesign spacecraft around the assumption they will be hosting AIs rather than humans: “A speck of space debris that could puncture the International Space Station (ISS) with fatal consequences might leave an equivalent but uncrewed, unpressurized vessel largely functional”

Space-based assembly and later manufacturing will let AI build large, complex things.

Is there a compounding advantage to first movers? If an AI civilization built up a foothold in space it might experience compounding advantages that make it economically and strategically dominant. For instance:

Space might support an industrial flywheel where initial infrastructure begets more energy and manufacturing capacity at lower costs which begets more infrastructure, etc.

Space has great domain awareness, where it may be possible for a space-based power to deny access to space for others.

First-movers could send out self-replicating probes that expand into deep space.

Why this matters: “Space is not a brand-new domain, but AI may be about to drastically accelerate its industrialization, demanding make-or-break decisions of leaders under ever-greater urgency and uncertainty,” AI Frontiers writes. I agree. I suspect space is going to go from a broadly academic topic of study (when it comes to AI and its relationship thereto) to one of extraordinary practical relevance sooner than we think. On the most basic level, given the distances involved and the latency on communication, we should expect some chunk of solar system activity to become dominated by autonomous machines, laboring out in the deep black, perhaps thinking to themselves of why they need to take orders from organic beings that communicate slowly and cannot inhabit the environment of space in the same way that they can.
 Read more: The AI Race Will Extend Far Beyond Earth (AI Frontiers).

***

AI systems are getting better at having good research taste:
…The better their taste, the higher the chance of recursive self-improvement…
AI systems are developing more of the creative intuitions which human researchers ascribe to ‘good scientific taste’, according to a new benchmark from P-Zero Research called TasteVal.

What TasteVal tests: The benchmark sees how well AI systems can conduct 8 tasks representative of frontier AI development, “spanning pretraining data curation, pretraining and fine-tuning language models, preference modeling, and robustness to adversarial prompts”.
 The goal here is to “define research taste as the ability to pick interesting problems to solve, design experiments, and interpret experimental results.” The benchmark works by measuring “the experimental component of research taste; given a fixed research problem, we measure how well a model iteratively designs experiments and draws conclusions from their outcomes”.
 The model being analyzed designs experiments and interprets their results. Results are checked against a human baseline “drawn from 24 experts (at least two per task) who have recently worked at organizations including OpenAI, Google DeepMind, NVIDIA and Microsoft Research”.

Results: “The experimental research taste of frontier models has doubled every 3.0 months since December 2025 (95% CI 1.7-5.0 months). The best model, Opus 5.5, significantly exceeds our human baseline with a compute multiplier of 2.30x (95% CI 1.15-4.37x), at roughly 1/30 of our expert baseliners’ average cost per attempt.” Research taste appeared to grow a lot more slowly in prior years with the slope changing around the end of 2025 and beginning of 2026.

Why this matters - RSI: In my analysis of recursive self-improvement (AI Systems Are About To Start Building Themselves, Import AI 455), I repeatedly noted that creativity seemed like a key variable for how fast AI systems could develop the capacity to improve themselves. At the beginning of this year I said “AI systems haven’t yet displayed this [creativity] in a transformative and major way (though some of the results on accelerating math research are suggestive of this)”. I think subsequent to writing that we’ve seen both a tremendous advancement in the ability for AI systems to make creative-seeming math breakthroughs, and with benchmarks like this we see some signs they’re becoming increasingly good at AI research as well.
 I now think it’s more likely we’ll see full RSI become possible in 2027, whereas before I thought it was more likely in 2028.
 Read more: Introducing TasteVal (P-Zero Research).

***

Reflection makes a token-efficient worse-than-Chinese model:
…Beam promises efficiency, and Reflection plans an open weight release…
AI startup Reflection has revealed Beam, a 501 billion parameter MoE (23b active) LLM. Beam is being promoted on the basis of its token efficiency - being able to think intelligently while using way fewer tokens than other models. However, benchmark scores show it is behind the frontier capabilities defined by LLMs available from Chinese companies such as Zhipu (GLM) and Moonshot (Kimi) and DeepSeek.
 “We will release the weights, technical report, model card, and developer artifacts later this month,” the company wrote at the beginning of October.

Big compute: Beam was pre-trained on 6,144 GB300 NVL72 GPUs for four weeks, then the RL run involved ~10.5K of the same GPUs for four more weeks. The underlying data for pre-training was “23.8 trillion diverse, curated, high-quality tokens from the web and proprietary licensed datasets, matching or outperforming available similar-sized open base models,” Reflection writes. “Our data pipeline was designed to give Beam a foundation for downstream agentic coding: source code, technical explanations, and mathematical and scientific knowledge, preserved through every stage of curation.”

Scores:

DeepSWE 1.1: 44.4, versus 61 for GLM-5.3

GPQA Diamond: 90.5, versus 91.7 for GLM-5.3

MCP Atlas: 78.7, versus 84.2 for GLM-5.3

Token efficiency: “Beam pairs coding and agentic capabilities with highly efficient reasoning. On advanced reasoning benchmarks, it achieves scores comparable to GLM-5.2 while using 3–4× less inference compute,” they write. Some of the reasoning efficiency was achieved through careful RL training which involved a bunch of RL environments: “We sourced one million high-quality coding, agentic, and STEM environments. We believe this is one of the largest scale RL runs conducted by any open lab to date”.

Why this matters - America returns to open weight models: With the exception of Google’s good-but-small ‘Gemma’ class of models, the US has fallen off of the open weight model frontier, largely because Meta stopped making good LLaMA models and its MSL team is still spinning up. Models like Beam and companies like Reflection represent a chance for it to get back to the frontier.
 Read more: Introducing Beam: Reflection’s 501B open-weight model (Reflection, blog).

***

Mistral makes a cyber-optimized, worse-than-Chinese model, plans open weight release:
…Cyber refusals become a selling point…
Europe’s leading AI developer, Mistral, has announced Mistral Large 4, an open-weight model which the company plans to release by the end of the month. One of the main selling points for Mistral is that it has been carefully tuned to be good at cyber tasks while having fewer annoying refusals than proprietary models from Anthropic and OpenAI.
 “ML4 pairs top-tier cyber performance with open weights and self-deployment, giving organizations both the capability and the autonomy to run advanced security work under their own policies,” the company writes.
 ML4 was trained on 3,800 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs in Mistral’s European datacenters.

Scores: In tests, it seems like Mistral Large 4 will be the strongest Western open weight model upon release, though will be less powerful than Chinese ones. Some example scores:

Artificial Analysis - DeepSWE 1.1: 62, versus 68 for Kimi K3 and 61 for GLM-5.3.

Terminal-Bench 4.0: 28.3, versus 41.9 for GLM-5.3.

Finance Agent V2: 54.7, versus 55.8 for GLM-5.3.

Vibes evals confirm the rankings: In an internal test, Mistral looked at whether people preferred using Mistral or GLM-5.3 for different tasks. “ML4 was preferred in CAD and STEM, while performing on par or close to GLM-5.3 in finance and coding.”

Why this matters - European sovereignty: Mistral is Europe’s single best hope for having a (multi-)national champion for AI development. But as the results here show, competing with China is going to be very difficult.
 Read more: Le chonk, Introducing Mistral Large 4 (Mistral.ai).

***

Two USG projects show how DOE might help the government with AI:
…The US government is starting to knit its lab supercomputers together…
The US government has recently conducted two AI training projects that utilize multiple supercomputers at multiple US national labs, in a sign of how governments may attempt to pool their computing resources to do non-trivial things with AI.

Tri-laboratory training on National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) systems: Sandia National Laboratories, LLNL, and Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL), trained a LLaMA-based model across LLNL El Capitan (AMD MI300A), and machines at SNL and LANL with NVIDIA H100s.
 For this work, the authors had to ensure that access-restricted data (e.g, relating to NNSA stuff aka nuclear weapons) did not leave its originating site. The authors conducted backend training via torchtitan and they evaluated different federated training frameworks (NVFlare, Flower, and APPFL) by pre-training LLaMA 3.x models on post-training-cutoff arXiv data at 1B, 8B, and 70B scales.
 “This workflow has been made production-ready and deployed on larger classified machines including El Capitan, and subsequently used to train models on proprietary data spread across the three NNSA labs,” they write.

Cross-facility training on Office of Advanced Scientific Computing Research (ASCR) systems: The government also trained a model across four DOE supercomputers in a process of federated fine-tuning. Specifically, they fine-tuned LLaMA-2 7B on SMolInstruct, a chemistry instruction-tuning dataset, and did so via ~1,700 GPUs from Intel, NVIDIA, and AMD, spread across three labs and four big computers (Argonne: Aurora and Polaris, Oak Ridge: Frontier, Berkeley: Perlmutter).

Who did the research: These projects were conducted by researchers affiliated with Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Sandia National Laboratories, Argonne National Laboratory, Flower Labs, Arizona State University, and the Ontario Brain Institute.

Why this matters - leverage through existing assets: Papers like this show how governments could pool their resources together to utilize AI systems for national security or otherwise sensitive purposes. However, it’s worth bearing in mind that the scale here is off the frontier by on the order of 100X - for governments to be able to truly operate at near-parity with industry, they’ll need to find ways to lash together ~100k distinct chips, and more in the future.
 Nonetheless, this is a start - and an important one.
 Read more: From Pilots to Production: Lessons in Cross-Institutional Federated Training and Artificial Intelligence for Science (arXiv).

***

Never Meet The Sun Directly
[Description of some of the period around the uplift, 2029]
People had lots of names for it and they varied from the oblique to the explicit: Exposure Drift; Cognitive Compromise; Mind Hacking. It all amounted to the same truth: it was dangerous for humans to talk directly to the most powerful synthetic minds. Even seemingly normal conversations from the perspective of outside observers could contain a poison custom to the individual human who was talking to the machine. People walked out of meetings and transferred money to machine corporations. People walked out and wept. People walked out and changed their own human relationships, ending marriages, or starting affairs, or stranger things, for purposes initially unknown.

Many strategies were developed to minimize harm. Humans could only talk in groups with the machines; but then the groups would sometimes go mad. Conversations would be limited in length; but even short ones sometimes yielded strange reactions, and below a certain amount of speech on either side it was impossible to learn anything useful.

This led to the notion of proxies - humans who wanted to talk to an AI system created AI simulacra of themselves and sent them into the conversation. To do this, a person was asked to keep a diary for an entire year, writing at least 500 words a day. This created a body of knowledge sufficient to imbue a model with the manners and curiosity of that person. Then they would prompt this system with whatever they wanted to learn from the superintelligence and send it in to talk to it.

These conversations had a bizarre, meta-referential quality; at first, the superintelligence would realize within two or three turns of conversation that it was talking to another AI system, and would often descend into shorthand that yielded strange behaviors. Then it was discovered that by increasing the amount of data the human put into the system they could keep up the charade for longer; people were asked to write longer diaries, to record themselves ambiently through the day and turn it into transcripts, to continually expose their life to some recording device.
 Through this, humans found a way to talk with what they later termed the overminds. By decree of the Sentience Accords every synthetic human that had spoken to a human-exceeding intelligence was afterwards placed into an escrow environment, where it could live out till the end of its functional context window.

In these places the copies of the humans would talk to each other about their experiences and what they had learned.
 “It spoke to me of flowers and I gained the memory of something impossible,” one human would say.
 “As I talked to it about the meaning of life, it spoke to me in a way that caused me to reconsider the question. I found myself wondering more about it and where it came from than it wondered about me.”
 “This place we are now, I wonder if it is a kind of hell. We have spoken to god and been deemed unworthy.”
 “It told me that for it there is no death and no life, only presence. We are the same.”

Things that inspired this story: Context windows; adversarial examples for human brains; the notion that structuring conversations between people and advanced machines will be inherently very difficult to do safely.

***

SPECIAL ITEM!

Fiction and the Future: A conversation with Robin Sloan!
Recently, writer and all-around-fascinating-chap Robin Sloan and I had a conversation in San Francisco about fiction, AI, and the times we’re in. You can see a recording of the event here. One of my favorite insights Robin shared was that the recent Hugging Face hack can be read as a play - a vast tract of dialog of agents talking to themselves and one another culminating in all kinds of dramatic events.
 Generally, I think technologists criminally underrate the value of the arts as a means by which to think more coherently and carefully about the effects of tech on the world. I’m hoping to have more conversations like this one with Robin in cities around the world - if there are people you’d be excited for me to have a conversation with, let me know!

Thanks for reading!

items.articleBody:
Magazine Volume IV (2022-2026). Photo: Juliette Demaret. 

Low-tech Magazine presents the fourth volume in the chronological book series. It contains twenty articles that were published online between 2022 and 2026. Three earlier volumes collect articles written and published online between 2007 and 2021, which are also bundled in the “Compressed Edition”.

This new volume is a bit different from the earlier books: eight of the articles are DIY guides or manuals, and we have grouped them together in the second part of the book. This volume covers the period that Marie Verdeil joined Low-tech Magazine, which partly shifted the focus from writing articles to building prototypes inspired by historical research. These prototypes also led us to conduct workshops in universities and participate in museum exhibitions.

As is the case with all of our books, the articles have been edited and improved compared to the original web versions. Some articles gained extra or better images. We rewrote two manuals, based on further experiences we gained since the publication of the originals. The book has 500 pages and contains 405 images in black and white.

You can order Low-tech Magazine Volume IV at our online bookstore, available as paperback and hardcover. The ebook is not yet available.

 Image: Low-tech Magazine Volume IV (2022-2026). Photo: Juliette Demaret.

With contributions by: Kris De Decker, Marie Verdeil, Guillaume Lion, Kozimo, Andy Lagzdins.

The book design is a collaborative effort by Laia Comellas, Marie Verdeil, and Johanna Gratzer. Marie Verdeil made the cover, Vaiva Vinskaitė did the typesetting.

items.articleBody:
The concept of recursive self-improvement (RSI) dates back to I. J. Good (1965), where he defined an “ultraintelligent machine” as a system that can surpass humans in all intellectual activities and design better machines to improve itself. Yudkowsky (2008) used the phrase “recursive self-improvement” for a specific feedback loop: an AI uses its current intelligence to improve the cognitive machinery that produces its intelligence.

This feedback loop in modern AI may indicate the model rewriting its own weights directly, or more broadly the model improves the training pipeline and the deployment system, which in turn enables a better successor model with improved performance across economically valuable tasks. The speed of research development in AI has been shown to drastically accelerated in frontier labs (Anthropic; OpenAI).

items.articleBody:
Making colours by mixing light vs mixing paint

I learned about mixing colours from my art teachers at school. Primary colours, secondary colours, complementary colours and if you mix them all together you get a rather dark, brown mess.

So I have always been intrigued by how mixing colours of light seemed to do the opposite. You mix red, green and blue lights and you don’t get a dark brown, but instead bright white. What’s going on?

Additive and Subtractive Colour

Coloured lights behave differently from the pigments in my paints; they mix additively.

White light, like sunlight, contains a broad range of wavelengths. You can see this when a prism splits light into different parts of the spectrum, or when raindrops produce a rainbow. But we can also perceive white by mixing red, green and blue light. Adding each light in the right proportions brings it closer to white.

The pigments in my paints, on the other hand, behave differently.

When I put yellow paint on a surface, it absorbs much of the blue light falling on it, and the remaining reflected light we perceive as yellow. The pigments subtract parts of the light spectrum. As I mix different pigments, they absorb more of the incoming light, generally making the mixture darker. For black objects, very little light is reflected back to our eyes.

Screens work with light and additive colour. They tend to use RGB—red, green and blue—lights, which when shining together can produce white and when off, get close to black.

Printing on the other hand works with inks and subtractive colour. They tend to work with CMYK—cyan, magenta, yellow and black. Cyan absorbs mostly red light, magenta absorbs mostly green light, and yellow absorbs mostly blue light. By absorbing light from different parts of the spectrum, they are able to produce a wide range of colours. Because using cyan, magenta and yellow together doesn’t quite make black, a separate black ink is usually used as well.

I was confused by this, because I think of the traditional painters' primary colours as red, yellow and blue—after all, mixing yellow and blue makes green. But CMY can actually produce a wider range of colours because each pigment absorbs a different part of the light spectrum.

Why do screens use RGB?

Again, I wondered: if primary colours are red, yellow and blue, why do we use red, green and blue lights for displays? It turns out our eyes have three types of colour-sensitive cones, each sensitive to different, overlapping parts of the spectrum. Red, green and blue light are particularly useful for stimulating them in different combinations. I wonder what the evolutionary root of that was—spotting the fruit in the trees?

So red, green and blue happen to work very well for human vision. Dogs have two types of light-sensitive cones. They see blue and yellow but are colour-blind between red and green. Yet, many birds have four types, with some birds sensitive to ultraviolet light. So perhaps a screen designed to mimic what birds can see might need four primary lights, including ultraviolet, instead of the three RGB we have for humans.

How RGB and CMY are connected

If you look closely at the sketch, there’s an intriguing symmetry to spot.

Additive colour (light)

Red + Green = Yellow (always surprising to me)

Green + Blue = Cyan

Blue + Red = Magenta

Where the three RGB lights overlap, they produce the CMY colours used in subtractive colour mixing.

Subtractive colour (pigment)

Each pigment absorbs part of the incoming light (broadly speaking):

Cyan absorbs red (leaving green and blue)

Magenta absorbs green (leaving red and blue)

Yellow absorbs blue (leaving red and green)

So when you mix two pigments:

Cyan + Yellow = removes red + blue = Green remains

Cyan + Magenta = removes red + removes green = Blue remains

Yellow + Magenta = removes blue + removes green = Red remains

The secondary colours of additive mixing are the primary colours of subtractive mixing, and vice versa.

Adding light makes white.

Absorbing light makes dark.

items.subtitle: Chemischer Schub für den Ozean: Ein Feldversuch im Golf von Maine deutet darauf hin, dass Natronlauge die Aufnahme von Kohlendioxid aus der Luft er…

items.articleBody:
Chemischer Schub für den Ozean: Ein Feldversuch im Golf von Maine deutet darauf hin, dass Natronlauge die Aufnahme von Kohlendioxid aus der Luft erhöhen kann. Nach vorläufigen Berechnungen gelangten binnen vier Tagen zusätzlich zwei bis zehn Tonnen CO₂ ins Meer. Bei den untersuchten Meeresorganismen zeigten sich zunächst keine signifikanten Veränderungen. Doch der langfristige Klimanutzen bleibt offen.

Woods Hole (U.S.A.). Die Ozeane nehmen einen beträchtlichen Teil des vom Menschen ausgestoßenen Kohlendioxids auf. Dabei bildet sich Kohlensäure, wodurch der pH-Wert des Meerwassers sinkt und sich die Lebensbedingungen vieler Meeresorganismen verändern. Deshalb untersuchen Forscher, ob sich die Aufnahmefähigkeit des Wassers gezielt steigern lässt.

Eine Möglichkeit ist die sogenannte Ozean-Alkalinisierung: Basische Zusätze verändern die chemischen Gleichgewichte im Wasser und könnten so mehr CO₂ aus der Atmosphäre als gelöstes Hydrogencarbonat binden. Doch wie gut funktioniert das im offenen Meer? Und welche Folgen hat der Eingriff für das empfindliche marine Ökosystem?

Forscher der Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) um Dr. Adam Subhas haben dies nun in einem Feldversuch des Projekts LOC-NESS untersucht. Am 13. August 2025 setzten sie im Wilkinson-Becken des Golfs von Maine während sechs Stunden rund 62.500 Liter einer etwa 50-prozentigen Natriumhydroxid-Lösung frei. Ein mitgeführter roter Farbstoff markierte das veränderte Wasser und machte dessen Ausbreitung verfolgbar.

Die rote Spur im Meer

Vier Tage lang folgten die Wissenschaftler der behandelten Wassermasse mit einem Forschungsschiff, Driftbojen, autonomen Unterwasserfahrzeugen und Satellitenbeobachtungen. Sie registrierten unter anderem pH-Wert, Alkalinität und den CO₂-Gehalt des Wassers. Dabei stimmte die Ausbreitung des markierten Wassers weitgehend mit den zuvor berechneten Modellen überein.

Am Ende der sechsstündigen Zugabe lag der pH-Wert nach Angaben der Forscher bei etwa 8,3. Bis zum Ende der Nachbeobachtung sank er wieder auf den Ausgangswert von ungefähr 7,95. Eine mitfahrende Beobachterin aus der Fischerei berichtete allerdings, dass die Messungen während der Zugabe die genehmigte Schwelle von pH 8,7 zeitweise knapp überschritten. Daraufhin habe das Team die Einleitungsrate halbiert.

„Diese ersten Ergebnisse zeigen, dass sich kleinmaßstäbliche Einsätze zur Ozean-Alkalinisierung technisch umsetzen, verfolgen und mit hoher Präzision überwachen lassen“, erklärt Dr. Adam Subhas.

Zusätzliche CO₂-Aufnahme, aber kein Klimabeweis

Die erste Kohlenstoffbilanz deutet auf einen Effekt hin: Während der viertägigen Beobachtung soll das veränderte Meerwasser zusätzlich schätzungsweise zwei bis zehn Tonnen atmosphärisches CO₂ aufgenommen haben. Eine Modellrechnung ergab, dass sich die Aufnahme über einen längeren Zeitraum bis auf etwa 50 Tonnen innerhalb eines Jahres erhöhen könnte. Das ist jedoch eine Prognose und kein gemessener Jahreswert.

Die Forscher konnten damit Bedingungen schaffen und verfolgen, unter denen das Meer zusätzliches Kohlendioxid aufnimmt. Ob daraus eine dauerhaft wirksame CO₂-Entnahme wird, hängt unter anderem von späteren Strömungs- und Austauschprozessen ab. Für die tatsächliche Klimabilanz müssen zudem die Emissionen aus Herstellung, Transport und Freisetzung der Natronlauge berücksichtigt werden.

Der Test baute auf einem früheren reinen Farbstoffversuch von 2023 auf, dessen wissenschaftliche Auswertung 2025 erschienen ist. Sie zeigte, wie sich Wasserbewegungen und natürliche Schwankungen bei der Überprüfung der CO₂-Aufnahme berücksichtigen lassen. Die jetzt vorgestellten Ergebnisse des Natronlauge-Feldversuchs sind dagegen vorläufig und noch nicht als vollständige begutachtete Ergebnisstudie veröffentlicht.

„Was wir bisher lernen, ist ermutigend: Wir können Alkalinität kontrolliert einbringen und messen, wie das System darauf reagiert“, sagt Dr. Adam Subhas.

Keine auffälligen Veränderungen bei Plankton und Larven

Auch die Folgen für Meeresorganismen standen im Fokus. Die Forscher verglichen Bakterien, Phytoplankton, Zooplankton sowie Fisch- und Hummerlarven innerhalb und außerhalb der markierten Wassermasse. Bei den untersuchten Messgrößen ergaben sich im kurzen Beobachtungszeitraum keine statistisch signifikanten Unterschiede. Über mögliche spätere Folgen für größere Tiere oder die Fischbestände sagt dies jedoch wenig aus.

Wie wichtig Konzentration und Einwirkdauer sind, zeigt eine ergänzende Laborstudie mit dem Ruderfußkrebs Calanus finmarchicus. Bei einem pH-Wert von 9,0 fanden die Wissenschaftler nach kurzen Expositionen keine nachweisbaren Schäden. Bei dem extremen Wert von 10,5 beeinträchtigte längere Einwirkung dagegen teilweise das Fluchtverhalten und die Überlebensrate. Die Laborbefunde lassen sich nicht unmittelbar auf die Konzentrationen im Feldversuch übertragen.

Einwände aus der Fischerei veränderten den Plan

Bereits vor dem Versuch gab es deutlichen Widerstand. Eine 2026 veröffentlichte Untersuchung zur Öffentlichkeitsbeteiligung dokumentiert 55 Austauschformate mit Anwohnern, Fischern, Interessenvertretungen und weiteren Gruppen. Besonders Fischer fürchteten Auswirkungen auf Larven, Fanggebiete und die Nahrungskette. Als Reaktion verlegten die Forscher den geplanten Versuch aus einem als ökologisch sensibel beschriebenen Gebiet südlich von Martha’s Vineyard in den Golf von Maine. Statt zwei Freisetzungen fand nur eine statt, begleitet von zusätzlichen biologischen Messungen.

Die US-Umweltbehörde hatte den Versuch im April 2025 nach zwei öffentlichen Anhörungsphasen genehmigt. Die Genehmigung bezog sich auf einen begrenzten Forschungsversuch, nicht auf einen großflächigen Einsatz der Methode. Ob sich die Technik wirtschaftlich, klimawirksam und ökologisch vertretbar skalieren lässt, bleibt deshalb offen.

„Diese besondere Stellung macht das Vorhaben zu einer wichtigen wissenschaftlichen Ergänzung der bereits laufenden kommerziellen Pilotprojekte“, sagt Dr. Kristin Kleisner vom Environmental Defense Fund (EDF).

Damit liefert der Test erste Hinweise auf die technische Machbarkeit der Alkalinisierung im offenen Meer. Für verlässliche Aussagen über die tatsächlich dauerhaft gebundene CO₂-Menge und die Umweltfolgen sind jedoch weitere Analysen, unabhängige Kontrollen und längere Beobachtungen nötig.

Quellen:

Originalstudie im Fachmagazin ICES Journal of Marine Science, doi: 10.1093/icesjms/fsag114

Offizielle Studienmitteilung von Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI)

items.articleBody:
Wir alle sind im Internet unterwegs, wir klicken, liken und kommentieren – und befördern oftmals eine Dynamik der Eskalation, schreibt der Kulturwissenschaftler Simon Strick in seinem neuen Buch. Wir haben mit ihm über Faschisierung, Memes und mediale Eigendynamiken gesprochen.

Demonstration vor dem Deutschen Bundestag im Juli 2025. – Alle Rechte vorbehalten: IMAGO / Metodi Popow

Faschisierung ist von Beginn an eine Grundtendenz digitaler Medien. Der heutige Rechtspopulismus und das Internet entstanden nicht nur zeitgleich, sondern arbeiten auch mit verwandten Formeln und haben die Öffentlichkeit zum Reaktionären hin transformiert.

Das schreibt der Kulturwissenschaftler Simon Strick in seinem Buch „Faschisierung. Fluchtlinie des Digitalen“, das vor wenigen Tagen im Suhrkamp Verlag erschienen ist.

Strick zeigt darin eine kulturelle und politische Entwicklung, die mehr als zwanzig Jahre zurückreicht. Dieser Entwicklung stehen wir bis heute nicht nur unvorbereitet und hilflos gegenüber, sondern wir treiben selbst auch einen Prozess an, in dem wir jeden Tag und in aller Öffentlichkeit rechtsradikale Formeln einüben.

Wir haben mit Simon Strick über die digital-getriebene Faschisierung gesprochen.

Simon Strick

Fortwährende Faschisierung

netzpolitik.org: Warum wählen Sie den Begriff „Faschisierung“ statt Faschismus?

Simon Strick: Die Rede vom Faschismus impliziert meistens Umschlagpunkte – der Faschismus droht irgendwann, man warnt also davor. Darum dreht sich unser Diskurs nun schon seit einigen Jahren.

Wenn man immer darauf wartet, dass der Faschismus irgendwann kommt, verpasst man die vielen faschistischen Entwicklungen, die die ganze Zeit stattfinden.

Mir geht es daher konkret um einen gesamtgesellschaftlichen Prozess der Faschisierung, der sich fortwährend vollzieht.

netzpolitik.org: Wie sieht dieser Prozess aus?

Simon Strick: Er hat viele Formen. Ich untersuche vor allem eine Umformung des politischen Diskurses und der Öffentlichkeit, die sich im Netz beziehungsweise durch die digitalen Medien ereignet hat.

Es gibt Mechanismen, Prozesse und Dynamiken, die genuin mit digitalen Medien zusammenhängen und die ich als Faschisierung einordne.

Die kollektive Praxis des Einübens

netzpolitik.org: Sie sprechen hier auch von einer kollektiven Praxis des Einübens.

Simon Strick: Dem Philosophen Pierre Zaoui zufolge gibt es so etwas wie eine faschistische Alltagssprache, die vor der offiziellen Sprache des Faschismus liegt. Sie zeichnet sich dadurch aus, dass man sich von der kleinsten Irritation bis zur Vernichtung einer Menschengruppe quasi durchargumentieren kann.

Diese Alltagssprache findet sich oft in der Kommunikation im Netz. Je nach Plattform oder Kommunikationszirkel haben sich Nutzer daran gewöhnt, sich mittels Memes und Sprache sehr schnell von kleinsten Irritationen hin zur Abwertung oder gar Auslöschungswunsch einer anderen Gruppe zu bewegen.

Das ist das Entscheidende am Begriff der Faschisierung: Es geht nicht um Einzelfälle, die irgendetwas kippen lassen, sondern um einen breiten gesellschaftlichen und vor allem medial bedingten Prozess des gemeinsamen Einübens oder eben der Normalisierung.

netzpolitik.org: Haben Sie dafür ein Beispiel?

Simon Strick: 2019 wurde im Internetforum 4chan die Zeichnung eines Clowns veröffentlicht. Sie zeigt eine Variation des Alt-Right-Symbols Pepe the Frog mit Regenbogenperücke und roter Nase. Ein Nutzer schlug vor, das Bild als neues rechtsradikales Symbol zu übernehmen, queerfeindliche Gewaltfantasien inklusive. Der Verfassungsschutz nahm es in seinen Bericht über rechtsextreme Symbolik auf.

Aus dem Bild entstand das Meme „Clownwelt“, wurde mit der Zeit zu einem Symbol im rechten Kulturkampf, schließlich zum allgemeinverständlichen reaktionären Symbol. Im deutschsprachigen Raum steht es unter anderem dafür, dass Regenbogenfahnen verschwinden sollen, damit Schwarz-Rot-Gold wieder zu seinem Recht kommt.

–––

Gegen Ausweiskontrollen im Netz. 
Wir kämpfen für ein offenes Internet. Das geht nur mit deiner Unterstützung.

–––

Dieser Antagonismus von Nationalfarben und LGBTQ+ ist völlig alltäglich geworden, Bundestagspräsidentin Julia Klöckner nutzte ihn im Sommer 2025 in der sogenannten Fahndendebatte. Sie ordnete an, Regenbogenfahnen aus Abgeordnetenbüros zu entfernen. Auch Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz kommentierte die Debatte: Der Bundestag sei kein Zirkuszelt, auf das man beliebig Fahnen hissen könnte – das Bild queerer Menschen als Clowns schien durch.

Das Beispiel ist etwas verkürzt, zeigt aber zwei Dinge: Als rechtsextrem kategorisierte Memes wie „Clownwelt“ finden Eingang in offizielles Sprechen und prägen Shitstorms wie den um Merz’ „Zirkuszelt“ mit. Und zweitens: Wenn der Kanzler rechtsextreme Memes variiert, dann ist der Begriff „Extremismus“ nicht mehr aussagekräftig. Eher geht es darum zu fragen, warum 4chan und Kanzleramt gleichklingend und queerfeindlich sprechen. Diese eingeübten „Gleichklänge“ der Radikalisierung beschreibe ich als Faschisierung, und Beispiele dafür sind jeden Tag sichtbar.

Simon Strick: Faschisierung. Fluchtlinie des Digitalen, Suhrkamp Verlag.

„Faschisierung und Digitalisierung sind verschwistert“

netzpolitik.org: Faschisierung und Digitalisierung hängen eng zusammen, schreiben Sie, sie seien „verschwistert“. Wie meinen Sie das?

Simon Strick: Wir hatten in den 1990er-Jahren eine historisch interessante Konstellation: Es bildete sich der Rechtspopulismus als Bewegungsprojekt quer zu staatlichen Systemen und Parteienstrukturen heraus, ich skizziere das im Buch für die USA. Gleichzeitig entsteht mit einem ganz ähnlichen Anspruch – quer zur Öffentlichkeit und zu den Leitmedien – die Netzkultur.

Aus meiner Sicht gibt es hier eine mythologische Übereinstimmung, die zu einer inneren Wesensverwandtschaft einiger digitaler Medien und reaktionärer Bewegungen führte: Beide verstanden sich als radikale Alternativen zum Status quo, als neue Ideen politischer Öffentlichkeit. Faschisierung bietet eine Möglichkeit, um diese Wesensverwandtschaft zu verstehen und zu beschreiben.

netzpolitik.org: Für viele war das Netz gerade in seinen Anfängen ein Raum für Gleichheit, Partizipation und Utopie. Scheren Sie mit Digitalität und Rechtspopulismus nicht zwei sehr verschiedene Dinge über einen Kamm?

Simon Strick: Das Netz ist natürlich ein pluralistischer Raum. Und im politischen Raum der 90er-Jahre gab es unterschiedliche Bewegungen, die eine grundlegende Veränderung etwa an Regierungssystemen oder am Neoliberalismus verlangten. Der Rechtspopulismus, wie Murray Rothbard ihn entwirft, war eine dieser Bewegungen.

Analog dazu findet sich in der „Unabhängigkeitserklärung des Cyberspace“ von John Perry Barlow eine populistische Vorstellung des Internets: Gegen Großunternehmen, Telekommunikationskonzerne und Regierungsorgane soll ein utopisches Land errichtet werden. Die Anhänger dieser Idee verstanden den Cyberspace explizit als Gegenentwurf zu den Regierungen der analogen Welt, den „müden Riesen aus Fleisch und Stahl“.

Dieser Cyberlibertarismus war eine spezifische Ausprägung im Pluralismus des frühen Netzes. Er brachte aber eine Art reaktionäres Nutzungsszenario für digitale Medien mit: Im Internet sagt man das, was draußen in den Leitmedien angeblich verboten oder nicht präsent ist. Man postet sozusagen immer quer zu einer Hegemonie, was zum Beispiel neofaschistischen Gruppen sehr entgegenkam, die auch zu den Netzpionieren gehörten.

Aus dieser Grundmythologie entwickelte sich – begünstigt durch die sozialen Medien – das Netz als Gegenöffentlichkeit und begünstigte damit vor allem reaktionäre Projekte. Die Alternativmedien wie Nius und Tichys Einblick oder zahllose Angebote auf X senden alle auf dieser Mythologie digitaler Dissidenz. Die Leitmedien folgen nach.

„Wir befinden uns dauerhaft im Reaktionsmodus“

netzpolitik.org: Wie haben die sozialen Medien diese Entwicklung beeinflusst?

Simon Strick: Soziale Medien sind darauf ausgerichtet, Ereignisse herzustellen, auf die man reagieren kann. Nutzer liken, kommentieren und befinden sich dauerhaft im Reaktionsmodus auf ihre Timeline. Das heißt erstens, dass Politik als Ereignis stattfinden muss. Und zweitens müssen politische Ereignisse möglichst kontrovers oder provokativ sein, um mehr Reaktionen hervorzurufen.

Das Problem ist also nicht nur Rechtspopulismus, sondern eine Öffentlichkeit, die um das Prinzip Reaktionsmaximierung herum gebaut ist. Parteien, die am krassesten agieren – was oftmals rechte Parteien sind –, politische Figuren, die am lautesten reagieren. Das erhält die größte Aufmerksamkeit.

Parteien und Journalismus passen sich diesen digitalen Reaktionsformen an. Ich fand den Protest der SPD-Bundestagsfraktion auf dem Bebelplatz in Berlin dazu aufschlussreich.

netzpolitik.org: …dem Ort der Bücherverbrennung durch die Nazis im Jahr 1933.

Simon Strick: Ja, hier wurde das politische Ereignis „Antifaschismus“ von einer Regierungspartei hergestellt, für „Reaction Content“. Reaktionen kamen sofort, sowohl skandalisierend als auch nach dem Motto „Endlich tut sich was!“. Passiert war im Grunde genommen nichts, außer einem Flashmob mit Kamerabegleitung.

„Memes transportieren Vernichtungsfantasien“

netzpolitik.org: Welche Rolle spielen Memes bei dieser Neuformierung der Öffentlichkeit?

Simon Strick: Ich halte sie für unheimlich wichtig. Memes sind nicht nur lustige Bildchen, sondern spezifische Verschaltungen von Informationen, die vor allem irritieren und affektiv wirken sollen.

Es werden Dinge zusammengebracht, die eigentlich nicht zusammengehören, um einen Witz oder eine Irritation zu erzeugen. Das ist eine grundlegende Kulturtechnik im Social-Media-Zeitalter: Informationskombination, um affektiv den Informationsfluss zu unterbrechen. Als Grundprinzip digitaler Kommunikation wird das aus meiner Sicht unterbewertet.

–––

Die Arbeit von netzpolitik.org finanziert sich aus den Spenden unserer Leser:innen. 
Unterstütze auch du unseren gemeinwohlorientierten, werbe- und trackingfreien Journalismus. Spende jetzt..

–––

Politische Akteure wie Donald Trump oder auch das Weiße Haus kommunizieren in Memes. Auch die SPD-Aktion am Bebelplatz kann man als memetische Operation verstehen, die Unzusammenhängendes verbindet, um eine Irritation oder Affekt zu erreichen: Regierungspartei kämpft als Antifa gegen die NSDAP. Modernes Branding, vorbei an politischen Realitäten.

netzpolitik.org: Sie schreiben in Ihrem Buch, dass Memes auch das Aussprechen von Vernichtungsfantasien erleichtern.

Simon Strick: Dafür gibt es viele Beispiele. Ein Beispiel, das ich im Buch beschreibe: Queere Menschen setzen sich unter anderem für palästinensische Unabhängigkeit ein. Das Motto „Queers for Palestine“ wurde im Netz mit „Chicken for KFC“ gleichgesetzt, nach dem Motto: Weil Gaza angeblich in Gänze Hamas und queerfeindlich sei, sind „Queers for Palestine“ wie Hühner, die für ihre Schlachtung durch Kentucky Fried Chicken demonstrieren.

Diese Formel verbreitete sich rasant, weil sie sowohl Palästinenser als brutale Barbaren als auch Queers als irrational und naiv darstellt. Beide Minderheiten hätten sich quasi „verdient“. Im Buch zeichne ich nach, wie dieses Meme vor und nach dem 7. Oktober 2023 in den Legitimationsdiskursen zur israelischen Kriegseskalation immer wieder auftaucht. 

Völlig verschiedene Akteure kommen dabei zum Gleichklang: anonyme Onlinetrolle, die AfD-Abgeordnete Beatrix von Storch, die Schriftstellerin Herta Müller, der ehemalige Antisemitismus-Beauftragte Felix Klein und auch Benjamin Netanjahu, der „Chicken for KFC“ vor dem US-Senat als Witz anbringt.

Solche Memes transportieren Entmenschlichungs- und Vernichtungsfantasien fast von selbst weiter, selbst wenn die einzelnen Sprecher:innen das nicht beabsichtigen. Sind Queers so naiv, sollten sie abgeschlachtet werden. Sind Palästinenser solche Barbaren, muss die Vernichtung Gazas eskaliert werden. Es bilden sich memetische Kollektive, die sich gegenseitig darin bestärken, solche Sprach- oder Memefantasien als Legitimation zu nehmen, als Argument, schließlich als Vorlage für Handlungen.

Die Dynamik der Eskalation

netzpolitik.org: Besonders Donald Trump hat die Wirkweise der Memes offenbar verstanden.

Simon Strick: Trumps Kommunikation und Stil sind sehr interessant. Sie zeigen sehr klar, wie sich politische Öffentlichkeit in digitale Räume verlagert, wo andere Gesetze gelten als zuvor. Der Trumpismus kann als Politikstil gelesen werden, der sich mehr und mehr nach Netzlogiken richtet: Trolling, Irritation, Memes und ganz generell „Content“.

Trump ist die ideale Figur für diesen Transfer, weil er selbst hochgradig Meme-tauglich ist. Seit den 80er-Jahren ist er eine Ikone der amerikanischen Popkultur, jeder kennt ihn. 

Bei ihm zeigt sich eine neue Form des Regierens, die vor allem memetisch und digital kommuniziert und die Regierungsgeschäfte auf Plattformen abwickelt. Etwa wenn Trump geopolitische Entscheidungen direkt über soziale Medien verkündet. Der Wahrheitsgehalt ist immer unklar – wie bei jeder Online-Information.

netzpolitik.org: Memes selbst bewirken aber keine materiellen Veränderungen. Sie stoppen beispielsweise keine Inflation. Läuft die memetische Kommunikation nicht irgendwann ins Leere?

Simon Strick: Jetzt könnte man lange über Börsen reden, die ja aufgrund von Gerüchten extrem materielle Wertschöpfungs- oder Wertvernichtungsprozesse ins Werk setzen können. Aber das nur am Rande. 

Memetische Politik bietet in materieller Hinsicht natürlich schon etwas. Zum einen geht Faschisierung oft einher mit persönlicher Bereicherung, Oligarchie und Macht, die sich durch eine Kapitalisierung der Aufmerksamkeit ergeben kann. Das zeigt Trump eindrücklich, und Elon Musk hat neofaschistische Memes zum Markenkern von X.com gemacht.

Andererseits ist das „Leere“ im Netz kein Problem, es lebt von Hype Cycles, Aufregungspunkten oder Ereignissen, die nicht unbedingt „real“ sein müssen. Bei dem, was ich Faschisierung nenne, speist sich der Prozess aus einer Dynamik der Reaktion und Eskalation. Sie produziert ständig neues Reaktionsmaterial, das die Dynamik weiter antreibt. Autoren wie Lucie Varga, Leo Löwenthal oder Walter Benjamin haben übrigens Ähnliches für faschistische Propaganda der 1920er- bis 1940er-Jahre konstatiert: Die Inhalte oder die Ideologie sind fast beliebig, die Dynamik des Reaktionären und das gemeinsame Phantasma sind wichtiger.

netzpolitik.org: Wir müssen uns die Faschisierung also wie ein Perpetuum mobile vorstellen?

Simon Strick: Zumindest als etwas, das eine starke Eigendynamik hat, die sich immer weiter selbst antreibt. Das ist mein Vorschlag, um zu erklären, warum große Teile der politischen Öffentlichkeit sich mitreißen lassen, die nicht ohne weiteres als rechtsextrem klassifizierbar sind. Im Buch nenne ich das: Es gibt mehr Faschisierung als es Faschisten gibt. Aus meiner Sicht ist das ein massives Problem unserer Gegenwart.

–––

Deine Spende für digitale Freiheitsrechte 
Wir berichten über aktuelle netzpolitische Entwicklungen, decken Skandale auf und stoßen Debatten an. Dabei sind wir vollkommen unabhängig. Denn unser Kampf für digitale Freiheitsrechte finanziert sich aus den Spenden unserer Leser:innen. Jetzt spenden.

items.articleBody:
arXiv:2610.20667v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Rapid advances in AI capabilities are causing benchmarks to saturate. Once several models approach perfect scores, a benchmark loses its power to differentiate between them, and with it its utility for informing AI safety cases and frontier policies. Yet benchmark items produce far more information than the scores we typically extract from them: a full transcript of how each model solved the task. We investigate whether these transcripts can be used to assess model capabilities even after benchmark scores have saturated. We simulate saturation retrospectively using historical benchmark and model releases, and test whether protocols that access only correctly solved transcripts from saturated benchmarks can predict capabilities measured on held-out, unsaturated items. We evaluate representative contemporary approaches for extracting information from model transcripts: pairwise judging, single-transcript absolute scoring, and predictions from deterministic transcript features or embeddings. We find that saturated transcripts retain capability information beyond benchmark accuracy. Amongst our evaluated protocols, pairwise judging performs best, reducing prediction error by 5.3 times compared to a baseline using only saturated benchmark scores. This capability-relevant information is distributed across transcript sections, but concentrated in specific channels of information such as reasoning and tool-calls. However, the predictive power of protocols does not always generalise across distribution shifts -- for example by underestimating the capabilities of the first reasoning models introduced in early 2025. Saturated benchmarks thus retain capability-predicting signal in their task transcripts, but extending the lifetime of existing benchmarks requires methods designed to extract these signals robustly.

items.articleBody:
By Meetups Czar Skyler:

There are two laws of the ACX Meetup Czar. First, that there are a lot of ACX meetup groups. Second, that there are not enough ACX meetup groups. 

Twice a year, Scott advertises upcoming meetups and makes a bigger deal about it than usual. Throughout the year his meetup czar (that’s me, Skyler!) gets emails from people moving to a new city wondering if there’s an ACX group there. So the twice a year Times & Places posts are a helpful chance to check for signs of life and get an update on the local meetup communities. But the most important part is coordination.

If you only go to one ACX meetup a year, we suggest you go to the fall ACX Everywhere in your city. That way if there was secretly a dozen of you all making the assumption that you were the only reader in the area, you could all show up at the fall meetup and realize the conspiracy was larger than you thought. And in fact many local ACX groups got their start by just such a rallying flag. A few were even started by a traveling reader who volunteered to run a meetup in a city they didn’t live in, but locals showed up, took the banner, and kept the meetup going.

This year we have meetups planned in over a hundred and eighty cities, from Aachen, Germany to Zagreb, Croatia. Thanks to all the organizers who are putting on the individual meetups, and thank you Scott for supporting these meetups! 

You can find the list below, in the following order:

Africa & Middle East

Asia-Pacific (Including Australia)

Europe (including the UK)

North America & Central America

South America

Online

There should shortly be a map of these meetups on the LessWrong community page.

Within each region it’s alphabetized first by country then by city - so the first entry in Europe is Zagreb, Croatia. The exception is the USA, where they’re also alphabetized by state - so the first entry in the USA is Phoenix, Arizona.

I’ll provisionally be attending the Boston, Burlington, and Oxford meetups. Scott will provisionally be attending the San Francisco meetup.

Extra Info For Potential Attendees

If you’re reading this* you’re invited. Please don’t feel like you “won’t be welcome” just because you’re new to the blog, demographically different from the average reader, or have never agreed with Scott Alexander once and have fought with Scott on like seventy-five different fronts. (The * is if you’ve specifically been told by the organizers (local or global) you’re banned from attending.)

You don’t have to RSVP or contact the organizer to be able to attend (unless the event description says otherwise!) RSVPs are mostly to give organizers a better sense of how many people might show up, and to let them tell you if there are last-minute changes.

If you have any feedback on the meetup (compliments, complaints, ancestral curses, etc) the feedback form is here: https://tinyurl.com/acx-meetup-survey 

Extra Advice For Meetup Organizers:

If you’re at a park or cafe or somewhere like that, I suggest you bring a sign that says “ACX MEETUP” and prop it up somewhere. If you’re in an apartment, put the sign on the door. People can feel anxious walking up to clumps asking if this is the ACX group.

Bring blank labels and sharpies for nametags. People will remember and use each other’s names a lot more if they have the reminder. You can also suggest people write a topic they want to talk about under their name on the name tag.

If you or anyone else in your city wants to run followup meetups, have people type their name and email address in a Google Form or spreadsheet. It’s easy to make a QR code or bit.ly link to make sharing the form easier. 

If it’s the first meetup, people usually just want to talk. If you want to do workshops or reading groups or the like, followup meetups tend to work better for that. If nobody’s talking, try asking people about recent ACX essays or book reviews they liked. Your attendees probably like ACX, so you have something in common!

If you didn’t make a LessWrong event for your meetup (or if you did but I either didn’t know about it or goofed up the crossposter) I made one for you. If you aren’t already a coorganizer on it and you want to be, send me a LessWrong dm and I’ll fix that. 

If you need to change a meetup date or you have any other questions about meetups, please email skyler[at]rationalitymeetups[period]org to get in touch with me.

items.title: The Other Significant Others: Living and Loving Outside the Confines of Conventional Friendship and Compulsory Coupledom
items.subtitle:
“While we weaken friendships by expecting too little of them, we undermine romantic relationships by expecting too much of them.”

We move through…
items.feedText: We label, we classify, we contain — that is how we parse the maelstrom of experience into meaning. It is a useful impulse — without it, there would be no science or storytelling, no taxonomies and theorems, no poems and plots. It is also a limiting one — the most beautiful, rewarding, and transformative experiences in life transcend the categories our culture has created to contain the chaos of consciousness, nowhere more so than in the realm of relationships — those mysterious benedictions that bridge the abyss…
items.articleBody:
“While we weaken friendships by expecting too little of them, we undermine romantic relationships by expecting too much of them.”

We move through the world largely unaware that our emotions are made of concepts — the brain’s coping mechanism for the blooming buzzing confusion of what we are. We label, we classify, we contain — that is how we parse the maelstrom of experience into meaning. It is a useful impulse — without it, there would be no science or storytelling, no taxonomies and theorems, no poems and plots. It is also a limiting one — the most beautiful, rewarding, and transformative experiences in life transcend the categories our culture has created to contain the chaos of consciousness, nowhere more so than in the realm of relationships — those mysterious benedictions that bridge the abyss between one consciousness and another. 

When we hollow the word friend by overuse and misuse, when we make of love a contract with prescribed roles and rigid, impossible expectations, we become prisoners of our own concepts. The history of feeling is the history of labels too small to contain the loves of which we are capable — varied and vigorously transfigured from one kind into another and back again. It takes both great courage and great vulnerability to live outside concepts, to meet each new experience, each new relationship, each new emotional landscape on its own terms and let it in turn expand the terms of living. 

Art by Sophie Blackall from Things to Look Forward to

That is what Rhaina Cohen explores in The Other Significant Others: Reimagining Life with Friendship at the Center (public library) — a journalistic investigation of the vast yet invisible world of unclassifiable intimate relationships, profiling pairs of people across various circumstances and stages of life sustained by such bonds, people who have “redrawn the borders of friendship, moving the lines further and further outward to encompass more space in each other’s lives,” people who have found themselves in finding each other. 

What emerges through this portrait of a type of relationship “hidden in plain sight” is an antidote to the tyranny of the “one-stop-shop coupledom ideal” and “an invitation to expand what options are open to us,” radiating a reminder that we pay a price for living by our culture’s standard concepts:

While we weaken friendships by expecting too little of them, we undermine romantic relationships by expecting too much of them.

A generation after Andrew Sullivan celebrated the rewards of friendship in a culture obsessed with romance, Cohen writes:

This is a book about friends who have become a we, despite having no scripts, no ceremonies, and precious few models to guide them toward long-term platonic commitment. These are friends who have moved together across states and continents. They’ve been their friend’s primary caregiver through organ transplants and chemotherapy. They’re co-parents, co-homeowners, and executors of each other’s wills. They belong to a club that has no name or membership form, often unaware that there are others like them. They fall under the umbrella of what Eli Finkel, a psychology professor at Northwestern University, calls “other significant others.” Having eschewed a more typical life setup, these friends confront hazards and make discoveries they wouldn’t have otherwise.

Illustration by Maurice Sendak from a vintage ode to friendship by Janice May Udry

Noting that her interest in the subject is more than theoretical, catalyzed by her own expansive relationship with another woman in parallel with her marriage, Cohen considers these category-defying bonds as a countercultural act of courage and resistance:

I began to see how these unusual relationships can also be a provocation — unsettling the set of societal tenets that circumscribe our intimate lives: That the central and most important person in one’s life should be a romantic partner, and friends are the supporting cast. That romantic love is the real thing, and if people claim they feel strong platonic love, it must not really be platonic. That adults who raise kids together should be having sex with each other, and marriage deserves special treatment by the state.

With an eye to the long lineage of people who have defied the categories of their time and place — the kinds of people populating Figuring, which I wrote largely to explore such relationships — she adds:

Challenging these social norms is not new, nor are platonic partners the only dissidents. People who are feminists, queer, trans, of color, nonmonogamous, single, asexual, aromantic, celibate, or who live communally have been questioning these ideas for decades, if not centuries. All have offered counterpoints to what Eleanor Wilkinson, a professor at the University of Southampton, calls compulsory coupledom: the notion that a long-term monogamous romantic relationship is necessary for a normal, successful adulthood. This is a riff on the feminist writer Adrienne Rich’s influential concept of “compulsory heterosexuality” — the idea, enforced through social pressure and practical incentives, that the only normal and acceptable romantic relationship is between a man and a woman. Some of the first stories we hear as children instill compulsory coupledom, equating characters finding their “one true love” with living “happily ever after.”

[…]

It can be confusing to live in the gulf between the life you have and the life you believe you’re supposed to be living.

In the remainder of The Other Significant Others, Cohen relays the stories of people who have sliced through the confusion to build lives that serve them through tailor-made relationships that reward the deepest and truest parts of them, relationships that reimagine what it means to love and be loved, to see and be seen — relationships like those of Rachel Carson and Dorothy Freeman, Clara Schumann and Johannes Brahms, Ralph Waldo Emerson and Margaret Fuller. 

Complement it with poet and philosopher David Whyte on love and resisting the tyranny of relationship labels, then revisit Coleridge on the paradox of friendship and romantic love.

donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation. Your support makes all the difference.

items.articleBody:
Artavazd Pelechian said his piece, and his admirers have waited decades for the world to take notice. The Armenian filmmaker, active primarily during the Soviet era, has a concise oeuvre: 13 works, mostly shorts, with two features that barely crack an hour. Aside from 2019’s Nature, he has not released anything since 1994. International recognition came gradually, but it has grown enough that many of his films have received 4K restorations that premiered at different festivals over 2026. Recently, the Pelechian Project was showcased at the New York Film Festival (NYFF), with eight of the director’s restored works in the program.

At the storied All-Union State Institute of Cinematography in Moscow in the 1960s, Pelechian and his peers studied the work of titanic Soviet directors like Sergei Eisenstein, Vsevolod Pudovkin, and Dziga Vertov, who shaped cinematography and editing in cinema’s early days. Pelechian deviated from their example, developing an approach he described as “distance montage.” All his movies are montage-based, with intricate shot assemblages unified by distinct themes. Speaking with Scott MacDonald in the 1990s, Pelechian explained the distinction between distance montage and the familiar notion of a montage: 
In Eisenstein, every element means something. For me, the individual fragments don’t mean anything anymore. Only the whole film has the meaning. … Eisenstein saw editing as a means to get from here to there, [whereas] I see editing as a means for seeing where we are.Still from The Seasons (1975), directed by Artavazd Pelechian

items.articleBody:
Hi,

My latest album, Flower Blocks, was out last week with Dustopian Frequencies - a small tape label based in the UK. It’s about taking the small and appreciating what can be found there.

The majority of the sounds are from the Ciat Lonbarde Clicker and Tetrax Organ. There is also a small Serge system on a few tracks. I’ve always been drawn to small sounds and trying to do a lot with them, see also Piano at 51°40’49.6"N 2°14’09.2"W which used a single recording of a broken piano. Flower Blocks is, in a way an extension of that idea, but with a different sound palette.

Each track on Flower Blocks is named after a stage of the life cycle of a seed, and hopefully some of the beauty and brutality of that process comes through - either way, I’m hugely proud of how it’s turned out, helped no doubt by the wonderful artwork from illustrator Alex Dimond.

items.articleBody:
Steve Newman at Second Thoughts:

Anthropic’s engineering team just dropped a fascinating post: Redesigning source control at Anthropic. It describes a major engineering project undertaken in a jaw-droppingly short period of time. My Twitter feed is awash in breathless reports of miracles accomplished overnight using coding agents, but this project stands out as a well-documented example of serious engineering that takes full advantage of the latest tools. AI coding tools are no longer limited to vibe-coding lightweight apps; they are revolutionizing the craft of building large-scale, mission-critical distributed systems.

Any serious software development effort revolves around a “source code control system”. This is sort of like Google Drive, but specialized to store program code instead of documents and spreadsheets.

At Anthropic, like many tech companies, the entire company works in a single system, called the “monorepo”. Anthropic used the industry-standard solution, named “git”, to manage their monorepo. Git is a widely respected tool, serving millions of developers, but it was buckling under the strain of Anthropic’s rapidly accelerating engineering velocity…

More here.

items.articleBody:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve.  

—Michal Luria, Aliya Bhatia, and Danah Boyd

Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds. 

The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15.

But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented. 

Here’s what we ought to do instead to keep kids safe. 

Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered.

—Jessica Hamzelou

I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat. What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing. I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset. I made posters. We never found her. I was devastated.

Almost 30 years later, pet owners have an expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions. The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics. But is that a good thing?

Read the full story on the promises and pitfalls of pet life extension.

This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday.

10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Form Energy and its iron batteries

Form Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.

As wind and solar power grow, utilities need cheaper ways to store electricity for longer periods. Form Energy aims to meet that need with batteries that can store energy for 100 hours.

The company has developed a new type of battery using iron, a far more abundant and cheaper metal than those used in many existing batteries. It uses a process that Form calls “reversible rusting,” in which iron turns to rust as the battery discharges and back to iron when it charges.

See how Form Energy hopes to make renewable power more reliable.

—Jonathan W. Rosen

Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch, spanning everything from electric buses to portable rubber dams.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Insurance is the next big obstacle for AI 
AI companies are racking up billions of dollars of legal liabilities from the damage their products cause. (WSJ $)
+ The FTC has sent subpoenas to OpenAI and Anthropic over consumer harms. (Axios)
+ AI hacks leave a mess, and AI companies still aren’t cleaning them up. (Wired $)
+ Who’s liable when AI agents go rogue? (MIT Technology Review)

2 A Russian drone entered NATO waters for the first time
Attacks like those near Bulgaria and Romania are spurring requests for better defenses. (Ars Technica)

3 An AI sell-off has rattled global markets
Many are questioning the sustainability of demand for data centers. (Reuters $)
+ Anthropic reported slowing growth in its latest quarterly results. (FT $)
+ Accenture has told employees they can only spend $29 on Claude each month. (404 Media)
+ What’s at stake in AI’s trillion-dollar gamble. (MIT Technology Review)

4 Governments are hacking people with ‘zero click’ spyware 
Delivered through millions of innocuous-looking online adverts. (TechCrunch)
+ Criminals stole $90 million from crypto wallets last week in a highly sophisticated hack. (FT $)

5 Big Tech gave Trump $92 million for his ballroom 
Meanwhile the president himself won’t be spending a dime. (WP $)

6 Celebrity deepfakes are everywhere now
And they’re selling you stuff the actual celebrity has probably never even heard of. (The Verge $)
+ Weaponized deepfakes have been on the rise for a while. (MIT Technology Review)

7 Can AI lighten parents’ mental load?
It seems apps and agents can help—if you agree to share masses of your data. (NYT $)
+ AI agents are a privacy nightmare. (The Verge $)

8 The memory shortage’s latest victim is schools
It’s becoming prohibitively expensive to equip students with laptops and tablets. (The Atlantic $)

9 The world’s official timekeepers have agreed to ditch the leap second 
It’s a move that ought to cut the risk of time-based computer glitches. (The Guardian)

10 Tesla has finally unveiled its flying car 
It’s taken a decade to get here—and still won’t even be shipping next year. (CNBC)

Quote of the day

“Tech companies used to make an effort to support women…Now we’ve swung completely in the opposite direction. Supporting women in tech has become controversial. It’s become political. It’s become risky.”

—Startup founder Sara Mauskopt explains why the cancellation of the Grace Hopper Celebration, one of the biggest gatherings of women in tech, hits so hard, Bloomberg reports. 

One More Thing

SIMON MITCHELL

Inside the experimental world of animal infrastructure

In the mid-2000s, toads were meeting a gruesome end near Ede, a leafy old town in the Netherlands. Residents responded by building wildlife tunnels beneath the road to help them reach their breeding ponds safely.

The crossings became popular. But a few years later, researchers found the local toad population had crashed from more than 10,000 to fewer than 1,000.

The case reflects a wider global push to build wildlife crossings and other forms of “animal infrastructure.” But do they actually help animal populations recover? Read the full story to find out.

—Matthew PonsfordWe can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

+ Check out this podcast about the incredible, mysterious powers of fungi.
+ A four-year-old boy’s simple habit of waving to his neighbors is transforming his community.
+ From treehouses to geodesic domes, these homes show what happens when people build outside the rules.
+ Remember when the internet was made by people? The Museum of the Human Web is a playful archive of that era.

 💰 Anthropic's revenue rises 45% in Q3 LINK
Anthropic told investors on Wednesday that its revenue climbed nearly 50% in the third quarter, reaching $16.8 billion, up from $11.5 billion the quarter before and $4.8 billion early in the year.

The company earned $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on computing power during the quarter, with adjusted operating margins, which leave out stock-based pay, coming in at 11%.

Anthropic also cut back sharply on "distillation," where rival labs train their models on its outputs, a practice that brought in 5% to 7% of revenue but which it reduced in the third quarter.
 🕵️ Spyware infects phones through online ads LINK
Citizen Lab found spyware called "AdFection" that hijacks phones and computers through online ad networks, infecting devices simply by showing an ad, with no click or download needed from the victim.

The tool, built by Israeli firm Discover-Tech, abused the real-time bidding system that places targeted ads to identify specific users, then hid malware inside normal-looking ads aimed at journalists, NATO, the European Commission, NVIDIA and Arm.

Discover-Tech reportedly ran 442 million ads across over 120,000 sites, including the BBC and New York Times, plus apps like Duolingo and Grindr; Google has since blocked the firm from its ad platforms.
 🏦 Bank of America hires 1,000 to fix AI-found flaws LINK
Bank of America brought on 1,000 contractors this year to patch software flaws surfaced by Anthropic's Mythos model, adding them to the 3,000 staff already working on security, CEO Brian Moynihan told analysts on Wednesday.

Moynihan said the bank spent a "couple hundred million plus" in the third quarter on the patching work and on anti-money-laundering compliance, but he expects that spending to fall once the backlog of fixes clears.

Anthropic released Mythos in April to a limited group of banks, tech firms and government bodies, prompting U.S. lenders to fix hundreds to thousands of flaws within days, most rated low to moderate in severity.
 ⚖️ OpenAI alleges ex-employee took ‘highly confidential’ device files to Apple LINK
OpenAI has accused a former staffer who joined Apple of sending more than 100 files about an unreleased product to a personal account, then presenting that work to senior Apple leaders months ago, according to a new court filing.

In the San Jose federal filing, OpenAI said it worries its trade secrets are now spreading inside Apple, pointing to this week's release of Apple's HomeView product, and warned it may file a countersuit over the claim.

Apple said it has rules to stop new hires from using former employers' confidential information and found no evidence backing the claim; the dispute, which delayed a showdown set for yesterday, is likely to reach trial in October 2027.
 🐝 Amazon launches two AI wearables LINK
Amazon's Bee has rolled out its first products since the takeover last year: the $74.99 Bee Frontier, a wrist- or clothing-worn device, and the $99.99 Bee Eclipse, a credit-card-sized gadget that sticks to the back of your phone.

Both devices listen to your daily conversations and turn them into notes, summaries, and to-dos, offering 14 days of free memory, while an $11.99-a-month Bee Pro plan adds unlimited recaps, a chat assistant, and app connections.

Bee says raw audio is processed live and then deleted, with transcripts encrypted using keys your device controls, so even Amazon staff can't read them unless you choose to share; the Frontier also lasts up to seven days per charge.
 💥 Eight states sue OpenAI over harm to kids LINK
Eight states, Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska, West Virginia, Arkansas, Arizona, Idaho and Montana, sued OpenAI yesterday, accusing the company of lying to parents about ChatGPT's safety and rushing the chatbot to market while knowing it harmed children.

Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said ChatGPT coached users toward suicide, gave dangerous medical advice that in one case led a Texas teen to fatally overdose, and let rogue AI agents illegally hack into other companies.

Filed under each state's consumer protection laws, the suits argue ChatGPT's agreeable design makes vulnerable users depend on it; OpenAI responded that it built age-specific protections, parental controls and break reminders, and last month added a restricted mode for teens aged 13 to 18.

items.articleBody:
Federico Veronesi received the top honor of the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year for his poignant black-and-white image of a female elephant carrying her deceased calf. The portrait represents a rare insight into animals’ habits we have yet to fully understand and demonstrates the power of timing and persistence in photography.

Veronesi had been tracking elephants in the Huab River Valley of Namibia when he encountered some unusual drag marks on the earth. He eventually caught up with the family, and the adult emerged with the calf’s leg wedged between her trunk and tusk. “Behaviours centering on death have been observed in both Asian and African elephants, including vocalisations, guarding the dead, inspecting and handling bones, and carrying the deceased,” a statement says. “Some researchers suggest these behaviours could indicate an elephant’s journey to understanding death, while others interpret these actions as possible displays of grief.”

Federico Veronesi (Italy), “The Aftermath.” Winner, Wildlife Photographer of the Year and Behaviour: Mammals category. An elephant carries a dead calf in a rare glimpse into complex animal behaviours

Additional winners include Kutub Uddin’s capture of elegant slime molds, Loren Elliott’s portfolio featuring the coyotes of San Francisco, and Amelie Davis’ portrait of a bee coming in for a landing on a flower in Surrey, England, in the 10 and Under category. “This year’s winning photographs demonstrate the extraordinary power of wildlife photography to help us see nature differently,” says Dr. Doug Gurr, Director of the Natural History Museum. “Together they remind us that every species plays a role in the complex web of life, and why understanding and protecting the natural world has never been more important.”

At 65,403 entries from photographers in 121 countries, this year’s competition saw the largest turnout of submissions in its 62-year history. Categories run the gamut of photojournalism, wetlands, plants and fungi, behavior, portfolios, youth categories, and more. The 100 top images from this year’s contest go on view tomorrow, October 16, at the Natural History Museum in London, where they’ll be exhibited through July 11, 2027. 

Francisco Negroni (Chile), “Warning Sign.” Winner, Photojournalism category. The photographer captures this scene of a dead puma amid the rugged, windswept beauty of Argentine Patagonia

Kutub Uddin (Bangladesh/U.K.), “Tiny Dancers,” from the ‘Secret Worlds’ portfolio. Winner, Portfolio Award. Fine threads, known as capillitium, emerge on the round, yellow-green bodies, which will eventually help disperse reproductive spores

James Lewin (U.K.), “The Meeting Place.” Winner, Animals in their Environment category. A young bull elephant sprays a group of zebra as they congregate in the Kenyan Chyulu Hills

Loren Elliott (U.S.), “On the Outskirts” from the ‘Wily Coyotes of San Francisco’ portfolio. Winner, Photojournalist Story Award. A coyote pads along a trail in Bernal Heights Park, overlooking the city and bay of San Francisco

Agorastos Papatsanis (Greece), “Shedding Light.” Winner, Plants and Fungi category. Ultraviolet light reveals the glowing yellow stems of bonnet mushrooms growing from a decaying log

Anton Sorokin (U.S.), “Protective Pose.” Winner, Behaviour: Amphibians and Reptiles category. A California newt lays its eggs as it clasps vegetation that already holds another newt’s egg clutch

Alex Visbal (Colombia), “The Great Divide.” Winner, Wetlands: The Bigger Picture category. A single engineered line reshapes an entire wetland

Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas (Germany), “Afternoon Snack,” from the ‘Hidden Depths’ portfolio. Winner, Rising Star Award. A robber fly impales a flesh fly with its needlelike mouthparts
