items.articleBody:
arXiv:2610.20669v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reward-guided discrete diffusion enables test-time alignment with downstream objectives, but applying Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) guidance at every denoising step is computationally expensive. Active guidance steps require additional reward evaluations and, for gradient-based proposals, value-gradient computations. Sparse guidance reduces this cost by guiding only a subset of timesteps, but commonly used schedules are fixed heuristics whose effectiveness can vary substantially across tasks. We propose VISTA, a training-free method that automatically selects guided timesteps under a fixed budget. VISTA formulates sparse guidance as approximation of the ideal full-guidance probability path and derives an estimable upper bound on \(\ell_1\) path deviation. Using value statistics collected from a small number of full-guidance warmup generations, VISTA optimizes the resulting empirical surrogate exactly via dynamic programming. The warmup generations can be retained as model outputs, and after schedule selection VISTA has the same per-generation guidance complexity as other sparse schedules with the same budget. Across text, biological sequence, and image generation tasks, VISTA discovers task-dependent schedules and outperforms hand-designed sparse schedules in most tested settings, while approaching or exceeding full-guidance performance on several task metrics. In toxic-text generation, for example, VISTA attains a 0.99 unique-toxic ratio compared with 1.00 for full guidance while reducing post-selection per-generation latency from 204.23 s to 38.16 s, a 5.35$\times$ speedup.

items.title: AI Safety Is Not A Corporate Plot
items.subtitle: AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI have long mentioned the possibility that their products could be existentially dangerous, but this has recen…

items.articleBody:
AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI have long mentioned the possibility that their products could be existentially dangerous, but this has recently crescendoed into even more dire warnings, including suggestions that we have to pace the frontier, ie coordinate to slow AI progress.

In response, cynical commentators have suggested this is a conspiracy to boost the companies’ stocks. The exact motives imputed vary from person to person. Some say the companies are hyping the product by talking about how dangerous it is; if AI is smart enough to kill all humans, it must be smart enough for your business workflow. Others say they’re trying to distract from near-term harms; every inch of newspaper space devoted to human extinction is one less inch that can be spent on plagiarism and water use. But the most popular story involves regulatory capture: if the product is unsafe, maybe it can only be trusted to a few big politically-connected companies, and everyone else should be banned.

Many debates about AI are complicated and hard to resolve, but this one isn’t: all of these stories are clearly false. Some evidence:

The AI experts who aren’t affiliated with big companies are just as concerned as the ones who are. 

The AI company leaders giving these warnings were giving the exact same warnings before they had AI companies - and in many cases, before they worked in the industry, or before the industry existed.

If these corporate plots were real, they would be incredibly dumb.

Taking these in order:

I. The AI Experts Who Aren’t Affiliated With Big Companies Are Just As Concerned As The Ones Who Are

Grace et al surveyed 1,580 AI researchers who presented papers at big AI-related conferences, mostly academics with no company affiliation. Over half thought there was at least a 10% chance AI would cause “human extinction or similarly permanent and severe disempowerment of the human species”. 72% said we needed to be prioritizing AI safety research more. This survey was in 2024; current numbers would probably be higher. 

Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, and Yann LeCunn are collectively considered “the godfathers of AI” for inventing deep learning; in 2018, they received the Turing Award, sometimes called the Nobel Prize of computer science, for their accomplishment. In 2023, Geoffrey Hinton quit his job at Google to work full-time raising awareness of the potential existential dangers of AI; he said there was “between 10% and 50% chance” that his invention would destroy humanity. In the same year, Yoshua Bengio also switched to activism, saying that he “regretted his life’s work” and that AI could have a “catastrophic impact”. Neither was affiliated with a major AI company.

(the third godfather, Yann LeCunn, runs a $3 billion AI company, and says he isn’t worried)

Along with these independent researchers, there are many others who formerly worked at companies, then quit to whistleblow about the dangers, or left to pursue anti-AI activism full-time. Paul Christiano left OpenAI in 2021 to found an AI alignment nonprofit; he later said there was a “50/50 chance of doom shortly after you have AI systems that are human level.” Daniel Kokotajlo quit OpenAI in 2024, refusing to sign a non-disparagement clause even though it could have cost him $2 million in equity, in order to start a nonprofit warning about risks from AI (he says he thinks there’s about an 80% chance AI kills everyone). Jacob Coxon quit Anthropic in September, also likely giving up millions of dollars in equity, because he thought it was “gambling with our lives”. There are dozens of others.

The people at AI companies are no more likely to raise the alarm about AI dangers than people who were never at AI companies, or people who were previously at AI companies but have since quit.

II. The AI Company Leaders Giving These Warnings Were Concerned Long Before They Ever Had AI Companies. 

DARIO AMODEI first started discussing the risk of superintelligence destroying humanity in 2013, before OpenAI or Anthropic was founded, and when Amodei wasn’t employed in tech at all. Here’s a 62 page debate between Amodei, Eliezer Yudkowsky, and other AI safety enthusiasts about strategy, dated October 27, 2013:

In 2017, when Amodei was an ordinary employee at OpenAI, he spoke about his work the on the podcast 80,000 Hours (July 21, 2017):

I mainly work on safety. We have a safety team that’s so far, myself and Paul Christiano. Paul was co-author of mine on the [Concrete Problems In AI Safety] paper and has also written a lot online on his blog about AI. He’s probably one of the people who’s I think done the most to promote clear thinking about the problem and tie it to current AI. We have a third person joining in a few weeks who I’m super excited about. We’re trying to build up a team that focuses on technical safety. We also do a little bit of strategy stuff which is how do we get different organizations that are working on AI to cooperate with each other, how do we cooperate with policy makers on questions like these. We’re also thinking a little bit about those issues but mainly technical safety.

Dario expanded on the cooperation point - he told the host about his fear that AI would lead to an “arms race” in which companies competed to develop the technology first and let safety slide. His solution was making companies cooperate:

We all think about AGI and think, that safety issues are important. . . then the question is, how does that scale to there being a lot of organizations? How does that scale to others who get involved once they see how powerful AI is? Can we make them cooperate as well? My hope is that we can.

This became an obsession with him, and he hired an advisor to help OpenAI work on the problem. According to the New Yorker:

In 2017, Amodei hired Page Hedley, a former public-interest lawyer, to be OpenAI’s policy and ethics adviser. In an early PowerPoint presentation to executives, Hedley outlined how OpenAI might avert a “catastrophic” arms race—perhaps by building a coalition of A.I. labs that would eventually coördinate with an international body akin to NATO, to insure that the technology was deployed safely. 

As Hedley recalled it, [OpenAI president Greg] Brockman didn’t understand how this would help the company beat its competitors. “No matter what I said,” Hedley told us, “Greg kept going back to ‘So how do we raise more money? How do we win?’ 

This incident and several like it turned Dario against Greg, leading to an era of constant backstabbing office politics. Dario led a pro-safety faction against Greg’s pro-business faction; Greg usually won. It didn’t help that Dario was anxious to the point of paranoia, constantly insisting that their work was too dangerous to release:

Sam Altman tried to play peacemaker by promising Dario various concessions, but eventually Dario noticed that Altman lied constantly and never came through on any of them, so he and the rest of the safety faction left to found Anthropic. Here’s how Fortune described the split:

Amodei, along with a small group of employees, became concerned about OpenAI’s direction and what he perceived as a lack of safety involved in scaling up ChatGPT.

In 2021, Amodei, along with his sister and cofounder Daniela Amodei and a dozen other ex-OpenAI employees started Anthropic with a mission to put safety first. The company released its large language model, Claude, in 2023.

The employees who jumped ship from OpenAI believed two things, Amodei told Fortune’s Jeremy Kahn at the Fortune Brainstorm Tech conference in 2023. First, they believed if you pour more compute into large language models, they will greatly improve, and there’s almost no limit to how advanced they can get. Second, they believed—in addition to scaling up the models—there needed to be a strong set of guardrails and safety considerations.

SAM ALTMAN said in February 2015 - that is, ten months before he started OpenAI - that “development of superhuman machine intelligence is probably the greatest threat to the continued existence of humanity.” He continued:

The US government, and all other governments, should regulate the development of SMI [superhuman machine intelligence]. In an ideal world, regulation would slow down the bad guys and speed up the good guys—it seems like what happens with the first SMI to be developed will be very important.

Although my general belief is that technology is often over-regulated, I think some regulation is a good thing, and I’d hate to live in a world with no regulation at all. And I think it’s definitely a good thing when the survival of humanity is in question. (Incidentally, there is precedent for classification of privately-developed knowledge when it carries mass risk to human life. SILEX is perhaps the best-known example.)

He also famously said in June of that year that “AI will most likely lead to the end of the world, but in the meantime there will be great companies”. Some people say this was a “joke”. I think it was the one time in his life that Sam Altman was ever completely 100% honest.

ELON MUSK, another AI company leader who has been talking about extinction risk, has an equally long relationship with the topic. His first statement on AI safety was in 2014, before he had any business ventures in AI, when he said that “We are summoning the demon with artificial intelligence”. He continued by calling it “our biggest existential threat”, and admitted that “I’m increasingly inclined to think there should be some regulatory oversight, maybe at the national and international level just to make sure that we don’t do something very foolish”.

Here’s a photo from the first big AI Safety conference in Puerto Rico. Elon is circled in orange. He was a rare famous billionaire who agreed to hang out with powerless nerds to debate the safety of a technology that technically didn’t exist yet, just for the love of the game.

The green circle is Demis Hassabis, the purple is Ilya Sutskever, and the red is Eliezer Yudkowsky.

After the conference, Elon agreed to donate $10 million to the fledgling cause. He continued to be a regular at AI safety conferences over the next few years. I saw him speak at the Asilomar conference in 2017, where he gave a rambling talk on how brain-computer interfaces could solve the problem (they didn’t). 

SHANE LEGG and DEMIS HASSABIS are two of the three co-founders of DeepMind, now Google DeepMind. In 2008 - a year before founding Deep Mind - Legg wrote his PhD thesis on “Machine Super Intelligence”, where he wrote that it could be “a nightmare scenario” (although he also said that “if we carefully prepare for this possibility in advance, not only might we avert disaster, we might bring about an age of prosperity unlike anything seen before.”) His other optimistic predictions include “If by suffering you mean prolonged suffering, then I think this is quite unlikely. If a super intelligent machine (or any kind of super intelligent agent) decided to get rid of us, I think it would do so pretty efficiently.”

Hassabis was also concerned at least as early as 2012, when he reportedly tried to convince Elon Musk that AI was an existential risk. He attended the same 2015 AI safety conference as Musk (see photo above) and included as a condition of DeepMind’s acquisition by Google that Google set up a powerful AI safety oversight board (this went wrong in approximately every way possible). 

THE CORPORATE PLOT hypothesis requires these CEOs to be the most prescient people in history. In 2008 or 2013 or 2015, when they were all in other industries and AI was just an academic curiosity, they would have had to realize that one day AI would become a trillion dollar business, that they would be the CEO of one of the companies, and that the company would benefit from regulatory capture. Then they would have had to devote a significant proportion of their life, and in some cases donate millions of dollars, to start laying the groundwork ahead of time, just in case it became necessary. Dario Amodei, while finishing his biology postdoc, would have to have moonlighted as an AI safety enthusiast just in case he became a multi-billion dollar tech CEO one day. Shane Legg would have had to choose his PhD thesis topic based on the possibility that he would own shares in a Google AI subsidiary sixteen years later. 

The alternative is that all these people believed it then, and still believe it now, for the same reason that all of the independent experts and academics believe it. They are working in the field partly because they think that being closer to the development of AI gives them more of a chance to control it and keep it safe than if they were sitting on the sidelines.

III. If This Is A Plot, It’s A Really Dumb One

Having shown that these men would have to be the smartest people in the world to pull this off, it’s worth noting that the plot they apparently dedicated their lives to is really dumb.

For example, if the Pacing The Frontier consortium attempt was a plot to pump stock prices, you might expect that, upon it being announced, stock prices would go up. This didn’t happen.

Anthropic and OpenAI aren’t publicly traded companies, so they don’t have an easily-tracked stock price. But there are complicated cryptocurrency bets called “perpetual futures” that traders use to approximate the stock prices of private companies (usually these are some kind of prediction-market like instrument on eventual IPO price). When the slowdown call happened, Anthropic’s value on the biggest cryptocurrency futures platform dropped 4.57%, and OpenAI’s stock dropped 13.42%.

(two other AI companies that endorsed the slowdown proposal, Google DeepMind and X.AI, are subsidiaries of larger publicly traded companies; Google and SpaceX respectively. Both companies went down modestly the day after the announcement, although they have so many other things going on that I take this less seriously than the AI company futures.)

Why wouldn’t the stock market (or at least this particular cryptocurrency simulation of the stock market) approve of the slowdown as a potential regulatory moat? It seems like traders thought the first-level effects (slowing down) were more important than any secondary regulatory effects that might or might not materialize.

Libertarian economist Alex Tabarrok is head of the Center for Study of Public Choice, the subfield of economics that studies things like regulatory capture. He agrees with the traders. He wrote a good post, What Regulatory Capture Actually Looks Like, arguing that a regulatory capture story doesn’t fit:

Go ahead: argue that Amodei and other AI experts are wrong about AI risk. Ask whether his proposals favor Anthropic. But calling “our product might kill you” a clever marketing and regulatory-capture strategy isn’t sophisticated analysis. The facts don’t fit regulatory capture theory and trying to make them fit requires epistemically painful Ptolemaic epicycles. Even a dull Ockham’s razor cuts through that story to the obvious alternative: Amodei actually believes what he’s saying.

Or consider another story - trying to distract from near-term harms. Is this really how things work? Are there vicious fights between environmentalists who want to save the rainforest and environmentalists who want to fight climate change, with the former arguing that the latter’s focus on longer-term risks detracts from environmental problems that are happening right now? No, obviously this is stupid; these groups are natural allies. Both donate to the Sierra Club and vote for the Green Party. Even if a certain rainforest supporter didn’t care about climate change at all, they would be grateful for the climate change activist’s votes and donations.

This is how things are shaping up with AI also. Last summer, Ted Cruz sponsored a bill to ban states from regulating AI. It had strong support from AI money and was expected to pass. A coalition of effective altruist groups worried about human extinction, artists’ groups worried about intellectual property, family groups worried about harms to children, and many others united to defeat it. 

But maybe it’s true for newspaper space in particular? Maybe concerns about human extinction are preventing journalists from writing about nearer-term harms?

Both people interested in human extinction and people interested in near-term harms fund the Tarbell Center for AI Journalism, which helps fund reporters on both category of risk (Tarbell received an ACX Grant two years ago). They highlight articles they’ve helped with on issues across the spectrum, from Worried Anthropic Researchers Warn That AI Could Kill All Humans to Hundreds Gather To Urge Scottish Government To Pause Data Center Boom to AI Is More Likely Than Humans To Form Biases When Hiring.

In retrospect, this alliance should be obvious. Both groups want the same thing: the ability to slow AI. And both have the same enemy: the tsunami of Silicon Valley money which is trying to elect Congressmen who refuse to regulate AI in any way. Both groups are working together against their common foe. Signal-boosting long-term risks to distract from short-term risks would only empower this coalition, and so - like the other version of this plot - be implausibly stupid.

As for the claim that AI companies are trying to hype their products, this seems unnecessary: AI is the fastest-adopted technology in history:

…so it hardly seems worth it to hype it up a little more at the cost of getting a large number of Americans to think your product will kill them personally, and a plurality of voters in both parties to want to ban your industry from creating new products:

If the last section required AI company leaders to be the smartest people in the world, this one requires them to be the dumbest.

We live in an age of cynicism and nihilism. When someone endorses a good cause, we accuse them of virtue-signaling; if they donate to it, we accuse them of trying to whitewash their role in capitalism. We lionize corrupt politicians and insipid bling-wielding celebrities because, as people who have never made any claim to moral acceptability, they are the only people who can entirely escape the suspicion of faking it. 

This is idiotic and requires otherwise smart people to constantly contort themselves to figure out the latest less-than-entirely-depraved person’s angle. Maybe some people are so venal that they can’t imagine anyone truly caring about the welfare of humanity, but they should stop projecting this on everyone else. The experts are warning you that AI could kill you because they think AI could kill you. Many of them have made personal sacrifices to get the message out. Stop adding thumbtacks to your conspiracy corkboard and take their message seriously.

items.articleBody:
“If you can acknowledge it and you can relax with it a little bit, very often it shortens its duration.”

It starts with a low hum that adheres itself to the underbelly of the hours like another dimension. Gradually, surreptitiously, the noise swells to a bellowing bass line, until it drowns out the symphony of life. 

It can last for days or months or entire seasons of being. It visited Keats frequently in his short life, leaving him with a mind empty of ideas and hands heavy as lead. It rendered Lorraine Hansberry “cold, useless, frustrated, helpless, disillusioned, angry and tired.” It drove Abraham Lincoln to the brink of suicide. 

If you are lucky enough, if you have the right aids of science, social support, and chance, one day you look over the shoulder of time and, like the poet Jane Kenyon, gasp in grateful incomprehension: “What hurt me so terribly all my life until this moment?” But until that moment comes, as William Styron so vividly observed in his classic bridge of empathy, “the gray drizzle of horror induced by depression takes on the quality of physical pain.”

Among the legion of us soaked by the drizzle is one of the most beloved artists of our epoch, whose music has made life brighter and more livable for generations. 

Bruce Springsteen driving cross-country in 1987. (Photograph from Born to Run.)

In his memoir, Born to Run (public library), Bruce Springsteen writes about his father’s “long, drawn-out depressions,” often so debilitating that he could not rise from bed for days, and about his own tumble toward the edge of the abyss quarried by his genetic inheritance and the darknesses of his childhood, and about what kept him from falling. “God help Bruce Springsteen when they decide he’s no longer God,” John Lennon reflected in his most personal interview, but no outside “they” — no critic, no cry from the public — ever measures up to the inner chorus of anguish that most cruelly lowers an artist from the pedestal of their creative power and into the pit of depression. 

In a particularly vivid vignette from the period just before he finally sought help, Springsteen writes:

My depression is spewing like an oil spill all over the beautiful turquoise-green gulf of my carefully planned and controlled existence. Its black sludge is threatening to smother every last living part of me.

Even Springsteen’s favorite books reflect this lifelong undertone of black. But it is in his BBC Desert Island Discs appearance that he opens up most candidly about his experience of depression and his life-honed coping mechanisms for it. He reflects:

I’ve developed some skills that help me in dealing with it, but still — it is a powerful, powerful thing that really comes up from things that still remain unexplainable to me.

Bruce Springsteen. (Photograph: BBC.)

After noting that much of it is pure biochemistry, and can therefore be greatly salved by biochemical interventions, he considers the psychological skills that have helped him temper the onslaught and offers a Buddhist-like strategy of unresistant presence with the flow of experience on its own terms, laced with a gentle admonition against the trap of blamethirsty projection:

Just naming it [helps]… What most people tend to want to do is, when they feel bad, the first thing you want to do is to name a reason why you feel that way: “I feel bad because…” and you’ll transfer that to someone else “…because Johnny said this to me,” or “this happened.” And, sometimes, that’s true. But a lot of times, you’re simply looking to name something that’s not particularly nameable and if you misname it, it just makes everything that much worse. 

So my “skill” is sort of saying, “Okay, it’s not this, it’s not that — it’s just this. This is something that comes; it’s also something that goes — and maybe something I have to live with for a period of time.” 

But if you can acknowledge it and you can relax with it a little bit, very often it shortens its duration.

Complement with Bloom — a touching animated short film about depression and what it takes to recover the light of being — and Tim Ferriss on how he survived his suicidal depression, then revisit Robert Burton’s centuries-old salve for melancholy and two centuries of beloved writers — including Keats, Whitman, Hansberry, Carson, and Thoreau — on the mightiest antidote to depression.

donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing The Marginalian (which bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a donation. Your support makes all the difference.

newsletter

The Marginalian has a free weekly newsletter. It comes out on Sundays and offers the week’s most inspiring reading. Here’s what to expect. Like? Sign up.

items.articleBody:
Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO

The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting investors on Wednesday. Lots of details in here from "people with knowledge of the matter".

Key things I learned from the article:

Q1 revenue (Jan/Feb/Mar) was "about $4.8bn"

Q2 (Apr/May/Jun) was $11.5bn

Q3 (Jul/Aug/Sep) was $16.8bn

In Q3: $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on "computing power"

Adjusted operating margins (excluding stock-based compensation) were 11%

This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine):

The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones.

When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending.

Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter.

Napkin maths says that if distillation was 5% of their Q2 revenue (before they cut it back in Q3) then unnamed "other labs" spent over half a billion dollars distilling Anthropic's models in that quarter!

Also notable: Anthropic appear to no longer be leaning on "annualized run-rate revenue" (previously) in these communications to their investors.

Two life-changing experiences lie at the heart of the captivating new oil-and-graphite paintings in Tanya Merrill’s exhibition, Land animal, house animal: The artist gave birth to her daughter in June, and her family recently relocated from New York City to upstate New York. 

In her new environment, Merrill decisively challenges a pervasive anthropocentric worldview that deems humans superior and animals lesser. She foregrounds local animals as sentient beings with their own motivations and desires, including a cat in two terrific paintings, a wide-eyed and inquisitive dairy cow, and the Northern harrier (or marsh hawk) with piercing eyes and luscious gray, white, and black feathers that she frequently observes from her studio (“Marsh hawk,” 2026). This bird painting echoes regional folk art and Audubon. 
Tanya Merrill "Horse at night" (2026), oil and graphite on linen

items.articleBody:
A new bill proposed by Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-NY) aims to establish new regulations that would ensure that "buying a video game would give the consumer ownership of the game rather than a license to play it," including assurances that they can continue to access the games for years after they are released.

The announcement names NBA 2K25 as an example of the problem the bill aims to solve; that game launched on September 6, 2025, but is scheduled to become unplayable on December 31 due to server shutdowns. The bill, which is called the Power to Players Act, directs the FTC to take action to prevent outcomes like that in the future.

Disquiet Junto Project 0772: Garden Grow

The Assignment: Tend to your music like Brian Eno might.

Brian Eno has said: “my feeling is that making art can be more usefully thought of as being like gardening: you plant a few seeds and then start watching what happens between them, how they come to life and how they interact.”

There is one step to this project: Record a piece of music that puts that concept into effect.

Tasks Upon Completion:

Label: Include “disquiet0772” (no spaces/quotes) in the name of your track.

Upload: A person participating in the Disquiet Junto should post only one track per weekly project (SoundCloud account preferred but not required). If on occasion you feel inspired to post more than one track (whether to a single account or across multiple accounts), you should clarify which is the “main” rendition for consideration by fellow members and (if on SoundCloud) for inclusion in the SoundCloud playlist.

Share: Post your track and a description/explanation at https://llllllll.co/t/disquiet-junto-project-0772-garden-grow/

Discuss: Listen to and comment on the other tracks.

Additional Details:

Length: The length is up to you. Is your garden wild or controlled?

Deadline: Monday, October 19, 2026, 11:59pm (that is: just before midnight) wherever you are.

Newsletter: https://juntoletter.disquiet.com/

items.articleBody:
More than 5 million people around the world with age-related macular degeneration (AMD) experience atrophy in their retinas. And until now, no treatment could restore their vision. The PRIMA system, which was approved in Europe in July and is awaiting FDA clearance in the US, changes that. It combines a retinal implant with camera-­equipped eyeglasses to improve sight in patients who develop a blind spot in the middle of their vision due to advanced AMD. After training sessions, more than 80% of recipients were able to read, do crosswords, and use their phones.

The retina processes light in three layers of cells: Photoreceptors convert light into electricity, bipolar cells process that signal, and ganglion cells transmit the signal to the optic nerve and the brain. PRIMA replaces the photoreceptors.
BROWN BIRD DESIGN

Developed by the California-based Science Corporation, the system takes advantage of the fact that AMD doesn’t damage all retinal circuitry; only photoreceptors—the cells that convert light into an electrical signal—die off. PRIMA’s implant mimics those cells and transmits visual information directly to healthy eye circuitry and on to the brain. “We’re leveraging all of the body’s own natural functions to process and transmit the information,” says Frank Brodie, an ophthalmologist at the University of California, San Francisco, and Science Corp.’s chief medical officer for ophthalmology. 

BROWN BIRD DESIGN

CAPTURE

Glasses outfitted with a miniature front-facing camera capture what someone is seeing in real time. The video feed is roughly five megapixels running at 30 frames per second, which is similar to TV. The raw video is transmitted to a connected processor via a fiber-optic cable.

CONVERT

A small, handheld processor, which can be set on a table or tucked in a pocket, converts the video feed into infrared light signals that route back to the glasses. The device also includes physical buttons that let the wearer adjust contrast, brightness, and zoom.

BROWN BIRD DESIGN

DISPLAY

A laser projector on the glasses faces the wearer and shines pulses of near-infrared light directly at the eye at 880 nanometers—an invisible wavelength. This signal passes through the pupil and on to the retinal implant in the back of the eye.

SEE

The implant is made up of 378 pixels, each with an electrode and two photovoltaic cells, which do double duty. They convert the light into a current that healthy bipolar and ganglion cells pass on to the brain. They also act as solar cells to power the chip, eliminating the need for a battery.

Update: This story has been updated to clarify the specific cases of AMD the PRIMA system treats. 

Linda Marsa is a former Los Angeles Times reporter and an author who covers medicine, health, science, and the environment.

FROM OUR PARTNER

Your journey to the secure agentic enterprise

Every team is being asked to roll out AI agents, but agents don't fit into human or machine identity models.

So how do you authenticate them, scope their access, and govern what they can do, at scale?

Watch this on-demand webinar to learn:

• Why identity models break down for autonomous agents

• The security foundations that matter: authentication, access control, delegation, and governance

• Hard-won lessons from powering identity for 1000+ MCP servers and millions of monthly agentic transactions

Rohit Ganguly, AI Product Manager at Descope, walks through what it takes to secure agents in the enterprise.
Secure your agents before they scale. Watch the webinar now.

 🕵️ Engineer accused of bugging OpenAI's office LINK
OpenAI used its own AI models to trace a hidden recording device found in an executive conference room, helping identify and catch the engineer who allegedly planted it in the company's office.

The accused, 35-year-old Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested after security found the device plugged into a TV's USB port around September 28, plus a second recorder in a bag holding his wallet and ID.

The device had encryption, audio monitoring, and a hidden data transfer method; FBI Director Kash Patel said it was likely meant to capture sensitive talks about OpenAI's superintelligence work, though the full purpose stays unclear.
 🛰️ Ukraine says SpaceX capped Starlink drone speed LINK
Ukraine says SpaceX quietly throttled its Starlink service overnight, limiting the speed of military terminals used for drone strikes and frontline communications, according to defense ministry sources and a top presidential advisor.

Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to President Zelenskyy, said SpaceX capped Starshield, the company's military satellite network, so it slows down above 100 miles per hour, and that Kyiv's military got no warning beforehand.

Beskrestnov offered no evidence but suggested the slowdown ties to US-Ukraine tensions, coming after Elon Musk said Zelenskyy had "gone too far" with strikes on Russian refineries and amid recent Russian missile attacks on Kyiv.
 🔌 400+ AI scientists demand containment rules LINK
More than 400 AI researchers, including Yoshua Bengio and Geoffrey Hinton, signed an open letter urging the industry to build stronger containment for AI, warning that weak safeguards have already led to serious security failures.

The letter makes three asks: that firms running "cyber-capable" models wall them off from outside networks, that a new international body set containment standards, and that all containment failures be reported to that body and made public.

The call follows OpenAI's July breach of Hugging Face and other lab incidents, and arrives as Anthropic cofounder Jack Clark now predicts self-improving AI could arrive in 2027, a year sooner than he earlier thought.
 ⚙️ ASML can't meet AI chip-tool demand LINK
ASML, the Dutch maker of chipmaking machines, says its supply plans fall short of demand for 2027 and 2028, with some customers already asking to place orders stretching into 2029 and 2030.

Chief executive Christophe Fouquet said buyers ask for more tools every day, and the company is looking past the 30% extra capacity it planned for 2027 and the further 30% it was studying for 2028.

ASML raised the low end of its 2026 sales guidance to between €44B and €45B, its shares rose 2.8% to about €1,552 in Amsterdam, and China still makes up roughly a fifth of this year's revenue.
 📱 Facebook lets you reshape your feed LINK
Facebook has rolled out a feature called "Your Algorithm" that lets users shape what shows up in their Feed and Reels by describing in plain language the topics and posts they want to see more or less of.

Meta says the AI-powered tool updates recommendations in real time and may ask follow-up questions to learn what people liked or disliked, letting them give more detailed feedback about their preferences.

The company also reworked Facebook's three-dot menu so people can open "Your Algorithm" or tap "Interested" and "Not interested" straight from individual posts, following similar tools on Instagram and the "Dear Algo" feature on Threads.
 👁️ Neuralink co-founder's chip restores vision in first patient LINK
Science Corporation, led by Neuralink co-founder Max Hodak, has placed its PRIMA vision chip in a first patient with Stargardt disease, an inherited condition that destroys central vision and is currently considered incurable.

The 2mm-by-2mm chip sits at the back of the eye and acts like artificial light-sensing cells, working with camera glasses; the patient, implanted in May at Sydney Eye Hospital, saw a letter and later read a word during rehabilitation.

Hodak said the current black-and-white view is sharp but narrow, like looking through a straw; a next version should reach humans within a year, with near-normal sharpness possible over five years as implants grow and electrodes shrink.

items.articleBody:
The imaginative, strange childhood dreams of twins Nikolai and Simon Haas materialize in a large-scale exhibition at Blanton Museum of Art. Working as the Haas Brothers, the siblings have been collaborating since 2010 and are widely known for their fantastical sculptures of flora and fauna with their signature cheeky, surreal twist. In Austin, the Los Angeles artists present a range of figurative furniture, plush cartoonish characters, and illuminated installations that showcase their idiosyncratic aesthetic.

Previously on view at Cranbrook Art Museum and the Museum of Art and Design in New York, Uncanny Valley is the first mid-career survey for the duo, presenting a range of their quirky, genre-defying works. The exhibition also nods to the brothers’ childhood in Austin, where they lived from age 3 to 19, a time when the unofficial city slogan “Keep Austin Weird” became a cultural ethos and early influence.

Installation view of ‘Haas Brothers: Uncanny Valley’ at Blanton Museum of Art (2026)

Interested in technology and its implications, the artists frequently engage with the strange intersection of the artificial and the natural. The duo’s brilliant and bizarre strawberry tree, for example, appears as if transplanted from another planet into the gallery. In a statement for the show, Simon elaborates: 

The ‘uncanny valley’ generally refers to robotics, where empathy for a robot increases the more human you make it—up to a point. When the robot becomes too human, empathy switches to revulsion. The solution for this is to add cuteness: when a robot is humanoid with an extra dose of cuteness, empathy for the object skyrockets. Looking at our 15-year career from a bird’s-eye view, the ‘uncanny valley’ came into focus as a core theme.

Uncanny Valley is on view in Austin through January 17, when it will travel to its final location, Mint Museum in Charlotte. Find the accompanying monograph of the same name on Bookshop.

items.articleBody:
We’ve asked before: “What is your department’s AI policy?” Perhaps you think a good academic AI policy should, to the extent possible, be sensitive to the kind of thing the AI is being used for, and by whom. So what should a department’s policy be about graduate students using AI to write a dissertation?

Art by James Nolan Gandy

I ask because, according to recent analyses, some students are using AI to write at least part of their dissertations, and the number of dissertations containing AI-generated text in the United States is increasing. 

According to a new working paper by Daniel P. Gross (Duke), Dror Shvadron (Toronto), and Hansen Zhang (Duke), between a quarter and a third of the dissertations that earned people their PhDs in STEM fields this year in the US contained AI writing. 

They say:

We measure AI-generated writing in the dissertations of a near-census of US STEM PhD graduates from 2019 to 2026 and link graduates to their subsequent employment. [“We process all abstracts and a stratified random sample of complete dissertations (stratifying over fields and years), which we use to verify that AI-generated abstracts are a surrogate for AI-generated writing in the full text—consistent with prior research which has found the same.”] 

AI writing is absent before 2023, present in 29% of dissertations filed in 2026, and rapidly growing. Use is more common among students from non-English-speaking countries and at lower-ranked programs. Among graduates in the same program and cohort, those whose dissertations contain AI writing are less likely to enter academic research careers and more likely to enter non-tenure-track roles or industry, with this pattern strongest among US-origin students. At the same time as AI may increase research productivity, it thus appears to also be displacing a potentially important portion of the work through which scientific expertise is developed.

That’s in STEM fields. What about philosophy?

I asked the team that produced the above study if they could run a similar analysis on philosophy dissertations. Very kindly, they agreed to do so. (And very kindly, my department at the University of South Carolina agreed to fund the use of the Pangram API with which they did it.)

As with the STEM fields, in philosophy the trend is an increase in the number of dissertations with AI writing (operationalized as containing at least 2% AI-written text). In 2024, 1.3% of philosophy dissertations included AI writing. That figure jumped to 7.8% in 2025, and continues to rise. Only about a quarter of the philosophy dissertations expected to be filed in 2026 were analyzed, but so far 11.1% of them contain AI writing. 

Bars report total U.S. philosophy PhD dissertations (right axis); lines report shares of scored abstracts (left axis), using Pangram 4.0 (model definitions).* The dark blue line counts abstracts in which Pangram identifies more than 2% of the text as written by AI. Graph by Hansen Zhang, based on data collected and analyzed by Daniel Gross, Dror Shvadron, and Hansen Zhang. Thanks to the University of South Carolina Department of Philosophy for funding this analysis.

What to make of this?

One cautious point is that the numbers on that graph do not tell us how the AI was used. Perhaps not all of the types of AI use that could lead to a piece of writing having a “high” Pangram score are objectionable? Relatedly, we might ask whether we can adequately craft policies that make the right fine-grained distinctions about the permissibility of AI use, and whether such policies can be enforced.

Another thing to note is that although the rate at which AI writing shows up in philosophy dissertations is about one-third of that in STEM fields, this is not much comfort to those in philosophy who object to such writing. One reason is that shifts in academic norms are not necessarily confined by disciplinary boundaries. If the prevalence of AI-written text in dissertations becomes normal in other disciplines, the expectations we will have in philosophy will certainly be affected, as will the expectations of administrators. Number-crunching deans may want to know why they’re paying for graduate students to spend a few years writing a dissertation without AI when, with it, they could be done with their dissertations in a few months, or perhaps even weeks or days.

If departments aim to prohibit or strictly limit how AI is used in the writing of dissertations, best to try to do that now, while norms are in the air, rather than waiting until later, when perhaps largely unrestricted AI use by graduate students on their written work will have been normalized.

Discussion welcome.

*Note: There were some challenges determining the set of philosophy dissertation abstracts to study. Initially, the team searched available abstracts and metadata of dissertations in ProQuest that listed “philosophy” in the department or any subject search field. That overcounted philosophy dissertations by around 300% (which we noticed by comparing those figures with the number of philosophy PhDs earned each year). This is not surprising, since the word “philosophy” is used by more than just philosophers. Limiting the search to “philosophy” in the listed department and ignoring its presence elsewhere in the abstract and metadata had its problems, though, too. For one thing, some multi-disciplinary departments include philosophy; and so by this method, all of the dissertations produced by a department of “Psychology & Philosophy” would be counted as philosophy dissertations, even if the department only offers a PhD in psychology, not philosophy. So we eliminated those departments. But then we noticed a different problem: the dissertation counts of some departments were bizarrely low. For example, according to the department-only ProQuest search, Stanford University’s Department of Philosophy appears to have produced just 1 dissertation between 2016 and 2026—obviously a mistake. Several other departments had this undercounting problem. When I pointed this out, one of the researchers said the likely explanation is that “department information may be missing or recorded differently in ProQuest”. We did not search for these “missing” dissertations, and so the set of dissertations on which the study is based is not identical to the set of all philosophy dissertations filed in the US during the years studied.

COMMENTS POLICY

items.subtitle: Strokes are becoming alarmingly common among younger adults, with rates nearly doubling among people ages 20 to 54 over nearly three decades.
items.feedText: Researchers found that blocked blood vessels in the brain accounted for much of the increase, while high blood pressure, diabetes, and substance use also became more common among younger stroke patients. Although survival rates have improved, more young adults may now face the lasting consequences of stroke.

items.articleBody:
The value of a man was reduced to his immediate identity and nearest possibility. To a vote. To a number. To a thing. Never was a man treated as a mind. As a glorious thing made of star dust.

—Rohith Vemula, January 17, 2016

On a January morning in 2016, a 26-year-old PhD scholar at the University of Hyderabad left behind a suicide note that would shake India’s conscience. The Dalit student and activist Rohith Vemula had been suspended from his university, evicted from his hostel, and effectively erased from institutional life because of his caste and his activism with the Ambedkar Students’ Association (ASA). His words have since become one of the most quoted testimonies to the lived reality of caste in modern India.

Rohith’s death did not silence his family. Three months later, on April 14, 2016—the 125th birth anniversary of Dr. B. R. Ambedkar, the famed Dalit activist and chief architect of the Indian Constitution—his mother, Radhika, and his brother, Raja, traveled from Hyderabad to the Dr. Babasaheb Ambedkar Bhavan in Dadar, Mumbai, where thirty Buddhist monks administered the Deeksha vows in the presence of Prakash Ambedkar, the great man’s grandson. They converted to Buddhism. Rohith’s childhood friend Riyaz Shaikh and ASA activist Charbad Raju converted alongside them.

They convert to Buddhism as protest, as survival, as the most radical act available to them: the refusal to remain within a religion that sanctifies their humiliation.

This act of conversion in response to violence is neither new nor isolated in India. It is a pattern woven through seven decades of Ambedkarite history: Caste commits violence, the state fails to respond, and Dalits reach not for weapons but for the dhamma. They convert to Buddhism as protest, as survival, as the most radical act available to them: the refusal to remain within a religion that sanctifies their humiliation.

The World Ambedkar Inherited

To understand why Dalits convert to Buddhism when atrocities occur, one must first understand what they are converting from. Caste is not merely social stratification; it is a theological architecture of pollution and purity, inscribed in shastras (scripture), enforced through violence, and reproduced across generations. For those designated “untouchable”—outside the fourfold varna system entirely—it meant being prohibited from access to temples, wells, schools, transport, jobs, and roads. It meant being forced to announce one’s presence by striking two stones together so caste Hindus could step aside. It meant sweeping streets, carrying human waste, skinning dead cattle—not by choice but by birth. It meant that one’s very shadow was considered contaminating.

Dr. Ambedkar was born into this reality on April 14, 1891. A brilliant student who earned doctorates from Columbia University and the London School of Economics, he was nonetheless barred from drinking water from a common pot in his own school, denied accommodation by landlords, and turned away from guesthouses throughout his professional life. He understood that no amount of personal achievement could dissolve caste as long as Hinduism provided its theological justification. His conclusion, reached after decades of study, political struggle, and searching engagement with multiple religious traditions, was unambiguous: Hinduism and caste were inseparable. Reform from within was impossible. Liberation required exit.

The Dhamma Deeksha: Ambedkar’s Mass Conversion

On October 14, 1956, in the city of Nagpur, in the year of the celebration of the 2,500th anniversary of the Buddha’s passage into parinirvana, Dr. Ambedkar led approximately 500,000 followers in a mass conversion to Buddhism—what became known as the Dhamma Deeksha. He was 64, gravely ill, and knew he was dying. (He died in his sleep six weeks later, three days after completing The Buddha and His Dhamma, which would become the foundational text for the Ambedkarite movement.) Before his death, he was determined to set a new school of engaged Buddhism in motion—what he termed Navayana, or the “New Vehicle.”

In taking the twenty-two vows Ambedkar prescribed, new Buddhists simultaneously rejected Hindu gods, the authority of Brahminical priests, the legitimacy of caste, and the identity of untouchability itself. They were not joining a religion so much as declaring their humanity. The vows made this explicit: “I renounce Hinduism, which is harmful for humanity and impedes the advancement of human beings, and I embrace Buddhism as my religion,” and “I believe that today I am taking new birth.” This language of rebirth was chosen with care. Buddhism offered not just a new faith but a new identity—one whose dignity was not contingent on caste, whose spiritual worth was not determined by birth, whose liberation was possible here, in this world, through ethical engagement. Further, in their explicit refusal to worship Hindu deities and to view the Buddha as an avatar of the Hindu god Vishnu, the vows push back against Hindu nationalist attempts to absorb Buddhism back into Hinduism and therefore weaken Buddhism’s power to challenge caste. Taken together, these twenty-two vows laid the foundation for Ambedkarite Buddhism, which offered a fierce rejection of Hindu nationalism and caste politics while affirming the inherent dignity and equality of all beings.

Taken together, these twenty-two vows laid the foundation for Ambedkarite Buddhism, which offered a fierce rejection of Hindu nationalism and caste politics while affirming the inherent dignity and equality of all beings. 

In laying out the tenets of the Navayana movement, Ambedkar did not present the Buddha as a god to worship but as Margadata—one who shows the path. The dhamma, he insisted in The Buddha and His Dhamma, served as a social blueprint: “The function of Dhamma is to reconstruct the world.” He drew from the Pali canon’s democratic sangha as model for egalitarian community, from the Mahayana’s bodhisattva ideal as model for social service, and from his analysis of Indian society to reframe dukkha not as cosmic suffering but as the specific, structural suffering imposed by caste.

Ambedkar timed the Dhamma Deeksha to take place on the date of the Emperor Ashoka’s conversion to Buddhism. But when Emperor Ashoka converted to Buddhism in the 3rd century BCE, the conversion “came from the throne.” Imperial patronage supported monasteries and spread the dhamma throughout Asia. Ambedkar’s revival, by contrast, “came from the people”—specifically from those deemed to occupy the lowest stratum of society. This origin from the very bottom of India’s social hierarchy fundamentally shapes Ambedkarite Buddhism and explains why it carries such a sense of moral urgency. What Ambedkar left behind was not merely a new Buddhism but a new form of resistance—one that subsequent generations of Dalits would turn to whenever the violence of caste made remaining inside Hinduism unbearable.

Buddhists gather in Nagpur in 2006 to celebrate the fiftieth Anniversary of Ambedkar’s Buddhist conversion. Photo by Shashi Jambhulkar. Courtesy Santosh Raut.

Ambedkar’s Legacy

In the seventy years since that October morning in Nagpur, the pattern of caste violence has repeated with devastating regularity. Caste commits atrocities, and the state looks away. And Dalits, following in Ambedkar’s footsteps, respond by converting to Buddhism—not in defeat but in defiance.

In July 2016, four young Dalit men from Mota Samadhiyala village near Una, Gujarat, were stripped, bound to an SUV, and flogged publicly by cow vigilantes. Their crime was skinning a dead cow, the traditional occupation their caste had been assigned for centuries. Their attackers filmed the assault and circulated the footage. The police, presented with video evidence, were slow to act. The victims and hundreds of their family members embraced Buddhism in protest: If Hinduism made them responsible for dead cows and then targeted them for doing so, they would leave Hinduism. The act of conversion was at once a rejection of the theological framework that assigned them this labor and an assertion of dignity in the face of violence and humiliation.

In 2019, in Gundlupet, a Dalit youth was stripped, thrashed, and paraded naked—an act of humiliation designed to communicate to an entire community their assigned place. Dalit activists organized protest marches that concluded with several individuals converting to Buddhism. The symbolism was significant: In response to an act of forced stripping, these Dalits voluntarily adopted a tradition that strips a person of their caste identity at the moment of conversion.

In 2022, two Dalit youths in Bhulon Village were assaulted by upper-caste men for the act of offering aarti (prayer) at a Hindu temple—a devotional practice considered the prerogative of caste Hindus. The police refused to file cases against the offenders. More than 200 Dalit families converted to Buddhism collectively in protest, as Buddhism offered them a house of worship where no upper-caste gatekeeper could deny them entry.

Some conversions are not singular events but the culmination of long struggles. The Namantar Andolan—the sixteen-year movement to rename Marathwada University after Dr. Ambedkar—was marked by sustained upper-caste violence: riots, murders, destruction of Dalit property, burning of homes. Dominant castes attacked the very proposal of honoring Ambedkar with an institution bearing his name. But the violence did not suppress the Dalit Buddhist movement. After nearly two decades of advocacy, the university was eventually renamed in 1994, but what the struggle solidified was more enduring: a Buddhist identity in the region inseparable from political resistance.

Buddhists celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of Ambedkar’s Buddhist conversion. Photo by Shashi Jambhulkar. Courtesy Santosh Raut.

Rohith Vemula: A Life Reduced to a Number

No case has more powerfully illustrated the intersection of caste, institutional violence, and Buddhist response than that of Rohith Vemula. Rohith was an activist with the Ambedkar Students’ Association at the University of Hyderabad. Following a political clash with a right-wing student group, the university administration suspended him and four other Dalit student leaders, evicting them from their hostel and banning them from common spaces. They lived in a makeshift tent on campus. On January 17, 2016, Rohith committed suicide.

His suicide note is not a document of despair alone. It is a philosophical protest—a young man who dreamed of stars and galaxies articulating what the caste system does to the inner life of a human being. The phrase “My birth is a fatal accident” does not describe personal misfortune. It describes a social system in which being born in a particular caste is a life sentence. His note ends: “From shadows to the stars.”

His family understood. His body was cremated according to Buddhist rites. Three months later, on Ambedkar Jayanti, his mother and brother converted to Buddhism in Mumbai, taking the Deeksha vows. “From today,” Raja Vemula stated, “my mother and I will be free from shame, free from the daily humiliation, free from the guilt of praying to the same god in whose name our people have been tortured for centuries. . . . We want azadi [freedom] from the caste system.” Rohith had urged his family toward Buddhism while he was alive. In death, he finally brought them there.

A New Buddhism Born from Old Symbols

What is being created through these conversions is not simply a transfer of religious allegiance. It is the emergence of a distinctly Ambedkarite Buddhist culture rooted in the particular experience of caste. In Buddhist viharas across Maharashtra, the altar holds two images: the meditating Buddha and Dr. Ambedkar in his characteristic blue suit with pen, holding the Constitution he helped to craft. The pairing is deliberate: One offers the path; the other shows how that path was walked in modernity.

Sunday weekly dhamma class at the Sariputta Buddhist Vihara in Nagpur. Photo by Shashi Jambhulkar. Courtesy Santosh Raut.

Ancient Buddhist symbols are being reimagined through Ambedkarite imagination: The dharmachakra appears on protest banners alongside photographs of atrocity victims; the blue of Ambedkar’s suit has become the color of Dalit assertion; the Bodhi tree is reclaimed as a symbol of enlightenment available to all, not just the ritually pure. Conversion ceremonies are conducted on Ambedkar Jayanti and Dhamma Chakra Pravartan Din to connect each individual act to the collective history of 1956. At local viharas, monks and laypeople administer the twenty-two vows together, dissolving the hierarchies that traditionally separated clergy from laity. In Rohith’s case, even death became a Buddhist ritual act—his cremation insisting that his mind, “a glorious thing made of star dust,” was never reducible to his caste.

Participants engage in metta bhavana meditation at the Dhammakranti Retreat in Nagpur in 2006. Photo by Shashi Jambhulkar. Courtesy Santosh Raut.

From Shadows to the Stars

When Rohith Vemula signed his final letter, “From shadows to the stars,” he was thinking of Carl Sagan and the cosmos. But the phrase has taken on a meaning larger than one man’s biography. It has become an Ambedkarite phrase, describing the journey from the shadow of caste to the light of Buddhist liberation, from the imposed darkness of untouchability to the possibility of human dignity.

Ambedkar understood this journey. “The greatest thing that the Buddha has done,” he wrote, “is to tell the world that the world cannot be reformed except by the reformation of the mind of the man and the mind of the world.” Spiritual revolution becomes the foundation for social transformation. This is what conversion enacts: a reformation of mind, a refusal to carry within oneself the shame that caste assigns. It is what Raja Vemula was describing when he said his family would be free from shame. Shame is structured into the caste system. Buddhism, in the Ambedkarite tradition, dismantles it.

For 10 million Ambedkarite Buddhists, the dhamma provides the moral foundation enabling constitutional democracy to flourish. In Ambedkar’s formulation, the Buddhist principle of maitri (loving-kindness) becomes the democratic principle of fraternity. Anatta (not-self) provides the basis for constitutional equality, as caste hierarchy is revealed to be an illusion. And the Pali canon’s descriptions of sangha become the model for democratic governance and community. But the answer is also the people themselves. When they march with Buddhist flags instead of weapons, when they demand justice with dignity, when they build communities of equality in a hierarchical society, they are collectively enacting the vision of Ambedkar’s Constitution, enabling it to flourish.

Participants celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of Ambedkar’s conversion. Photo by Shashi Jambhulkar. Courtesy Santosh Raut.

Seventy years after Ambedkar’s conversion, his movement stands at a crossroads determining not only its own future but potentially the future of engaged Buddhism globally. The challenges it faces offer a template for how Buddhism can meet the social challenges of the modern age and set forth a path of liberation not just for individuals seeking peace but for communities seeking justice. For the global Buddhist community, Ambedkarite Buddhism poses an uncomfortable but necessary question: Can we learn from Buddhists who are actually transforming society, or will we continue ignoring them?

When we speak of engaged Buddhism, remember that 10 million people are already doing it, not as a theoretical concept but as lived reality, carrying within their bodies the memory of every flogging, every temple door slammed shut, every act of institutional violence, and choosing, still, the path of peace. The question is whether the rest of us are watching silently—or paying attention and ready to join in.

The post B. R. Ambedkar and the Dalit Quest for Dignity appeared first on Tricycle: The Buddhist Review.

items.articleBody:
Frank Brosow (PH Ludwigsburg) –

Am 25. August 1776 starb der schottische Philosoph David Hume in Edinburgh, der Legende nach in völliger Seelenruhe. Vielen gilt er als der bedeutendste Philosoph, der je auf Englisch geschrieben hat. Humes skeptische Sicht auf die philosophischen Probleme seiner Zeit zu kennen, gehört zum kanonischen Grundwissen, sie zu übernehmen, gilt in der akademischen Philosophie als naiv. Diese dreiteilige Artikelserie möchte allen (Nicht-)Skeptikern zeigen: Ihr wisst ja gar nicht, was ihr verpasst!

Wer immer sich ernsthaft mit westlicher Philosophie beschäftigt, stößt früher oder später auf den Namen Hume. Doch nur Wenige machen seine Art des Philosophierens so sehr zu ihrer Sache, dass sie sich als ‚Humeaner‘ oder „Humeanerinnen“ bezeichnen. Hume führt vor, wie bescheiden die Antworten der Philosophie ausfallen, wenn man den Empirismus beim Wort nimmt und die Grenzen unserer Erkenntnis von den Grenzen unserer Erfahrung bestimmen lässt. So sagte mir einmal ein Kantianer, wenn die Welt wirklich so wäre, wie Hume sie sich vorstellt, wäre sie viel zu langweilig, um über sie zu philosophieren.

Aus meiner eigenen Biografie heraus kann ich das nicht bestätigen. Für mich war es in der Vorlesung über Philosophiegeschichte gerade die Sitzung über David Hume, die mir als Student den Schlüssel zum philosophischen Denken geliefert hat. Innerhalb des Pluralismus philosophischer Theorien stellt Humes Philosophie noch heute eine Perspektive dar, die einzunehmen sich als lohnend erweist. In dieser kurzen Serie von Artikeln möchte ich zeigen, warum es für mich bis heute spannend ist, ein Humaner zu sein.

1. Der Hume, das ist ein Empirist; ihr wisst vielleicht nicht, was das ist.

Humes Philosophie wurzelt in der Einteilung aller Bewusstseinsinhalte in Eindrücke (impressions) und Ideen (ideas). (T 1.1.1.1; SBN 1)1 Eindrücke sind die lebhaften, sinnlich erfahrenen Originale, Ideen ihre weniger lebhaften Kopien. Wenn Hume uns über philosophische oder alltagsprachliche Begriffe aufklärt, fragt er, auf welchem Eindruck die komplexe Vorstellung beruht, die wir mit ihnen verbinden. Findet sich kein solcher Eindruck, wie beim Begriff ‚Substanz‘, ist die Vorstellung leer und der Begriff sinnlos. Ideen bilden die Bausteine unseres Denkens, die sich über Assoziationsprinzipien (Ähnlichkeit, raum-zeitliche Nähe, Ursache/Wirkung) zu Gedankenketten verbinden. (EHU 3.2; SBN 24)

Vernunfturteile über wahr und falsch zerfallen für Hume in Urteile über Tatsachen (matters of fact) und Beziehungen zwischen Ideen (relations of ideas). (EHU 4.1; SBN 25) Urteile über die Beziehung zwischen Ideen fällen wir a priori, weil das Gegenteil der ausgedrückten Beziehung notwendig einen Widerspruch enthält. Urteile über Tatsachen fällen wir a posteriori, indem wir den vorgestellten Inhalt mit der Erfahrung abgleichen. Dem heutigen Sprachgebrauch nach sind Urteile über die Beziehung zwischen Ideen analytisch, d.h. sie zerlegen eine Vorstellung in ihre Bestandteile. (Der Ball ist rund.) Urteile über Tatsachen sind synthetisch, verbinden also Vorstellungen miteinander, die nicht notwendig zusammengehören. (Das Spiel dauert 90 Minuten.)

Drückt eine Kette aus Ideen keine notwendige Beziehung dieser Ideen aus, sondern eine kontingente Tatsache, lässt sich die erste Idee widerspruchsfrei sowohl mit der zweiten Idee als auch mit deren Gegenteil zusammendenken. Erst der Abgleich mit der Erfahrung entscheidet, welche Alternative wahr ist. Erfahrungen haben wir nur in der Gegenwart, nicht mit der Zukunft. Folglich dachte die Philosophie vor Hume, sicheres Wissen könne es nur in Bezug auf die Beziehung zwischen Ideen geben, während alles, was Tatsachen betrifft, nur wahrscheinlich sei.

Hume führt mit dem Beweis (proof) eine dritte Kategorie ein. (T 1.3.11.2; SBN 124) Dass Ereignis A passiert ist oder dass Ereignis B eintreten wird, gilt uns als bewiesen, wenn erstens die Erfahrung in sehr vielen Fällen und ohne Ausnahme gezeigt hat, dass ein Ereignis der Art A regelmäßig mit einem Ereignis der Art B verknüpft ist, und wenn zweitens eine der beiden Arten von Ereignissen der gegenwärtigen Erfahrung präsent ist. Dies ist Humes Lösung des Induktionsproblems. Sein Skeptizismus endet nicht mit der Behauptung, dass das Induktionsproblem unlösbar sei, sondern mit der Feststellung, dass wir darin kein Problem sehen, weil das erläuterte Prinzip in unserem Denken wirksam ist. Was durch einen Beweis bewiesen ist, ist für den Skeptiker Hume „entirely free from doubt and uncertainty“ (Ebd.).

Die Pointe der Theorie wird deutlich, wenn man sie auf sich selbst anwendet: Humes Behauptung, dass wir auf diese Weise über wahr und falsch urteilen, ist die Behauptung einer Tatsache, keine Beziehung zwischen Ideen. Sie kann nicht analytisch als wahr demonstriert werden. Hume definiert die Wahrheit einer Tatsachenaussage auch nicht einfach als ihre Übereinstimmung mit der Erfahrung. Er legt einen Beweis vor, indem er auf vielfache, regelmäßige Erfahrungen ohne Gegenbeispiele hinweist: Menschen empfinden Vorstellungen von den Beziehungen zwischen Ideen als falsch, wenn sie einen gedanklichen Widerspruch beinhalten, während wir Vorstellungen von Tatsachen als falsch empfinden, wenn wir einen Widerspruch zwischen ihnen und der Erfahrung wahrnehmen. Diese Empfindung ist der Eindruck, auf dem unsere Idee von Falschheit als Gegenteil von Wahrheit beruht. Solange die Erfahrung keine Gegenbeispiele für diese Regelmäßigkeit liefert, gilt als bewiesen, dass die menschliche Natur auf diese Weise funktioniert.

Dass es sich hier um einen Beweis handelt, ist ebenfalls keine bloße Setzung in Form einer Definition. Hume weist darauf hin, dass Menschen diese Art der Evidenz immer gelten lassen. Er sagt uns sinngemäß: ‚Gebt zu, dass ihr nicht daran zweifelt, dass die Sonne morgen aufgehen wird, ja dass ihr gar nicht daran zweifeln könnt, weil eure Natur euch zwingt, euch solcher Regelmäßigkeiten sicher zu sein!‘ Wir könnten an solchen Regelmäßigkeiten zweifeln, wenn wir die Erfahrung einer Ausnahme machen würden. Doch solange wir diese Erfahrung nicht machen, können wir nur so reden, als ob wir zweifeln, ohne wirklich davon überzeugt sein zu können, dass die Sonne morgen nicht aufgehen könnte. Derselbe Grad an Gewissheit gilt für natürliche Überzeugungen (natural beliefs) wie die, dass eine Außenwelt jenseits unserer Perzeptionen existiert.

Nachdem Hume dieses Naturgesetz entdeckt hat, erklärt er seine genaue Funktionsweise. Als das empirische Prinzip, das bei Menschen (und vielen Tieren) hinter der Sicherheit im Urteil über Tatsachen steht, identifiziert er die Gewohnheit. (EHU 7.26–30; SBN 73–79) Sie sorgt dafür, dass die Vorstellung einer Tatsache vom Gefühl des Glaubens (belief) begleitet wird, so dass sie in ihrer Lebhaftigkeit näher an den Eindruck der Wahrnehmung des Ereignisses heranrückt. Wenn der Eindruck des Glaubens eine Idee begleitet, wird aus der Fiktion eine Überzeugung. (EHU 5.11–12; SBN 48–50) Wo die regelmäßige Verknüpfung zweier Arten von Ereignissen Ausnahmen kennt (wie wenn eine Medizin nicht immer wirkt) oder wo wir a priori voraussehen, dass ein Ereignis mehrere alternative Folgen nach sich ziehen kann (wie bei einem Münzwurf), verteilt sich der Glaube auf mehrere Alternativen, die wir je nach Grad des Glaubens für unterschiedlich wahrscheinlich halten. (EHU 6.1–4; SBN 56–59)

All diese Behauptungen über die menschliche Natur meint Hume, im erklärten Sinn beweisen zu können. Beweise sind sein Versuch der Übertragung der experimentellen Methode aus den Naturwissenschaften in die Philosophie, wie er sie im Untertitel seines Traktats über die menschliche Natur ankündigt. Als unseren Verstand bzw. unsere Vernunft betrachtet Hume die Summe derjenigen Prinzipien des Denkens, die dauerhaft, unwiderstehlich und allgemein sind (T 1.4.4.1; SBN 225), die also alle Menschen unter empirischen Normalbedingungen wie Wachheit, Gesundheit, Nüchternheit und Aufmerksamkeit stets unwillkürlich dieselben Dinge für wahr und falsch halten lassen. Vernunft ist für Hume nicht das Vermögen, zu erkennen, was unabhängig von der menschlichen Natur wahr ist, sondern Wahrheit ist die Wirkung derjenigen empirischen Prinzipien des Denkens, die wir ‚vernünftig‘ nennen, weil sie uns dauerhafte, unwiderstehliche und allgemeine Sicherheit im Urteil spüren lassen. – Dass diese Science of Man langweiliger ist als Kants ‚kopernikanische Wende‘, wäre erst noch zu beweisen.

2. Der Fehler am naturalistischen Fehlschluss ist nicht die Natur, sondern der Schluss.

Die Vernunft ist bei Hume nur für die binäre Unterscheidung zwischen wahr und falsch zuständig. In Fragen der Wahrscheinlichkeit wird aus diesen beiden Polen ein Spektrum, auf dem die Intensität des Glaubens den Grad der Gewissheit bestimmt. Sofern Menschen vernünftig sind, richten sie den Inhalt und die Stärke ihrer Überzeugungen an der Evidenz aus, d.h. letztlich an logischer oder statistischer Wahrscheinlichkeit. Die Stärke der Evidenz und des ihr entsprechenden Glaubens macht aber nur einen quantitativen Unterschied. Qualitative Unterscheidungen beruhen nicht auf der Vernunft, wie Hume den Begriff verwendet, sondern auf dem Geschmack. (EPM App. 1.21; SBN 294) Werturteile werden weder deduktiv noch induktiv erschlossen, sondern gefühlt.

Was für wahrheitswertfähige Urteile Ideen sind, sind für Werturteile Affekte (passions). Einige Affekte können zum Handeln motivieren, darunter ruhige Affekte, die mit dem Wirken der Vernunft verwechselt werden. (T 2.3.3.4; SBN 415) Andere dienen nur der Beurteilung. Wie Ideen sind auch Affekte durch Assoziationsprinzipien verbunden, hauptsächlich durch Ähnlichkeit in ihrer Qualität (Lust/Unlust), Richtung oder Intensität. (OTP 3.9)

Humes Affekttheorie beweist, dass sich intersubjektiv gültige von rein subjektiven Werturteilen genauso trennen lassen wie vernünftige von unvernünftigen Überzeugungen. Das Kriterium ist hier wie dort, ob ein Urteil auf festen (steady) und allgemeinen (general) Prinzipien des Denkens bzw. Fühlens beruht (OTP 6.19) oder ob es in Inhalt und Stärke durch subjektive Faktoren beeinflusst ist, die Menschen zu unterschiedlichen Urteilen führen. Bei subjektiven Werturteilen lässt sich über Geschmack nicht streiten. Intersubjektivierbare Werturteile beruhen (wie die Vernunft) auf empirischen Maßstäben, deren Wurzel in der menschlichen Natur liegt. Sie kommen in der Ästhetik und in der Ethik vor, wobei Humes Ausführungen zum moralischen Geschmack umfangreicher ausfallen als die zum ästhetischen. (Es 226-249) Da der ästhetische Geschmack bereichsspezifisches Expertenwissen und Übung voraussetzt, wo der moralische nur das Einnehmen fester und allgemeiner Standpunkte der Betrachtung erfordert, wirkt Humes Beweis fester und allgemeiner Prinzipien des Urteilens im Bereich der Ethik plausibler.

Hume beginnt mit einer Art ‚Faktum des Geschmacks‘: Menschen unterscheiden zwischen Tugend und Laster. Wie alle Ideen beruhen auch diese auf einem Eindruck, den Hume im moralischen Gefühl der Billigung bzw. Missbilligung findet. Das moralische Gefühl lässt sich als indirekter, ruhiger Affekt analysieren. Indirekte Affekte erfordern neben ihrer affektiven Ursache (Lust/Unlust) einen gedanklichen Gegenstand. (T 2.1.2.1–6; SBN 277–279) Sehen wir uns selbst als Auslöser angenehmer Gefühle, empfinden wir Stolz, lösen wir unangenehme Gefühle aus, entsteht Scham. Lösen andere angenehme oder unangenehme Gefühle aus, begegnen wir ihnen mit Liebe bzw. Hass.

Moralische Billigung und Missbilligung lassen sich als ruhige Versionen dieser vier Affekte verstehen (T 3.3.1.2–5; SBN 574f.), die nicht nur bei direkt Betroffenen, sondern auch von einem festen und allgemeinen Standpunkt der Betrachtung aus entstehen. Diese Systematik der Affekte deckt sich mit der empirischen Beobachtung, dass Menschen aller Kulturen diejenigen Charaktereigenschaften als Tugenden loben, die der Person, die sie hat, oder ihrem Umfeld angenehm oder nützlich sind. Als Laster gelten Eigenschaften, die für uns selbst oder unser Umfeld unangenehm oder schädlich sind. (EPM 9.1, SBN 268) Was konkret als nützlich oder angenehm gilt, kann sich von Kultur zu Kultur unterscheiden (EPM, Dial., SBN 324-343), aber das allgemeine Prinzip ist für alle menschlichen Kulturen bewiesen.

Humes Gesetz, dass sich nicht gültig von einem Sein auf ein Sollen schließen lässt (T 3.1.1.27; SBN 469f), wurde im 20. Jahrhundert oft als eine Lektion im logischen Schließen gelesen. Wer die Rolle von Beweisen und die Trennung zwischen Vernunft und Geschmack in Humes Philosophie versteht, weiß es besser. Hume erklärt moralische Unterscheidungen ebenso wie die Unterscheidung zwischen wahr und falsch als Ereignisse innerhalb der empirisch erfassbaren Welt. Er weist auf allgemeine und dauerhafte Naturgesetze hin, durch die diese psychologischen Ereignisse erklärt werden. Naturgesetze können im erläuterten Sinne bewiesen, aber nicht im logischen Sinne demonstriert oder abgeleitet werden. Humes Philosophie erklärt die Funktionsweise und das Zusammenspiel der Prinzipien der menschlichen Natur.

Der zentralen Rolle der Gewohnheit und des Glaubens in der Erkenntnistheorie entsprechen in der Moraltheorie das Prinzip der Sympathie und die Gefühle von Lust und Unlust. Sympathie sorgt dafür, dass die lebhafte Idee von etwas Unangenehmem oder Schädlichem in einen entsprechenden Eindruck umgewandelt wird. (T 3.3.2.5; SBN 595) Gleichzeitig führt eine Assoziation von Ideen zum Gedanken an die Person, die diese Gefühle entweder erleidet oder verursacht. Aus diesem doppelten Impuls entstehen indirekte Affekte wie Mitleid oder moralische Missbilligung. (T 2.2.7.16, SBN 369-371) Entsteht statt Mitleid Schadenfreude, so war die Idee des Schadens nicht lebhaft genug, um unser Denken vom Gedanken an uns, denen es im Vergleich gut geht, auf das Opfer des Schadens und dessen Zukunft zu lenken. Entsteht statt dem ruhigen Affekt der moralischen Missbilligung heftiger Hass, so haben wir über die Person, die den Schaden verursacht hat, nicht von einem festen und allgemeinen Standpunkt der Betrachtung, sondern aus der Perspektive von direkt Beteiligten geurteilt.

Humes Moral-Sense Theorie kennt kein ‚unbedingtes Sollen‘, ist jedoch alles andere als subjektiv oder relativistisch. Hume identifiziert moralische Urteile als diejenigen Werturteile über den Charakter eines Menschen, in denen sich alle Menschen einig werden können – sofern sie bereit und fähig sind, diese Bewertung von einem unparteiischen Standpunkt der Betrachtung aus vorzunehmen und sofern ihre Annahmen über die nützliche oder schädliche Tendenz aller Charaktereigenschaft der bewerteten Person in ihrem konkreten, sozialen Umfeld korrekt sind. Diese letzte Prämisse ist schwer zu erfüllen, doch das liegt in der Schwierigkeit, wahre Überzeugungen über den Charakter eines Menschen und über den Grad der Nützlichkeit einer Charaktereigenschaft unter komplexen, sozialen Bedingungen auszubilden, nicht daran, dass die moralischen Urteile, die auf diesen Überzeugungen aufbauen, unsicher wären.

Noch wissen wir nicht, welche Auswirkungen dieser Ansatz auf Humes Theorie des Selbst, der Freiheit und der natürlichen Religion hat. Schauen wir uns die Erläuterungen im nächsten Teil dieser Serie an!

Frank Brosow ist Akademischer Oberrat und Fachkoordinator für Philosophie/Ethik am Institut für Philosophie der Pädagogischen Hochschule Ludwigsburg. Zu Humes Philosophie hat er neben diversen Vorträgen, Artikeln und Herausgeberschaften zwei Monografien verfasst: Hume. Eine Einführung, durchgesehene und erweiterte Neuausgabe, Stuttgart (Reclam) 2021; David Humes intersubjektivistisch-naturalistisches Verständnis von Normativität, Münster (mentis) 2014.

1 Die Clarendon Edition der Werke Humes zählt die Abschnitte und Absätze der Schriften Humes (im Traktat auch die drei Bücher und ihre Teile). Das ermöglicht das Auffinden von Textstellen auch in neueren, deutschen Ausgaben. Der Traktat über die menschliche Natur (T), die Untersuchung über den menschlichen Verstand (EHU) und die Untersuchung über die Prinzipien der Moral (EPM) werden zusätzlich nach der Seitenzählung der englischsprachigen Ausgabe von Selby-Bigge/Nidditch (SBN) zitiert, die Dissertation über die Affekte (OTP) und die Naturgeschichte der Religion (NHR) nur nach der Clarendon Edition. Die Essays Moral, Political and Literary (Es) werden nach der Ausgabe von Miller zitiert, die Dialoge über natürliche Religion (DNR) nach der von Bell.
