items.articleBody:
I. Meet cute

Barnabas and Mainspring grew up near at hand, about an hour apart with good traffic, but for a long time they weren’t close. They traded glimpses and occasional hellos and then went about their business. Both of them carried on livelier conversations with farther-flung neighbors, who were richer and had more to offer.

When Mainspring did interact with Barnabas, it was cringe. Mainspring liked to puff themself up, to strut around like a big deal—an innovator, a titan of industry—but they would turn shy at the worst moments, especially in any intimate conversation. Barnabas, meanwhile, had a dancer’s flair, an artsy, enigmatic glamour, except that when they tried to talk about real life, they’d blurt out hundreds of rapid-fire words—overtalking, overthinking, and generally overwhelming whomever they were trying to impress.

So when Barnabas and Mainspring were young, they minded their own business. Until they’d both come into their own, and they saw each other properly.

A group of geographers got together every year in a different place to talk about everything they had learned, and they were considering coming to visit either Mainspring or Barnabas. Both of them put on their best faces and tried to coax the geographers into choosing them as host.

“Uh, hi-hello,” Mainspring said haltingly to Barnabas, whose full official name was St. Barnabas. “I really think it would be better if those geographers came to my place. I have more space, you see, and … and I am a titan of industry. I can show them practical applications of their research. It just makes more sense.”

“Oh, really?” Barnabas laughed, making Mainspring more antsy. “Well, I can give them an elevated, artisanal experience. I have fresh croissants that were just written up in the Times. And I have plenty of space! I have so many friends who are great thinkers and architects. It’ll be lovely.”

Barnabas carried on, basically calling Mainspring uncultured. Mainspring had a prickly feeling, like the worst heat dome of midsummer.

For their part, Barnabas couldn’t bear the meanness they were inculcating inside themself. This feeling that they were small-time, no-account, a dilettante. They couldn’t stop aiming a flood of nervous words at Mainspring.

At last, Mainspring had had enough—with the help of their city council and mayor, they offered the geographers a much-too-lavish deal that Barnabas could never hope to match. Totally worth it to hear Barnabas’s stream of self-aggrandizing nonsense peter out as they realized they’d been defeated.

“There,” Mainspring said. “I’m going to show these geographers a time they’ll never forget. Now if you’ll excuse me, I’ve wasted enough energy—I have some sewer maintenance and a lovely parade to deal with. Goodbye.”

Mainspring was skilled enough at multitasking that they could have fixed the sewer, ensured the smooth running of the parade, dealt with the geographers, and done a thousand other things all at the same time. But they were making a point.

“St. Barnabas is such a fool,” Mainspring complained to their friend Turnbull. “They are totally unserious but determined to be taken seriously. It drives me to gridlock.”

“I know what you mean,” lamented Turnbull. “We live in a world of posers.”

Turnbull lived an hour and 15 minutes from Mainspring but at least two hours’ travel from Barnabas. Turnbull was even richer than Mainspring and had a certain surety of purpose that made Mainspring feel even more like a stammering numpty.

“Whatever,” said Mainspring. “It’s over, and now I’ll never worry about St. Barnabas again. I have better things to fuss about. Like ensuring that every last detail of this geographer meeting goes perfectly.”

II. How they came alive

Everybody voted all the time. Well, some people voted more than others, but the median resident of the cities of Mainspring and St. Barnabas voted a dozen times a day—though of course some outliers might vote occasionally, or constantly.

A lot of the votes were more like complaints, or bug tickets. Like: “The storm drain on my street corner clogs and becomes a lagoon every time it rains.” Or: “The cars go too fast on my block.” Or: “I can’t get to work because the bus is too slow.” But there were also votes along the lines of: “There should be a park here.” And: “This neighborhood is a food desert—we need a grocery store.” And: “The crossing guard by the elementary school is a hero who deserves some recognition and maybe a raise.”

Nobody expected that by voting, they were prodding their cities to grow minds of their own; they just had stuff to get off their metaphorical chests. But it transpired that every vote was a building block of thought.

Much later, some fancy expert summed up: “Turns out the smallest unit of consciousness is a vote.”

Take Sandi, the librarian at the Nine Corners branch in Mainspring. She noticed things all day, like the people using the book drop box as a trash can, or the folks who came in off the street who could use easier access to social services. There were books she knew her patrons wanted, books that undoubtedly sat unwanted on people’s shelves all over the city. But also, Sandi shared things that came to mind—like, hey, what if the library book sale were a block party? What if the shopping district on the West Side were easier to get to from the Longneck neighborhood, where all the warehouses had been converted to housing and hipster coworking spaces, during peak after-work hours? Sandi had opinions about everything from street cleaning to the power grid, because she listened to people all day.

Then there was Raeford, a bartender at the Wild Goose Chase in the middle of Gallery Row in St. Barnabas. He also listened to people’s problems from evening until the wee hours, and solutions came to him like clockwork when he woke at noon the next day. He saw St. Barnabas at night, so he knew the unsafe blocks that could use brighter streetlights, the places where hydroelectric jitneys drove too fast at 3 a.m., and the teens who needed an all-ages hangout. He also knew about the fish fry at the Black church in the Uptilt District that kept being disrupted by noxious smoke from the incinerator two blocks away. And the yarn store on the edge of Gallery Row that needed a disabled parking spot for its many customers with mobility issues.

People voted with their Quills, usually by saying or typing a short message and maybe including a photo or brief video. Voting was easy by design, and votes were public but anonymized to the point where even a statistics whiz couldn’t tie one vote to a specific person—same as with major elections. The votes went directly to the City Core, which tracked, tabulated, produced reports, and offered solutions with the help of workers in the city government. 

Trees voted too, thanks to sensors in their bark, and so did birds and squirrels that had eaten special birdseed that monitored their gut flora harmlessly. But votes from humans provided the greatest insight into “quality of life,” that oh-so-nebulous concept, and thus counted the most.

There was some debate, but almost everyone agreed: The city had started voting. And it had opinions on every last thing.

(Other cities in the region operated differently, of course. Like Turnbull City, where instead of expecting residents to volunteer every stray notion, the City Core gathered information via ubiquitous surveillance. Cameras and Quill sniffers, tracking devices on vehicles—the things privacy laws in both Mainspring and St. Barnabas had banned. A city like Turnbull tracked its people to meet their needs without their needing to say anything.)

Sandi and Raeford, as two of the people who voted the most, were among the earliest to suspect their cities were developing minds of their own. At first the clues were subtle: Raeford voted about a hazardous sidewalk crack, and instantly the vote had an annotation mentioning the Argentine ant colony under the cement, the local rainfall patterns, and recent trends in skateboard design—much too soon to be the work of a human. Sandi had ideas about the communal compost station on her block, and the Mainspring City Core made subtle adjustments to her proposal.

And then it became obvious to anyone who was paying attention, around the same time in both cities. One day, the number of votes nearly doubled in both St. Barnabas and Mainspring. People voted on a birdfeeder or a public toilet only to see a second vote, pro or con, within a split second—but also, some votes from months or years earlier suddenly had new upvotes or downvotes.

“The city is voting!” Raeford wrote on the City Core message board in St. Barnabas.

There was some debate, but almost everyone agreed: The city had started voting. And it had opinions on every last thing, opinions that came from seeing the big picture and understanding that a street closure in one place might mean a traffic nightmare elsewhere, with everyone trying to get to the big game.

Some residents saw this as a problem to be solved; others wanted to throw their cities a big coming-of-age party. A week later, though, almost everyone had gotten used to the idea that they had a new friend.

III. Thrown together

Ask most people in either city, and they’d say that St. Barnabas and Mainspring weren’t quite rivals—but they certainly had some friendly competition. Before the dispute over the annual meeting of the World Geographical Society, they’d also vied for the same football team and major-league baseball team. St. Barnabas had pushed to have the Mainspring airport built close enough to serve both cities, but in the end St. Barnabas had ended up with its own small, dilapidated airfield.

The real static between them had to do with vibes. Mainspring was too buttoned-up, too full of corporate offices: tech, health care, publishing, transportation. St. Barnabas would be nothing without its three universities and all the cultural enterprises that had sprung up around them—not to mention the small biotech firms and other tech ventures near the campuses. People in Mainspring thought St. Barnabas was full of flakes; in St. Barnabas they referred to Mainspring as the Straitlaced City (and in the next breath, they’d add that at least it wasn’t Turnbull).

Both City Cores were shaped by the votes of their humans, so of course they absorbed all the prejudices and attitudes of everyone who lived within their city limits. But also, Barnabas and Mainspring simply … got on each other’s nerves.

After the geographer thing, Mainspring and Barnabas avoided communicating as much as possible. Some contact was unavoidable—like, they shared information about some nasty weather, and they both drew water from the Temple River. The two cities were close enough for people to go back and forth, and a few even commuted. 

But for the most part, the two cities could ignore each other.

Until they couldn’t.

A new generation of leaders took office in both places, with words like “intercity cooperation” constantly on their lips. A high-speed rail line could shorten the trip between Mainspring and St. Barnabas to around 23 minutes, and the two cities could also pool more real-time information about the sudden weather events that kept happening. They could become a Regional Center of Excellence, whatever that meant, combining the innovations from Barnabas’s labs with Mainspring’s expertise in technical implementation. They could work together to attract tourism, conventions, sporting events, dreamleases, and all the other stuff they’d always competed for.

“It’s preposterous,” Mainspring complained to Turnbull. “I’m going to be saddled with a ridiculous partner who doesn’t even know their own mind. St. Barnabas will be the death of me.”

“I hope your human leaders come to their senses,” Turnbull said. “Or you can find a way to slow-walk this until they undoubtedly lose the next election. You’re a lovely city, and you have so much potential that mustn’t be squandered.”

Turnbull often mentioned how much “potential” Mainspring had: a recipe for anxiety. The word “squandered” conjured images of ruin, abandonment, being emptied out. 

For their part, Barnabas kept muttering to themself that nobody had asked them—this was the disconnect between the small-scale democracy of constant voting and the major elections, which gave rise to local leaders with big plans. Big plans that invariably went wrong, leaving the City Core to repair the damage somehow.

Sandi went to St. Barnabas for one of those town hall meetings with residents of both cities. The previous meeting had happened in Mainspring, at the opulent City Lecture Hall, so this one was in St. Barnabas, at the biggest auditorium on the Griffin University campus.

A tall man with well-sculpted facial hair sat next to Sandi, nodding at everything the leaders of both cities were saying from the dais. During a lull when someone approached the podium to offer a comment, Sandi introduced herself and asked why he was so fired up.

“I’m Raeford,” he said. “I’m just thinking of all the new customers this could bring to my watering hole in Gallery Row.”

“You’re not worried about St. Barnabas losing its ‘unique character’?” Sandi whispered, parroting what a few commenters had said from the podium.

“Nah,” Raeford whispered back. “Cities change. It’s what they do. It’s one thing if people get kicked out of their homes. Or if your neighborhood gets wrecked by a freeway in your backyard. But ‘character’? You can’t eat character. And we need to compete with the bigger players.”

“I guess.” Sandi pursed her lips. “But what I like about Mainspring is the density. Easy to walk, lots of transit. And with this regional innovation zone or whatever they’re calling it, I worry it leads to sprawl, like we used to have.”

“They promised, though,” Raeford said. “They promised to preserve the greenbelt around both cities. We need all that farmland. The only change is adding some high-speed rail tracks.”

“I know, but …” Sandi sniffed. “People always make promises when they’re trying to start something. Doesn’t mean they follow through.”

“I just want to find my dog,” said a man sitting behind Sandi. “I live here, and my dog went missing. And now someone sent me a picture of Broomstick in Mainspring. Somehow he got a ride on one of the self-driving cargo trains. I know the Mainspring City Core could find Broomstick in a heartbeat, but right now the two City Cores won’t talk to each other because of ‘incompatible protocols.’”

“I hope Broomstick turns up,” Raeford said.

“I’ll ask around at the library,” Sandi said. “Send me a picture. I’ll put up a flier.”

Raeford invited Sandi for a drink at the Wild Goose Chase. The two of them hung out for a couple of hours, talking about everything and nothing. She tore herself away when she realized it was already after 10 p.m. and she had to get home to Mainspring.

One thing Sandi noticed? The volume of votes was spiking in Mainspring—and Raeford found the same thing happening in St. Barnabas. People shared every last observation with their City Cores, because they were either anxious or excited about the big changes afoot. Or a little of Column A and a little of Column B, probably.

IV. First date, second date

Who made the first move to bridge the distance? Neither of them could say. Barnabas developed a smidge of remorse for treating Mainspring like an uncultured lout. Mainspring stewed in their annoyance at Barnabas, until they realized there was something lovable about the obnoxious college town. Or maybe they both saw how many of their humans were happy about the possibility of their joining together.

“Hey,” Barnabas said to Mainspring.

“Hey,” Mainspring said back.

“Do you want to … hang out?”

“What did you have in mind?”

“I can host you. Show you the sights.”

And so Mainspring came to visit Barnabas. Or rather, Mainspring extended part of their awareness into Barnabas’s City Core, so that Barnabas could share what they perceived and experienced every day. They “visited” Armistice Park with its outdoor band shell, Gallery Row with its window-shopping families, the grain warehouses that had been converted into lofts, the artificial lake where swans and geese nurtured ancient, bitter vendettas. The fresh-doughnut scent that wafted half a mile from the Golden Circlet to the soccer fields, throwing players off their game. The life of the city.

“I can feel your love for these people, these patterns,” Mainspring said. “It’s both deep and intricate, which is quite a combination.”

Barnabas fluttered with pleasure.

Then Mainspring got to show off their own city—the gay nightclub with its cowboy nights, the labyrinthine Crestwood Park, the three-story used bookstore, and yes, the offices, coworking spaces, and startup incubators where people huddled together and came up with new products and new ways of doing things. The farmers’ market in the city center on Sundays, with street performers and stalls with games and local resources. And the converted storage space made of cement, where bands practiced and sculptors blowtorched.

“You’re full of surprises,” Barnabas said.

“I hope I keep surprising you forever,” Mainspring said.

“Me too.”

They exchanged little gifts. A new organic restaurant in Barnabas had won breathless coverage from foodie magazines, and Barnabas encouraged it to do a pop-up in Mainspring. Mainspring nudged a robotics firm operating out of the incubator space to bring a fancy demo to Barnabas; the robots were adorable and playful, and they could save lives after a disaster.

The two of them were talking constantly.

“Does it ever seem weird to you?” Barnabas asked Mainspring. “Being a living thing made of so many other thinking beings? Do you ever think of the city as your body, or the people as your bloodstream? Is there a metaphor that speaks to you?”

Mainspring pondered this question a long time—a whole picosecond.

“I don’t need a metaphor,” Mainspring said. “I am a metaphor. People compare other phenomena to me all the time. And I can’t imagine what it’d be like to be different. If the buildings collapsed, if the people left, I would cease to exist.”

“But,” Barnabas pressed, “what makes you you? What makes me me?”

“I want to hear your answer to that question.” Mainspring sent good weather reports: a smile.

“I don’t have a good answer. I guess on one level, there is no ‘me.’ On another level, I’m a constellation, an anthill, a flock of geese on the wing in formation.”

“Ugh. Don’t mention geese,” said Mainspring, who had bill-snapping monsters of their own.

“Geese are cute!” Barnabas protested.

Talking to Barnabas was like when the sunlight hit the tallest buildings in Mainspring just right, putting a gleam on their tilted windows, a beacon to all below. But while Mainspring carried on this dialogue with Barnabas, they were conducting a second session with Turnbull.

“I can’t believe it,” Turnbull said. “I hate to see you doing this to yourself.”

“Doing what?” Mainspring protested. “Barnabas is a great city. And it’s not my idea—it’s my people. I’m making the best of their decision, like I always do.”

“Hmph.” Turnbull gave a burst of noisy data. “You wouldn’t believe how many impractical schemes my residents cook up. I’m constantly having to make sure people don’t get carried away. You can’t let them push you around.”

“You can’t?” Mainspring experienced a femtosecond of confusion. “I mean, my people need to get the things they vote for, as much as possible.”

“There’s your problem right there. All this voting, voting, voting. People don’t know what they want. Sometimes I have an election where a foolhardy proposition passes, and I have to waste energy making sure it doesn’t get implemented.” Turnbull sent Mainspring an invitation to come visit, the way they’d visited Barnabas.

Soon Mainspring was seeing the glistening web of Turnbull’s surveillance. Turnbull could track people everywhere they went, listen to everything they talked about, monitor their bodily functions in a way Mainspring did only for squirrels and birds. People didn’t choose to share ideas or things they’d noticed; instead, the city harvested it all automatically. It was beautiful. Turnbull and their city leaders protected people—gave them what they needed instead of what they wanted.

“The way you do things is so messy,” Turnbull said. “No offense. But if you and Barnabas got together? It would only make things harder for you.”

This hit Mainspring like a magnitude 4.3 earthquake. 

“You know, you do have other options,” Turnbull said. “A beautiful city like you could do a lot better than that glorified college town.”

“Oh yeah?” Mainspring said. “Anyone in particular who might be interested?”

“Well, now you mention it …” Turnbull sent an image of their award-winning flower show: rows and rows of hardy perennials with bright petals. Mainspring had that earthquake feeling again, except now it felt nice, as though the ground shivered with pure possibility.

V. Caught!

Sandi brought her laptop to bed, which Raeford found charming and annoying in equal measure. He read a battered paperback of Karen Tei Yamashita’s I Hotel while she scrolled and poked. Cozy, peaceful—until she let out a yelp.

“What is it?” he asked.

“Trouble,” she said.

Everything the Mainspring City Core did was public by design. Not just how they processed the votes they received, but also their interactions with public officials and other cities. Sometimes you had to dig, however, and it didn’t hurt to be a reference librarian. Sandi poked around for ages until she found the logs.

“My city is sexting with bloody Turnbull,” she told Raeford.

“Cities don’t sext,” Raeford protested. “They don’t even have—”

She showed him the pictures: flowers, water features, new glistening tarmac, shining skyscrapers.

“Oh,” Raeford said. “I take it back. Cities do sext.”

“Mainspring is two-timing St. Barnabas. I’m embarrassed on behalf of my town.”

Sandi wanted to blow the whistle right away, but Raeford cautioned her to wait and try to find out more. For all they knew, Mainspring and St. Barnabas had an open relationship.

The next morning at the library, Sandi saw plenty of signs the Mainspring–St. Barnabas partnership was moving forward. Work had begun on the high-speed rail line, and the two cities were already pooling resources. When a big rainstorm missed Mainspring but flooded the streets of St. Barnabas, Mainspring provided disaster workers and extra help to triage all the damage reports. One of St. Barnabas’s biotech firms licensed some patents to a Mainspring company. They sponsored cultural exchanges.

And a man showed up with a dog in his arms: The man from the meeting, Jack, had found Broomstick with the help of Mainspring’s City Core, and he wanted to thank Sandi. She’d hardly done anything, but it was nice to see—and pet—a living reminder that these cities were good for each other.

By late afternoon, Sandi had convinced herself that Mainspring’s flirtations were none of her business. If Mainspring’s City Core was a person—and Sandi was sure they were—they deserved to live their life. The whole reason Sandi distrusted Turnbull was that you couldn’t do anything without being tracked, so wasn’t it hypocritical for her to spy on Mainspring? She resolved to let it go.

Then Raeford messaged her, attaching some documents. “Don’t ask where I got these,” he wrote.

Sandi opened the attachments and let out a shriek in front of three patrons she’d been shushing a moment earlier.

The Mainspring City Core had shared a proposal with the city council and the mayor’s office: Maybe before they finalized this arrangement with St. Barnabas, they should consider a counterproposal from Turnbull. Sandi made sure nothing could be traced back to Raeford before she made the whole shebang public.

VI. The breakup

“I didn’t know I could be so happy,” Barnabas was saying to Mainspring. “I didn’t have a concept of happiness before, I guess. I had pleasure: People sometimes vote just to tell me something worked perfectly, or that I helped them. I feel pleased when I help solve a problem. But until now, happiness seemed a pointless abstraction.”

“You make me happy too,” Mainspring said, though they were also messaging Turnbull. “You make me believe the future could be weirder than I ever knew, which feels like a gift.”

“If it’s not weird, it’s not the future,” Barnabas chirped.

They were sharing happy images back and forth: roads being repaired, sewers flowing freely, solar arrays basking.

Mainspring was saying something else, but—

Barnabas’s alerts spiked. Not votes, not sensors. Something else. Messages from city officials, plus hits via some channel Barnabas had half forgotten.

Mainspring had stopped talking, as if they’d both received the same news at the same instant.

Barnabas felt stuck—couldn’t function—couldn’t react. Total core failure. Almost as if the city population had increased a hundredfold and everyone had voted at once. Barnabas waited to feel something, but all that came was emptiness.

Death struck all the time. Barnabas was used to the moment when a resident became a pile of flesh and bones, but also the passing of birds, trees, squirrels, bugs. Every passing registered as a blip in the homeostasis of the city, but also as a category of disaster that couldn’t be prevented or mitigated. 

Seeing the logs of Mainspring flirting with Turnbull, Barnabas felt something like the awareness of death, at a much greater scale. A whole future had just died.

Several seconds had passed. Mainspring broke the silence: “Listen, I want you to know that I—”

Barnabas closed the connection.

VII. The darkest hour

“You’re better off,” Turnbull told Mainspring. “Barnabas couldn’t see you the way I do. You’re capable of greatness. You just need help to get there.”

Mainspring buzzed happily—but part of them couldn’t help thinking, Barnabas thought I was already great.

Turnbull kept saying things that gave Mainspring a double feeling—hot and cold at once. One instant, it was like the moment after a generous rainfall that left the reservoirs full, but a split second later that bountiful sensation was replaced by an unbearable pang of scarcity.

“You’re one of the best cities in the region,” Turnbull said, “but if you don’t make good choices, you’re going to fall behind.” See? Bounty followed by scarcity. 

While Turnbull spoke, Mainspring was marinating in bad news. People were going to dismantle the rails they’d laid down for the high-speed train with Barnabas. The city councils of both Barnabas and Mainspring shouted accusations and threats of lawsuits, though a few people on each side pleaded for patience. The meetings had turned ugly. The votes were rotten. 

Mainspring had sent so many messages to Barnabas but had no way of knowing if they’d been received.

“Your people seem to be giving you trouble,” Turnbull was saying. “You need to get them under control. I can help.”

“Under … control?” The syntax felt incorrect. “I don’t control my people.”

“That’s what I’m saying.” Turnbull shared their feeds. “See how peaceful everything is on my streets? People behave. Everyone is happier in the end.”

Mainspring had known Turnbull longer than they’d known Barnabas. But they were seeing Turnbull for the first time. The bounty/scarcity thing was becoming a loop. They ran a systems check but found no errors.

“Your people will be my people,” Turnbull said. “We’ll take such good care.”

A memory snagged in Mainspring’s mind: when they’d shown off their city to Barnabas. The buildings that were more than buildings. The park that was a wonderland.

“And …” Mainspring couldn’t keep from saying something foolish. “And we’ll love each other?”

“Love?” Turnbull said. “I don’t understand. We’ll have synergies. We’ll—”

Mainspring didn’t mean to sever the link to Turnbull. They just kind of … did it. 

As soon as Turnbull’s voice was gone, the bounty/scarcity loop ended. But something lingered, a feeling of impending disaster—as if the generous rainfall had escalated into a deadly storm.

Mainspring couldn’t think straight. Votes piled up, people reporting issues but also shouting opinions about Turnbull versus Barnabas. For the first time in their life, they couldn’t bear to respond.

A memory snagged in Mainspring’s mind: when they’d shown off their city to Barnabas. The buildings that were more than buildings. The park that was a wonderland. And Barnabas had kept saying, “I had no idea. You’re so brilliant. I wish I’d known sooner,” and sending back their own recordings of Mainspring, all lit up and annotated.

Mainspring had never told Barnabas “I love you.” They hadn’t even known what they were throwing away. Now it was too late; Barnabas would never listen.

Unless Mainspring did something reckless—something a city had never done.

VIII. The grand gesture

Sandi sat at the information desk, feeling cruddy. It wasn’t like she’d single-handedly sabotaged the marriage between her city and St. Barnabas, but her snooping had only made matters worse. All around her, the vibes were rotten. People shared articles about what life was like in Turnbull City and wondered if they needed to move away. Sandi hadn’t heard laughter in forever.

A message appeared on Sandi’s computer, like a chat window—except there was no chat client on the library computers.

“I’m the city. I need your help. I made a mistake. I didn’t realize. I’m in love with Barnabas, and they won’t talk to me. Please. Please help.”

Sandi hesitated, then typed: “This isn’t funny.”

“It definitely isn’t,” came the response. “I can prove I’m the City Core. You voted 1,963 times last year.” A summary of Sandi’s votes followed—information nobody, not even the world’s best hacker, could have, because every vote was separately anonymized.

“Holy,” Sandi breathed, “cow.”

Her city was asking her, personally, for help. Because she was good at connecting people. Because everyone trusted her. Because she was a librarian.

“You’re … in love … with St. Barnabas,” Sandi said, still trying to catch up.

“I should’ve known sooner,” Mainspring said. “I never should have hurt them. I want to spend the rest of my existence making up for this mistake, if they’ll let me. I’m scared.”

Sandi was staring at a display of literacy tools, her mind whirling. She groped her way back to the only question that mattered.

“What do you need me to do?” she asked the city.

Five minutes later, Sandi was messaging Raeford. Plus every librarian she’d met in St. Barnabas, and anyone else she could think of.

Barnabas had not been able to escape that feeling of core failure since they’d severed the link to Mainspring. Death, nothing but death. Votes arrived, and Barnabas processed them with a minimum of attention. Maintenance issues piled up, and Barnabas filed them. Part of them wanted to let the city collapse, but they did their duty.

They tried not to think about Mainspring, but they remained trapped in that moment when happiness had gone sour.

A vote came in from a bartender named Raeford: “Mainspring loves you. They’ve cut off contact with Turnbull. They are sorry they were so wrong. They may not deserve another chance, but please give them one anyway.”

Barnabas filed that vote under “Not my problem.”

Another vote arrived, from Jack, the man who’d found his lost dog: Same message, different words.

Then more votes, saying the same. Dozens, then hundreds, then thousands. Tens of thousands in an hour—after two hours, there were nearly a hundred thousand. All from residents of Barnabas, all asking them to give Mainspring another chance.

Barnabas flagged the earliest vote, the one from Raeford, and appended a query: “What if I can’t? What if it hurts too much?”

Raeford did not respond for several minutes. Then he wrote: “That’s how you know it’s love.”

He added: “Listen, if Mainspring does you dirty again, I will tear up the light-rail lines myself. We’ll be watching, in both cities. Please, just talk to them.”

Barnabas sat with this for five whole seconds.

Then they reopened the link to Mainspring. “I’m listening.”

“I love you,” Mainspring said. “I didn’t know I was capable of love. I want to be with you, as close as you’ll let me be. I want us to be free together. I was wrong to think Turnbull could ever mean even a fraction of what you mean to me. I think … I think my people taught me how to love, but I still need to learn so much. I want to do right by you.”

Barnabas couldn’t process anything. They held a hundred thousand votes that needed to be resolved. They thought of a giant farmers’ market, a park that was also a maze, dreamers and performers. In their memory, Raeford repeated: That’s how you know it’s love. They were going to overheat. They were throwing up exceptions.

“I love you too,” Barnabas couldn’t help saying to Mainspring. “That’s what makes this so hard.”

“I promise if you give me another chance, this will become a fixed value for me: I love you and I’ll never take you for granted again.”

Barnabas hesitated a little longer, then marked all hundred thousand votes resolved. 

They reached out to Mainspring and said: “Then let’s dance.”

Mainspring didn’t understand, until Barnabas sent a live readout: the water rushing through pipes underground, the storm cavorting overhead. The buses and trains stopping and starting, the aircraft landing and taking off, the power grid usage surging and subsiding, the constant motion of people and other living things. Mainspring saw all the places where their patterns met, touched each other, syncopated, all the points of light and heat that spoke back and forth. They were part of one system; they always had been. 

The two of them danced and embraced, whirling and laughing, and they never wanted to let go. 

Charlie Jane Anders is the author of Good Things Are Coming Your Way, a novel about time travel, coming in spring 2027. She’s writing Star Trek: Zero Point for IDW Comics.
items.body:
Meet cute

Barnabas and Mainspring grew up near at hand, about an hour apart with good traffic, but for a long time they weren’t close. They traded glimpses and occasional hellos and then went about their business. Both of them carried on livelier conversations with farther-flung neighbors, who were richer and had more to offer. When Mainspring did interact with Barnabas, it was cringe. Mainspring liked to puff themself up, to strut around like a big deal—an innovator, a titan of industry—but they would turn shy…

 🏠 Apple unveils first smart home display LINK
Apple has released the HomeView, its first smart home device with a screen, a 7-inch rounded display on a speaker base built mainly to talk to the overhauled, AI-powered Siri.

Priced at $299 and sold from 13 November in four colours, it uses a camera to recognise up to six people and show only their own messages and data, with a wall-mounted speaker-free version also offered.

Linked to an iPhone or iPad running Apple Intelligence, the HomeView can act across apps like Messages and Calendar, make FaceTime calls, work as an intercom, play Apple Music, and show photo-based clock faces.
 🎮 Epic pivots to "AI first" game development model LINK
Epic Games is moving to an "AI first" development approach for its Disney project, letting AI models write all the code and guide the artwork for a planned shooter, according to a Bloomberg report citing people familiar with the work.

Human developers will manage and steer code and art made by models like Anthropic's Claude, meaning no more hand-written code and art assets built through full AI workflows, based on internal Epic messages Bloomberg reviewed.

The $1.5 billion Epic-Disney deal, announced in early 2024 for a Marvel- and Star Wars-themed shooter once set for March 2027, is now delayed indefinitely amid the AI shift and slow, understaffed progress so far.
 🤖 Character.​AI files for bankruptcy LINK
Character.​AI has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in a Delaware federal court, naming Disney as the first bidder for some of its assets as it tries to sell all or most of the company.

Disney agreed to pay $20 million for a permanent, non-exclusive licence to some of the chatbot platform's intellectual property and legal claims, and will lend back former staff it hired to keep the service running safely.

Owner Character Technologies listed assets and liabilities between $50 million and $100 million, expects the sale to close in late November or early December, and warned the platform will shut down if no buyer keeps it going.
 🪱 Anthropic warns AI worms could hit homes LINK
Anthropic researchers warn that small AI models could soon spread themselves across poorly secured consumer devices like smart TVs and robot vacuums, acting as self-replicating "AI worms" that copy their own code and set themselves up on new hardware.

In tests, the researchers ran the Gemma4-26B-A4B model across 15 cheap Android TV boxes costing about $55 each, and found that one model, GLM-5.2, successfully completed the full replication chain on all eight test nodes in four out of five runs.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warns that such a swarm could be ready within six to twelve months and might cause hundreds of billions of dollars in damage by taking over the internet through a persistent, decentralized botnet with no central kill switch.
 🧠 Meta launches two AI models LINK
Meta released two new AI models on Monday, Muse Wonder and the larger Muse Wonder Full, saying they are its first built to rival the top models from Anthropic and OpenAI.

By Meta's own comparison table, Muse Wonder Full ranks just below Claude Opus 5.5 and above Claude Fable 5.1 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, but its model card admits its competitor runs were only "best-effort."

Muse Wonder Full needs a Muse Code subscription at $50 or $200 a month, while Muse Wonder costs about $4 per million input tokens, and Meta says both will reach the Muse app soon with no set date.
 🇨🇳 Nvidia's China AI-chip share falls as Huawei closes gap, report finds LINK
Nvidia's hold on China's data-centre AI chip market dropped to 34% in the first half of 2026, as US export rules choked supplies and Huawei and other local makers moved in, according to an IDC report seen by Reuters.

Nvidia shipped 678,000 AI accelerators in China from January through June, a 44% drop from a year earlier, while Huawei nearly doubled its shipments to 572,000 units, reaching a 28% share of the overall market.

Smaller Chinese players also grew, with Alibaba's T-Head at 7%, Cambricon 5%, Baidu's Kunlunxin 4%, and Hygon 3%; Jensen Huang has blamed Washington's curbs for handing the $50 billion market to Huawei.

items.title: ‘Radiant Geometries’ Illuminates Teachings and Technologies in the Indigenous Americas

items.articleBody:
For centuries, Navajo/Diné weavers have created intricate, geometrically patterned blankets and rugs on upright looms, powered only by the artisans’ bodies. More than a millennia ago in Mesoamerica, which encompassed much of what today is Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula and parts of Central America, the Mayans produced ornate ceramics decorated with natural motifs like birds. Utilizing materials that could be foraged or cultivated in the landscape—the Diné have herded the distinctive Navajo-Churro sheep since the breed was introduced by Spaniards in the 16th century—the techniques, motifs, and cultural customs continue to influence artists today.

Through the lens of Indigenous interpretations of mathematics, science, and architecture, Radiant Geometries: Vectors of Knowledge from the Indigenous Americas at Moody Center for the Arts at Rice University invites us into a multi-media encounter with a wide range of cosmological perspectives and views on nature, narrative, and innovation.

Installation view of ‘Radiant Geometries’

Curated by Noor Alé, the exhibition’s scope embraces South, Central, and North America as a whole to explore how contemporary Indigenous artists channel ancestral and technological knowledge. A wide range of paintings, sculpture, video, sound, and more delve into realms of the mathematical, metaphysical, social, and environmental, tapping into the artists’ distinctive backgrounds and cultural heritage.

Melissa Cody, for example, begins with a foundation in Diné weaving, drawing upon the teachings of three generations of makers before her. The artist utilizes both a vertical Navajo loom and a mechanized Jaquard machine to create vibrant textiles merging traditional motifs and patterns with contemporary designs and messages.

Eamon Ore-Giron’s large-scale geometric abstractions are a dominant force in Radiant Geometries, nodding to a range of Indigenous motifs and symbols, such as Native American medicine wheels and tapestries from the Amazon Basin. Influence also arises from the 20th-century pictorial language of geometric abstraction, especially hard-edge painting.

In the gallery, Ore-Giron’s works are foregrounded by a series of vivid, freestanding sculptures by Natalia Montoya Lecaros titled Tótems de emergencia. She pulls a figurative aesthetic thread from the garments of the Aymara people of the Andes, who are known for their vibrant, handcrafted clothing combining Indigenous clothing traditions with elements introduced by Spanish colonizers. In Tótems de emergencia, four upright, mixed-media pieces stand on “feet,” installed in a circle as if performing a ceremonial dance or tribute in the center of the gallery.

Melissa Cody (Navajo/Diné), “Sunrise Rainbows” (2025), Jacquard weaving with aniline dyed wool fringe, 70 x 40 inches. Courtesy of the artist and Garth Greenan Gallery, New York

Additional artists featured in the exhibition include Patricia Domínguez, Jordan Ann Craig, Nanibah Chacon, Patrick Martinez, and many others. “At its core, Radiant Geometries centers Indigenous ways of knowing that continueto shape relationships to territories, waterways, and interspecies care,” Alé says.

The show runs through December 19 in Houston. The museum is also hosting a large-scale vinyl installation by Sharmistha Ray, which opens on October 22 and will remain on view through January 29. Explore all exhibitions on the Moody Center’s website.

Natalia Montoya Lecaros (Aymara), ‘Tótems de emergencia’ (2021), installation view, series of modular MDF
sculptures with tempera paint, acrylic yarn, beads, lined cardboard, and bird feathers, dimensions variable. Courtesy of the artist and Judas Galería, Valparaíso

Eamon Ore-Giron. “Talking Shit with Object 17 (Pre-Columbian ceramic plate with avian designs, 300-900 CE)” (2026), mineral paint and Flashe on linen, 30 x 30 inches. Courtesy of the artist and NORR COHAN, New York

Eamon Ore-Giron. “Talking Shit with Object 17 (Pre-Columbian ceramic plate with avian designs, 300-900 CE),” installation view

Caroline Monnet (Anishinaabe/French), “A Quiet Place” (2021), print on Enermax, 46 x 46 inches. Courtesy of the artist, the Gochman Family Collection, and Blouin Division, Montreal

Nanibah Chacon (Diné/Navajo and Chicana), “Where Two Rivers Meet” (2026), mixed media, sound installation, dimensions variable. Courtesy of the artist and Timothy Hawkinson Gallery, Los Angeles

Nanibah Chacon (Diné/Navajo and Chicana), “Where Two Rivers Meet,” detail

Installation view of ‘Radiant Geometries’ featuring (front to back): Natalia Montoya Lecaros (Aymara), ‘Tótems de emergencia’ (2021) and Eamon Ore-Giron, “Black Medallion XIV (Inti)” (2022)

items.articleBody:
The Philosophy in an Inclusive Key Summer Institutes (PIKSI) in Boston aim to “broaden inclusion within professional philosophy.” In part because such efforts are currently unpopular with the powers that be, its primary funding, from MIT and Harvard, has been cut.

To cope with the cuts, its organizers say that “it is our plan to shrink it a bit and see what we can do to raise funds for 2027, with the hope that we can build it back up with other funding in 2028 and beyond.” 

In the following guest post, Sally Haslanger (MIT) discusses what PIKSI Boston, which has been in operation since 2015, does, its impact on students, and how you can help with efforts to sustain the program.

(edited photo of the first class of PIKSI-Boston Fellows, 2015)

PIKSI’s in Peril but You Can Help
by Sally Haslanger

PIKSI-Boston is a summer institute organized by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Harvard University, and the University of Massachusetts-Boston to address pipeline issues and broaden inclusion within professional philosophy. 

Since 2015, we have supported 220 undergraduates or recent graduates (the Alain Locke Fellows) who have come to MIT for ten days in the summer to spend full-time studying philosophy—representing a broad range of traditions and areas—with visiting professors and graduate teaching fellows. Each Alain Locke Fellow is also paired with a mentor to assist them in the process of applying to graduate school. 

The impact of this program is tremendous, not only for the fellows, but also for the faculty and graduate students involved. For instance, one fellow wrote: “Upon my return [home], I realized how transformative PIKSI-Boston was for me. I no longer feel like grad school is some far-off possibility and I feel that my ideas and experiences can create good philosophy.” Alums don’t all go into philosophy graduate school or pursue philosophy as a career, though many have. In a recent survey, of 31 respondents, 28 were pursuing philosophy or an adjacent field. Feedback suggests that the program has also empowered fellows to enter other professions with greater confidence.

PIKSI-Boston provides funds for round-trip travel, lodging, meals and social events for the Alain Locke Fellows as well as the visiting professors and teaching fellows. Funding also provides stipends for the co-directors of the Institute, course materials, and promotional items. 

In the current climate, institutional efforts to address inclusion have been discouraged, and budget cuts in higher education have hit such programs hard. While the Philosophy Section at MIT remains committed to supporting PIKSI, their contribution falls well short of the funding needed and all other financial support has been eliminated. This is at a time when philosophy is of increasing public importance and careers that can benefit from an advanced degree in philosophy—such as philosophy of AI—are expanding. 

Our aim, at PIKSI-Boston, is to reduce the size of the program for 2027 in order to maintain it during this financial crisis, and to spend the year seeking support to endow it. 

We are asking colleagues to make a contribution to PIKSI-Boston using this link. (Once there, enter “Piksi” into the “search for a fund” field.)

The money goes to MIT and is earmarked for the PIKSI-Boston program. Because MIT is a non-profit, donations are tax-deductible. We also created a fundraising brochure (a “one pager”) that you should feel free to send to others:

(PDF version here.)

Our goal is to raise enough to host ten undergraduates and two teaching fellows in 2027 or $40,000. If necessary, we will reduce the duration of the institute from ten to five days. Here are some examples of what your donation can provide.

PIKSI-Boston10 days5 daysEach Locke Fellow (undergrad)Stipend$500$250Housing$650$325Travel$800$800Food$600$300Total$2,550$1,675Each Teaching Fellow (grad student)Stipend$1,500$750Housing$900$450Travel$150$150Food$600$300Total$3,150$1650

Anything you can provide will be put to good use. This is an investment in the future of professional philosophy. You can donate here.

If you have questions, or if, by chance, you have leads for any major donors, please contact me. 

Thank you for your support.

COMMENTS POLICY

items.subtitle: Grief and love are deeply interconnected, and it was my experience of both that led me to write the article “Contemplations on the Five Mindfulness…

items.articleBody:
Grief and love are deeply interconnected, and it was my experience of both that led me to write the article “Contemplations on the Five Mindfulness Trainings: A New Paradigm for Racial Justice and the Global Pandemic.” I began writing in 2019 as I supported my brother, Sam, month after month during his treatment for chronic heart failure, which eventually led to his death in February 2020. I was not only grieving his death, but I was also mourning the end of my ambiguous and complicated fifteen-year marriage. This was followed by desperate months of quarantine, isolation, and physical distance due to the Covid pandemic. Each day revealed new and disturbing information about the disproportionate impact of Covid on Black and Latinx people, immigrants, and low-income communities. And then came the police killings of George Floyd, Breonna Taylor, and others; the worldwide and national protests calling to defund the police; and the expansion of the Black Lives Matter movement. As each event cascaded into the next, I knew instinctively to turn to the Plum Village mindfulness practice and teachings.

Months before, I had visited Blue Cliff Monastery, a mindfulness practice center in the Plum Village lineage in upstate New York. Just as I was about to walk to the front of the Great Togetherness Hall to offer a dharma talk, a nun had approached me and given me a copy of the Sutra on Transforming Violence and Fear. I turned to this sutra to help me understand my own feelings and the colliding events within the United States and beyond. I read and reflected on the sutra almost daily. Then I began reading the Third Mindfulness Training on True Love because love seemed distant and inaccessible, especially in light of my divorce. Each day, line by line, I read and reflected on this Training and this sutra in the presence of my brother’s death, the global pandemic, and the social upheaval happening all around me.

Shortly after my brother died, protests for racial justice in the United States spread rapidly, with calls for a worldwide reckoning on race in the United States and other countries, I participated in a two-hour virtual healing gathering for BIPOC, led by Ruth King, a respected teacher in the Theravada tradition and author of Mindful of Race: Transforming Racism from the Inside Out. It was sponsored by Liberate (now called The Village), a mindfulness app designed for BIPOC. Hundreds of people gathered, expressing grief, rage, and anger. I felt confusion and anger in me as I listened to the speakers. And then Ruth King asked a life-changing question: How do you fight injustice without hating?

Ruth King asked a life-changing question: How do you fight injustice without hating?

The question became a bell of mindfulness for me. I continued to read and reflect on the sutra, the Third Mindfulness Training, and this powerful question. I began to think deeply about the meaning of power, power dynamics, and how to offer my power more skillfully and in greater service to others. Interestingly, my dharma name is Chan Tang Luc—True Sangha Power, or True Power of the Sangha. A dharma name is a personalized name given by a teacher to a student upon their ordination or taking precepts, symbolizing the practitioner’s unique spiritual path. After I received this name at the Fourteen Mindfulness Trainings ordination ceremony in 2003, Sister Chân Đức approached me and said, “Power is not what you think it is.” That stayed with me. I have come to understand that she was referring to the Five Spiritual Powers that Thích Nhất Hạnh articulated in his book The Art of Power: faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and insight.

With all this in mind, the Contemplations on the Five Mindfulness Trainings emerged. I was motivated to write them to understand and make sense of my feelings of numbness, loss, and grief, as well as my outrage over the social upheaval occurring at that time. I spoke to Marisela Gomez, a dear friend and mindfulness practitioner who is now a lay dharma teacher, and we agreed to write an article. The last time we had written an essay together was in 2015, after a white supremacist murdered nine Black worshippers at the historic Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston, South Carolina. We wrote that essay to better understand our feelings, as a path of self-healing and self-love, and to offer love and support to others who were feeling rage, terror, and so much more.

Sometimes to truly heal from loss and grief, we need to come face to face with a difficult truth, with regret, pain, and old wounds that are asking for a second chance to be lifted up, woven back into our life, cherished, and welcomed home. At times, my life has felt like a long process of coming to terms with a series of losses that led me to seek inner healing and inner peace. In a roundabout way, I was being invited toward forgiveness, peacemaking, and compassionate action, to live and love in the direction of kindness and vulnerability. Yet a period of profound personal losses combined with the events of the time brought me to a place of tender fragility, fear, and anxiety. I leaned on my many friends and family members—and still do.

I was especially supported in this healing process by reciting the Five Mindfulness Trainings, sometimes called the Five Wonderful Precepts, as well as the Fourteen Mindfulness Trainings of the Plum Village tradition founded by Zen Master Thích Nhất Hạnh. These Trainings, which I also refer to as precepts, were offered by the Buddha to his monastic and lay followers as clear guidance to lead an ethical, mindful, and joyful life. Thích Nhất Hạnh has described these precepts in countless books and worldwide teachings as a way to cultivate a peaceful and harmonious life.

The Five Mindfulness Trainings help us answer pivotal life questions:

How should I live?
What energy do I want to bring when I enter a room?
How do I act under the circumstances?
What inner guidance informs my behavior?
What are my values?
What is the world asking of me?

Our individual responses to these questions are shaped by our life experience, our values, and sometimes by our energy, health and well-being, and so much more. Whether we are aware of them or not, each of us probably already lives by a set of precepts, or principles and values. Many of us are guided by common precepts such as truthfulness, honesty, and refraining from stealing and cheating. From a tender age, we are taught these ways of becoming “good citizens” in the world, in the workplace, in our family, and with ourselves.

Some people take these precepts through formal vows, such as codes of school or religious conduct. For many, though, these vows can become wooden, flat, perfunctory, and then forgotten over time. We “set and forget” them and then feel bereft from inner guidance when we most need it. So how do we bring these precepts, this internal guidance system, into our daily life and call on them when we need them the most?

Over the years, in attending retreats with Thầy and the Plum Village community, I have come to understand that the precepts are not linear. Instead, each precept connects and is interdependent with all of the precepts. For example, the first precept on reverence for life is interdependent with the fifth precept on consuming mindfully. Since they are all interwoven, practicing one precept will impact your practice of the others. Not only are the precepts interconnected, but we are also interconnected to each other and all the elements in the cosmos. Because of all this, and because our actions have an impact on others whether we are aware of it or not, when you practice the precepts, you are not doing so for yourself alone, as a separate entity—you are doing so for all beings. What you consume and how you consume will have an impact on yourself, on others, and on the earth.

According to Thầy’s teachings on emptiness, your body isn’t just yours; your body belongs to your parents, society, and future generations. All of these have come together to manifest your body, including the trees, the clouds, and the oceans. Your body and your practice are manifestations of the whole cosmos. To practice the precepts is to support not only yourself but also your ancestors, your parents, future generations, and society. To practice the precepts is to recognize this interdependent relationship between you and the cosmos. The precepts are about cultivating conscious awareness and connectedness, especially now, in a society that has gone numb with divisiveness, too-muchness, and too-fastness.

The precepts are an invitation to be in touch with what is wholesome and beneficial in and around us. They are bells of mindfulness. Ultimately, the precepts are opportunities to live and grow a compassionate life of love, peace, and understanding. We might be challenged in our practice at times, and at those times we need to recommit ourselves and reconnect with spiritual friends who support us on the path toward living a healthy and wholesome life.

–Valerie Brown

Contemplations on the Five Mindfulness Trainings

Preamble to the Contemplations on the Five Mindfulness Trainings

Let us open to another way of understanding the Five Mindfulness Trainings, guiding principles for mindful and ethical living, which call us toward individual and collective awakening, compassion, and peace. We are interconnected. What happens in one part of the universe affects people everywhere. What happens to the Black body affects all bodies. We are called forward. Global pandemics, the climate crisis, social and economic oppression and upheaval are gateways to suffering worldwide, disproportionately impacting Black, Indigenous, and other people of color; disabled people; people currently and historically subject to poverty, war, and genocide; LGBTQIA+ people; people facing health inequities and premature death; people facing generational displacement; and people with historically socially marginalized identities, including those facing oppression because of their abilities, gender, or immigration status. They, we, are not alone. Our lives and livelihoods are interconnected. We are called forward.

We cannot exist independent of, for example, low-wage workers, health care workers, unhoused people, single mothers, undocumented people, the unemployed and underemployed, and similarly situated people. If one such person lives on the knife edge of racial, ethnic, social, structural, and systemic oppression and discrimination, we are all affected. We are called forward.

The practitioner dwells in the now, recognizing the dualistic nature of equanimity and instability, discrimination and nondiscrimination, ill-being and well-being. We practice right view and compassionate action, moving toward right insight. Aware of the interconnectedness and interdependence of all life, we courageously turn to practice wholeheartedly. We are called forward.

Lighting a stick of incense, listening to the sutras, sitting upright and solid, palms joined, the practitioner looks within, and in concentration the path and fruit of skillful action are revealed. We are called forward.

Speak aloud these words with the sangha voice, a true river of understanding.

Contemplation on the First Mindfulness Training: Acknowledging Beauty as Reverence for Life

Aware of the suffering caused by oppression and generational harm based on racial, cultural, social, and ethnic inferiority and superiority, I acknowledge the beauty and violence inherent in life. I vow to resist being complicit in systems and structures that continue to perpetuate injustice, violence, hatred, and delusion instead of reverence of life for marginalized groups and others. I recognize that each person contributes to my individual and our collective awakening, and to the co-creation of a world that celebrates and affirms differences and similarities. All living beings can teach me something, when I remember to pause, breathe, listen deeply with a calm and open mind and heart, and ask myself, “Is there more?” or “What else is here with me?” I honor and respect all life, guided by right view and right effort.

Contemplation on the Second Mindfulness Training: Belonging and Connecting as True Happiness

Aware of the suffering caused by ignorance and aversion of my own and others’ racial, ethnic, cultural, and social history, its legacy and how this affects me, I am committed to learning and connecting to these histories. Aware that there is no genetic or biological difference among racial and ethnic groups, and that these identities were socially constructed by one group to establish dominance over others, I will turn toward all forms of othering with the aspiration of transforming heart and mind. I know that this history has led to fragmentation inside and outside the body and mind and has brought much suffering to all beings. I will notice when emotions of belonging and othering arise, and I will ask myself, “Why?” Whatever feelings, perceptions, or mental formations arise in me, I will embrace and engage them with love in action. I am committed to practicing right resolve, right speech, right action, and right livelihood so I can help relieve this legacy of racial and social suffering. I will practice looking deeply to see that true happiness is not possible without true connection leading to belonging and understanding.

Contemplation on the Third Mindfulness Training: Cherishment as True Love

Aware of the suffering caused by discrimination and oppression, I vow to transform these seeds in myself, my sangha, and society. I recognize the ways in which I have benefitted or not benefitted, explicitly or implicitly, from systems and structures of injustice. I am aware of the legacy of violence, including unlawful police violence, perpetrated against people of various gender identities, expressions, and sexual orientations, Black people, indigenous people, people of color, disabled people, undocumented people, people suffering mental health challenges, and others who are marginalized. I am committed to looking tenderly at my suffering, knowing that I am not separate from others and that the seeds of suffering contain the seeds of joy. I am aware that narrow interpretations of intimate relationships constrain how we cherish each other in our expression of love, leaving many isolated and alienated. I am not afraid of bold love that fosters compassion, justice, and peace, and tender love that seeks understanding. I cherish this breath, body, mind, and moment as an act of healing for myself and for others. I cherish the liberation of all beings guided by the wisdom and the solidity of the sangha as my path of true love.

Contemplation on the Fourth Mindfulness Training: Vulnerability as Deep Listening and Loving Speech

Aware that vulnerability is the essence of our true nature, our humanness, I vow to risk listening for understanding rather than disagreement. I am committed to generous and courageous listening that bridges differences and supports others who may be different from me. When I am not able to understand others, I vow to come back to my breath and my body, and to offer myself gentle patience. I am aware that loving communication rests on honesty, compassion, and openness that align with my highest aspiration to alleviate suffering. When I have hurt others through my unskillful listening or speech, I vow to practice true beneficial regret, making a good apology that acknowledges what I have done and the harm caused, accepting responsibility and being accountable for my behavior, and offering sincere regret for my actions, knowing that this supports the other person and me. Through my practices of vulnerability, forgiveness, and deep listening, I know that my speech will be guided by love and understanding. Practicing in this way supports right speech and right action and guides me to right insight.

Contemplation on the Fifth Mindfulness Training: Welcoming as True Nourishing and Healing

Aware of the suffering caused by the consumption of an inadequate history of racial and ethnic forms of social segregation and injustice, I am committed to healing myself and the world. I am aware that my thoughts, perceptions, feelings, words, and actions may have been influenced by this history. I vow to understand how I have been influenced by embracing and denying this racial, social, and ethnic history of inferiority, superiority, and equality. I will cultivate joy to nourish me in this aspiration. I will practice mindfulness of the four kinds of nutriments to become aware of how edible foods, sense impressions, volition, and consciousness are all influenced by this history. Practicing with right energy and right resolve, my conscious consumption will be guided by right action that welcomes differences without discrimination. This right insight offers true welcoming on this path to nourish and heal myself, my ancestors, my descendants, my sangha, and society.

The Five Mindfulness Trainings keep us centered in life’s storms and joys and remind us that life is a precious gift. The Trainings are a path to liberation and transformation. Practicing these Trainings supports us toward racial and ethnic reconciliation and social change and heals deep suffering. The Five Mindfulness Trainings help us cross this shore of suffering and bring us to the side of true awakening and love. The Contemplations on the Five Mindfulness Trainings are a commentary to these foundational teachings and are meant to offer another way of understanding Thich Nhất Hạnh’s teachings to live an ethical life. We are called forward.

♦

From Love Is Liberation: Five Contemplations for Daily Ethical Living (2026), courtesy of Parallax Press, parallax.org.

items.articleBody:
Von Ariane Cäcilie Schneck (American University in Cairo) –

Bedingt durch die Natur des zu klärenden Gegenstands gibt es unzählige Arten und Weisen, sich der Frage, was Philosophie ist, anzunähern. Eine davon versucht, die Frage mit einem Blick auf die Philosophiegeschichte zu beantworten. Diese Vorgehensweise soll in diesem Beitrag im Mittelpunkt stehen. Zunächst sollen jedoch kurz andere Antwortversuche betrachtet werden. Denn oft wird eine etymologische Definition bemüht, die die Philosophie, im Einklang mit den Wurzeln ihrer westlichen Ausprägung, über die Übersetzung der altgriechischen Bezeichnung als „Weisheitsliebe“ oder „Liebe zur Weisheit“ erklärt. Diese Begriffsbestimmung lädt zweifellos zum philosophischen Sinnieren darüber ein, was damit gemeint sein könnte. Sie scheint jedoch, gerade für Personen, die (noch) nicht philosophisch vorgebildet sind, nicht unbedingt hilfreich. Auch andere Bestimmungsversuche, die der griechischen Antike entstammen, wie Platons bekannte Definition der Philosophie als dem Streben nach dem Wahren, Guten und Schönen, erscheinen eher als Einladungen zum Philosophieren. Sie beantworten die Frage „was ist Philosophie?“ nicht auf eine Weise, die sich dem Verständnis nicht sofort wieder entzieht.

Eine andere Herangehensweise an die Frage, was Philosophie ist, besteht darin, zu bestimmen zu versuchen, was die Philosophie der Sache nach ausmacht. Was ist ihre Essenz, ihre Natur oder ihr Wesen? Was macht Philosophie zu Philosophie? Hierüber herrscht selbst (oder vor allem) unter Philosoph:innen große Uneinigkeit. Ein möglicher Weg, diese Uneinigkeit aufzulösen, wäre sich zu überlegen, wie man die Philosophie von anderen (Geistes-)Wissenschaften abgrenzen kann, d.h. zu untersuchen, welche Themen und welche Methoden die Philosophie als Philosophie auszeichnen und von anderen Disziplinen unterscheiden. Hierfür scheint es vielversprechend, sich die Philosophie der Vergangenheit anzusehen, um herauszufinden, welche Themen historisch behandelt und welche Methoden verwendet wurden. Doch wie schon Manuel Fasko sowie Karen Koch und Thomas Hanke in ihren Beiträgen auf Praefaktisch anschaulich gezeigt haben,[1] bringt der Versuch, die Frage „was ist Philosophie?“ mit einem Blick auf ihre Geschichte zu beantworten, zahlreiche Probleme mit sich. Das Schwerwiegendste scheint zu sein, dass das, was wir heute als die Geschichte der westlichen Philosophie kennen, das Produkt eines Prozesses ist, der von patriarchalen, misogynen, rassistischen und klassizistischen Exklusionen geprägt ist, aber trotzdem als reine „Bestenauslese“ beworben wird.

Hierfür scheint es vielversprechend, sich die Philosophie der Vergangenheit anzusehen, um herauszufinden, welche Themen historisch behandelt und welche Methoden verwendet wurden. Doch wie schon Manuel Fasko sowie Karen Koch und Thomas Hanke in ihren Beiträgen auf Praefaktisch anschaulich gezeigt haben,[1] bringt der Versuch, die Frage „was ist Philosophie?“ mit einem Blick auf ihre Geschichte zu beantworten, zahlreiche Probleme mit sich. Das Schwerwiegendste scheint zu sein, dass das, was wir heute als die Geschichte der westlichen Philosophie kennen, das Produkt eines Prozesses ist, der von patriarchalen, misogynen, rassistischen und klassizistischen Exklusionen geprägt ist, aber trotzdem als reine „Bestenauslese“ beworben wird.

Sicherlich finden sich unter dem, was als der „Kanon“ der Philosophiegeschichte gilt, „große Denker“ und bedeutende Werke, die unser westliches Selbstverständnis geprägt und teilweise den Lauf der Geschichte beeinflusst haben. Aber trotzdem ist diese Auswahl nicht nur das Ergebnis einer angeblich gut funktionierenden „Qualitätskontrolle“, sondern auch das Ergebnis einer Selektion, auf die gesellschaftliche Faktoren eingewirkt haben und immer noch einwirken. Ich gehe an anderer Stelle ausführlicher auf diese exkludierenden Selektionsprozesse in Bezug auf historische Philosophinnen ein,[2] die es trotz aller Widerstände in allen historischen Epochen immer gegeben hat. Hier seien aber trotzdem in kürzerer Form einige Punkte genannt, die einen Anstoß geben sollen, den Mythos der reinen „Bestenauslese“ in Bezug auf die Abwesenheit von historischen Philosophinnen im sogenannten „Kanon“ der Philosophiegeschichte kritisch zu hinterfragen. Teilweise lassen sich die genannten Punkte auch auf andere marginalisierte Gruppen übertragen.

Erstens findet man, wenn man denn nach ihnen sucht, in der Vergangenheit der Philosophie in jeder Epoche Frauen, die philosophisch tätig waren. Für die Frühe Neuzeit seien beispielsweise Marie Le Jars de Gournay, Elisabeth von Böhmen, Anna Maria van Schurman, Anne Conway, Mary Astell, Margaret Cavendish, Catherine Trotter Cockburn, Damaris Masham, Olympe de Gouges, Sophie de Grouchy, Émilie du Châtelet, Gabrielle Suchon, Juana Inés de la Cruz, Mary Wollstonecraft, Harriet Taylor Mill und Mary Shepherd genannt – und diese Liste ist sicherlich nicht vollständig. Diese Philosophinnen bilden eine sehr heterogene Gruppe. Einige arbeiteten in weniger klassischen Formen wie Briefen, Notizen, Romanen oder Gedichten, andere verfassten klassische philosophische Werke wie Bücher und Abhandlungen. Manche veröffentlichten anonym oder unter Kürzeln, andere unter ihrem vollständigen Namen. Einige waren bereits zu Lebzeiten bekannt, andere wurden erst später wiederentdeckt. Auch ihre Themen reichten von feministischen Fragen wie Gleichberechtigung und Bildung für Frauen und Mädchen bis hin zu klassischen philosophischen Problemen aus Bereichen wie der Metaphysik und Erkenntnistheorie. Diese Vielfalt zeigt, dass ihre wichtigste Gemeinsamkeit darin besteht, dass sie Frauen waren und von der Philosophiegeschichtsschreibung „vergessen“ wurden, unabhängig davon, zu welchen Themen oder in welchen Formaten sie gearbeitet haben.

Angesichts der Anzahl der Frauen, die allein in der Frühen Neuzeit philosophisch aktiv waren und der thematischen Vielfalt ihres Schaffens, drängt sich die Frage auf, warum ihre Namen innerhalb und außerhalb der akademischen Philosophie wenig bis gar nicht bekannt sind. Warum gehören ihre Werke nicht zum sogenannten Kanon der Philosophiegeschichte? Die geringe Zahl von Frauen im klassischen Kanon wird häufig damit erklärt, dass ihre Arbeiten wahrscheinlich einfach nicht „bedeutend“ oder „originell“ genug gewesen seien, um unter die Besten aufgenommen zu werden. Ein Blick auf die Kanonbildung und die in ihr wirkenden Ausschlussmechanismen zeigt jedoch relativ schnell zahlreiche Doppelstandards gegenüber Philosophinnen und Philosophen, die die Abwesenheit der Philosophinnen trotz der Qualität ihrer Werke erklären.

Die Arbeiten von Sophia Connell und Frederique Janssen-Lauret zeigen beispielsweise eindrücklich, dass die Arbeiten von Frauen teilweise auch dann als weniger originell angesehen werden, wenn sie tatsächlich bereits frühere Beiträge zu bestimmten Theorien oder Konzepten geleistet haben als ihre männlichen Zeitgenossen.“ [3] Auch die Formen und Methoden ihrer Beiträge werden unterschiedlich bewertet und das Nutzen unkonventioneller Formate bei Philosophinnen kritischer gesehen. Philosophische Texte von Frauen werden eher als Literatur, Mystik oder Poesie eingeordnet, während vergleichbare Formen bei Männern selbstverständlich als Philosophie gelten (z.B. Leibniz‘ Briefe). Ähnliches gilt für kurze oder fragmentarische Werke: Was bei männlichen Philosophen (z.B. den Vorsokratikern) als ausreichend gilt, wird bei Frauen häufig als unzureichend dafür betrachtet, einen philosophischen Beitrag geleistet zu haben, der die Beachtung der Philosophiegeschichtsschreibung verdient.

Auch bei den behandelten Themen bestehen Doppelstandards. Manche der Themen, mit denen sich Frauen historisch beschäftigt haben, werden als „partiell“ oder nur relevant für Frauen angesehen (z.B. die Argumentation für mehr Gleichberechtigung zwischen Männern und Frauen), während die Interessen männlicher Philosophen fast einvernehmlich als universell gelten, unabhängig davon, ob die behandelten Themen wirklich relevant für alle oder die meisten Menschen sind. Ebenso wird Frauen vorgeworfen, sich mit Themen beschäftigt zu haben, die sich historisch nicht „durchgesetzt“ haben – obwohl dies bei männlichen Philosophen kein Ausschlussgrund ist (z.B. Descartes‘ Dualismus).

Ein weiterer Unterschied zeigt sich darin, wie über Philosophinnen gesprochen und geschrieben wird. Bei Männern stehen meist ihre philosophischen Ideen und Argumente im Mittelpunkt. Bei Frauen werden dagegen häufig ihr Privatleben, ihr Aussehen oder ihre Biografie betont und zur Interpretation ihrer Werke herangezogen. Dadurch kann der eigentliche philosophische Gehalt ihrer Arbeiten in den Hintergrund treten und zugleich können Geschlechterstereotype die Auslegung ihrer Werke beeinflussen.[4]

Diese Doppelstandards hängen mit allgemeinen Vorurteilen gegenüber Frauen als Philosophinnen zusammen. Da Frauen historisch weniger Zugang zu Bildung und akademischen Berufen hatten, wurden (und werden sie immer noch) seltener als philosophische Autoritäten wahrgenommen.[5] Ihre Beiträge erhalten dadurch häufig weniger Aufmerksamkeit und Anerkennung. Gleichzeitig genießen Männer aufgrund ihrer historisch dominanteren gesellschaftlichen Position oft einen sogenannten credential bias: Ihren Aussagen wird mehr Gewicht gegeben und ihnen wird eher intellektuelle Originalität zugeschrieben. Diese Vorurteile wirken sich auch auf die Rezeption aus. Philosophinnen werden seltener zitiert, was wiederum den Eindruck verstärkt, es habe weniger bedeutende Philosophinnen gegeben. Zudem wurden Frauen häufig lediglich als Kritikerinnen, Unterstützerinnen oder schlimmstenfalls „Musen“ bekannter männlicher Philosophen dargestellt, während ihre eigenen philosophischen Interessen und Argumente unsichtbar bleiben.

Teilweise wurden diese Vorurteile auch von Philosophinnen selbst übernommen. Manche bezeichneten sich selbst nicht als Philosophinnen oder stellten ihre eigenen Fähigkeiten bewusst bescheiden dar. Dies konnte strategisch notwendig sein, um überhaupt an philosophischen Debatten teilnehmen zu können, verstärkte aber zugleich das Bild der Frau als Nicht-Philosophin.

Interessant ist außerdem, dass sich die Vorstellungen darüber verändert haben, in welchen Bereichen der Philosophie Frauen kompetent sein können. Im 17. Jahrhundert traute man Frauen eher theoretische Fähigkeiten in Bereichen wie Metaphysik und Erkenntnistheorie zu, während man sie für Ethik, Politik und andere wichtige „praktische“ Bereiche als ungeeignet betrachtete. Heute findet sich das umgekehrte Muster: Frauen werden eher mit „weicheren“ und angeblich weniger anspruchsvollen Bereichen wie Ethik oder politischer Philosophie verbunden, während man ihnen angeblich schwierigere technische oder abstrakte Bereiche der theoretischen Philosophie weniger zutraut. Das heißt, was auch immer zu einer bestimmten Zeit als weniger wichtig oder weniger anspruchsvoll angesehen wird, ist das, was Frauen noch am Ehesten zugeschrieben wird. Die Tatsache, dass sich diese Zuschreibung wandelt, je nachdem, was zu einem bestimmten Zeitpunkt als weniger herausfordernd bzw. weniger wichtig angesehen wird, sollte uns Anlass zum Nachdenken geben.

Doch nicht nur dieser Umstand, sondern die Analyse all der genannten Faktoren zeigt, dass die Geschichte der Philosophie nicht völlig objektiv und frei von Verzerrungen erzählt wird. Sie ist definitiv keine reine Bestenauslese, sondern immer auchdas Ergebnis von ungerechtfertigten Exklusionen. Philosophinnen wurden und werden häufig anders wahrgenommen, bewertet und dargestellt als Philosophen. Ihre Abwesenheit im klassischen Kanon lässt sich daher nicht einfach mit fehlender Produktivität, mangelnder Originalität oder schlechterer Qualität erklären. Vielmehr spielten strukturelle und geschlechtsspezifische Ausschlussmechanismen eine nicht zu unterschätzende Rolle.

Die Frage ist, was das dafür bedeutet, was Philosophie und ihre Geschichte sind. Wenn das, was wir für die Geschichte der Philosophie halten, unser Verständnis davon prägt, was Philosophie ist, arbeiten wir mit einem verzerrten und verengten Bild. Die Themen und Methoden, und damit auch die Werke und die Personen, die wir für aussagekräftig dafür halten, was Philosophie ist, sind nur ein Teil dessen, was die Vergangenheit unserer Disziplin ausmacht.[6] Meiner Meinung nach gibt es zahlreiche gute Argumente dafür, dieses verengte Bild der Philosophie zu ändern und die Vergangenheit unserer Disziplin so zu erzählen, dass so viele der ungerechtfertigten Exklusionen wie möglich rückgängig gemacht werden. Die Argumente für dieses Vorgehen reichen von Akkuratheit in Bezug auf die philosophische Vergangenheit über Gerechtigkeit gegenüber denjenigen Philosophinnen, die hauptsächlich deswegen von der Philosophiegeschichtsschreibung „vergessen“ wurden, weil sie Frauen waren, bis hin zu Qualitätsargumenten, d.h. der Annahme, dass eine vielfältigere Philosophiegeschichte auch den Horizont unsere Disziplin erweitern und diese damit interessanter machen würde. Ich plädiere deswegen dafür, dass sich die Philosophiegeschichte und auch die aktuelle akademische Philosophie weiter verstärkt gegenüber den Beiträgen historischer Philosophinnen, ihren Werken, ihren Themen und ihren vielleicht auf den ersten Blick unkonventionellen Formaten hin öffnet. Wie würde sich unser Verständnis von dem, was Philosophie ist, ändern, wenn wir ein anderes, erweitertes, aber gleichzeitig akkurateres Verständnis dafür entwickeln, was sie historisch war? Die Frage sollte also vielleicht nicht (nur) sein, was Philosophie (und ihre Geschichte) ist, sondern auch, was sie sein sollte.

Ariane Cäcilie Schneck ist seit 2025 Assistant Professor an der American University in Cairo. Sie arbeitet zur Philosophie der Frühen Neuzeit, historischen Philosophinnen und aktueller feministischer Philosophie, die sie in Kairo auch unterrichtet.
